lawyer:
Md Khurshid Alam Khan, Advocate ------- For the Petitioner. 
Abdul Kuddus Miah, Advocate ------- For Opposite-Party No.1.
parties:
Jalil alias Abdul Jalil   ------- Petitioner
Vs. 
Manikjan Bibi and others ------- Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Md Arayesuddin J : Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order, dated 25-9-2003, passed by the learned District Judge, Comilla, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 7 of 2003, allowing the appeal on contest after setting aside the judgment and order, dated 14-1-2003, passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla, in Miscellaneous (Pre-emption) Case No. 7 of 1976, allowing the same on contest should not be set aside.

2. Fact necessary to dispose of this Rule, In brief, is that preemptor-opposite-party instituted pre-emption Case No.7 of 1993 in the Court of the Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla, seeking pre-emption of the land schedule No.1. In that pre-emption petition she alleged that land of schedule-1 originally belonged to (1) Chand Gazi, (2) Hosenuddin and (3) Shamsher Ali. Chand Gazi died leaving only son Yeas in and Yeasin died leaving five daughters-Pre-emptor and opposite party Nos.6 to 9 and two sons-opposite-party Nos.4 and 5. He had another daughter named Mirjan who died during his lifetime. Shamser Ali died leaving heirs opposite- party Nos. 10 to 13 and Hosenuddin died leaving one son named Nawab Ali-opposite-party No.3. In the pre-emption application, preemptor-petitioner alleged that she is not only a co-sharer by inheritance but also a co-sharer by purchase, as she purchased some land from Sayedunnessa and Obaidul Hoque by two registered deed Nos. 164 and 171 dated 6-2-1991. That the opposite-parties Nos. 14 to 25 are co-sharers by purchase and opposite-party No.3 without issuing any notice upon the pre-emptor-petitioner sold the case land to pre-emptee-opposite-party No.1 at a consideration of Taka 1,50,000 by the registered deed dated 4-12-1995. Pre-emptor- petitioner had no knowledge of this transfer. She came to know of the transfer on 6-12-1995 and after taking certified copy on 7-12-1995 has filed this pre- emption case.

3. The pre-emption case was contested by the present petitioner and opposite-party No. 2 by filing a written objection in which they alleged that pre- emptor-opposite-party No.1 is not a co-sharer in the case holding. The case land appertains to SA Khatian No.18 and they have mutated their names in Mutation Case No. 717 of 1979-80 and the Jama has been separated and has been fixed at Taka 9 and accordingly, separate Khatian No.76 has been prepared in their names and they are paying rents separately. So, they claimed that the Jama and holding of the case land have been separated. Therefore, pre-emptor-opposite-party No.1 being a stranger is not entitled to pre-empt the case land.

<u>4. On behalf of the pre-emptee-petitioner, the learned Counsel Mr Md Khurshid Alam Khan submitted that the learned District Judge erred in law to set aside the impugned judgment and order of the trial Court. The learned District Judge misconceived that the pre-emptor-opposite-party is not a co-sharer in the suit case, as the holding and the Jama of the case land have been separated by the Mutation Case filed by the present pre-emptee- petitioner and a separate Khatian No. 76 has been prepared in his name. So, the learned Counsel submitted that the learned District Judge did not consider Exhibit Ka which is the separate Khatian prepared by the Mutation Case No. 717 of 1979-80. So, he submitted that pre-emptor-opposite-party is not a co-sharer in the case Jote. Further he submitted that subsequently when the pre-emptor-opposite- party found it difficult to cope with her claim, she claimed the case land by way of contiguous owner. But she did not implead all the contiguous owners of the case land and has not given any boundary of the same. So, the learned Counsel submitted that the trial Court considered all these things in detail and by his judgment and order dated 14-1-2003 disallowed the pre-emption case. The learned Counsel submitted that the learned District Judge without showing any reason in support of his decision set aside the judgment and order which bears no legal value. In this regard, the learned Counsel has relied in the case of Fatema Bibi vs Manik Lal Somaddar reported in 50 DLR (AD), 97 and submitted that the Hon'ble Appellate Division in that case filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (Act No. XXVIII of 1951) observed that since the Khatians are different, the pre-emptor cannot be held to be a co-sharer in the case holding and as such she is not entitled to pre-emption. The learned Counsel Mr Khan submitted that the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge is not sustainable in the eye of law.</u>

5. On behalf of the pre-emptor-opposite-party No.1, the learned Counsel Mr MA Kuddus Miah submitted that petitioner filed the pre-emption case on the basis of co-sharership and as kabala purchaser and also she is a contiguous owner. He submitted that in the pre-emption petition and in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in section 96 it has been mentioned that if a portion or share of a holding of a Raiyat is transferred, one or more co- sharer/tenants of the holding may, within four months of the service of notice given under section 89 of the said Act, apply to the Court for the said portion or share to be transferred to himself or themselves. He submitted that mutation Khatian does not mean the division of the holding and by mutation Khatian co-sharership does not extinguish. He submitted that the learned trial Court committed error to dismiss the pre-emption case opining that pre-emptor-opposite-party is not a co-sharer. She is a co-sharer by inheritance and by purchase: So, he submitted that the leaned Appellate Court considered all these things and allowed the pre-emption case by allowing the appeal and set aside the impugned judgment and order of the learned Joint District Judge. To substantiate his submission the learned Counsel Mr MA Kuddus Miah has relied in the case of Joynal Abedin Mollah vs Atiar Rahman reported in 2 BCR (AD), 431 and submitted that the holding of the case land has not been separated by the separation of the Jama. So, the learned Counsel submitted that the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge needs no interference by this Court. Accordingly, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

<u>6. We have perused the impugned judgment and order of both the Courts below together with the miscellaneous application and written-objection and the exhibited documents filed by the parties in this miscellaneous case. It is found that by Exhibit Ka a separate Khatian has been prepared in the name of Nawab Ali at a Jama of Taka 9 in Mutation Case No.717 of 1979-80. That Khatian was approved by the then Circle Officer (Revenue), Barura, on 15-4- 1980 and since then Nawab Ali is paying rents as per his separate Khatian. Now, what would be the implication of this mutation case in the original Khatian and holding? In the case of Fatema Bibi vs Manik Lal Samaddar and others their Lordships of the Appellate Division held that when the Khatians are different, the pre-emptor cannot be held to be a co-sharer in the case holding and not entitled to pre- emption. This decision of the Hon'ble Appellate Division was given in a case filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. In paragraph No. 6 of this case the Hon'ble Appellate Division has given the detailed observation which runs as follows:</u>

<u>"It appears that pre-emption was sought for in respect of 0.05 acres of land in plot No.991 under SA Khatian No.185, whereas the pre- emptor purchased land from Plot No. 99l appertaining to separate SA Khatian No.179 and, as such, she was not a tenant in the case holding. The Lower Appellate Court found that the pre- emptor was not a tenant of the case holding No.185, whereas the respondents were co- sharers by purchase. Hence, Lower Appellate Court rightly held that the pre-emptor had no locus standi to file the pre-emption case in respect of land of SA Khatian No.185. In both the Khatians plot No.991 is a common plot, but pre-emptor being not a co-sharer in SA Khatian No.185 it was rightly held by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division that the application is not maintainable. The learned Single Judge also affirmed the finding of the Lower Appellate Court that the land in question being non-agricultural in nature, the application under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act was not maintainable. The learned Single Judge having correctly decided the point of maintainability of the application for Pre- emption the same calls for no interference."</u>

<u>7. In the case of Alfazuddin Ahmed vs Abdur Rahman reported in 8 MLR (AD) 153 = 55 DLR(AD) 108 their Lordships held that separation of tenancy/Jama Khatian disentitled the petitioner from the right of pre-emption. Co-sharership in a tenancy of non-agricultural land ceases through two different ways one is partition of land and the other is separation of the tenancy by splitting up the Jama Khatian. Though this case was under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, but the principles laid down therein are the same. The learned District Judge failed to consider the implication of the separation of the Jama and preparation of separate Khatian in the name of the present petitioner and on erroneous view be set aside the impugned judgment and order of the Joint District Judge and allowed the pre-emption case. In the deed of transfer the scheduled land has been shown by mentioning the old Khatian and holding, but the purchaser-pre-emptee after his purchase separated the Jama and the Khatian as per the aforesaid mutation case and by opening separate Khatian in his name. So, we find that the holding has been separated and the pre- emptor-opposite-party cannot claim pre-emption of the case land. Lastly, the pre-emptor-opposite-party rested her claim on the contiguous owner. But no schedule of the case land has been furnished and in the pre-emption case none of the contiguous owners has been made party. Therefore, her subsequent claim as a contiguous owner also fails. Under such circumstances we find merit in the Rule.</u>

8. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order, dated 25-9-2003. passed by the learned District Judge, Comilla, in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 7 of 2003, is hereby set aside and those of dated 14-1-2003 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Comilla, in Miscellaneous (Pre-emption) Case No. 7 of 1996, is hereby upheld.

Send down the LC records to the Court concerned at once for information and necessary action.

End.

lawyer:
S. R. Pal with S. C. Das ------ For the Petitioner.  

K. Z. Alam, D.A.G. Mahmudul Islam  ------ For the Respondents.
parties:
M/s. Khan Bros. Ltd  ------ Petitioner.
Vs.
Govt. of Bangladesh  ------ Respondents.
full_judgment:
K. Hossain, J.—This writ petition is at the instance of M/s. Khan Brothers Ltd. a private limited company and raises a short but important question of law in that the properties held by a company registered within the territories now comprising Bangladesh during Pakistan regime, could be said to be abandoned property, in terms of section 2 of Presidents Order No. 16 of 1972 (hereinafter referred to as Abandoned Property Order). To appreciate these point facts as emerge from the affidavits of the parties may be set out. Khan Brothers Ltd. is a private limited Company with seven share-holders, divided into five thousand shares as on 28.2.72 the day Presidential Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated. Of the seven share-holders, lion's share was held by Khan. A. Sabur and he were the life Managing Director holding 2369 shares. Among the other six share-holders, one M. A. Samad who held 200 shares, has been admitted to be a Pakistani, and was not resident in Bangladesh at that time. The other five members of the Company have been asserted to be the nationals of Bangladesh and resident in Bangladesh. The Company had a Board of Directors consisting of four members including the Life Managing Director. They are Q. A. Rashid, Mrs. N. R. Khanam and Rouf Khan. After the creation of Bangladesh on the surrender of the Pakistani occupation Army, on the 16th of December, 1971, on 31st of January, 1972 Q. A. Rashid was appointed Director-in-charge of the Company. On 22nd February, 1972 Khan A. Sabur against whom charge of collaboration under the Collaborator's Order, 1972 was hanging, surrendered before the S. D. O. (s) at Dhaka. In his absence the Company was run by the Director-in-charge and the Board of Directors. Upon some instruction from the Government, the Additional Deputy 'Commissioner of Khulna on 29.8. 72, took over the management of the assets of the Company which consisted of a jute godown and jute bailing press at Daulatpur, Khulna. On 1.9.72 a representation was made by Q.A. Rashid the Director-in-charge to the Government for the release of the properties asserting, that they are not 'abandoned property'. But on that date a Gazette Notification was issued by the Government in the following terms:

"GOVERNMENT OF PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH

MINISTRY OF INDUSTRIES

INDUSTRIES DIVISION

NOTIFICATION

"No. Ind. M-XVI-9(12)172/199(5)—1st September 1972 In exercise of the authority given by the Articles 4 and 5 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972 (President's Order No. 16 of 1972) and the rules made thereunder, the Ministry of Industries is pleased to take over with immediate effect and until further orders the management of M/s. Khan Brothers Ltd., Daulatpur, Khulna, including all its properties and assets whenever located in Bangladesh and to put it under the Management Board Group-A-Khulna Area. The Management Board shall operate this unit and generally conduct all its affairs including operation of Bank accounts.

M. N. Islam.

Deputy Secretary".

This Notification is under challenge, and has given rise to the question of law set out above. On 6th December, 1973, Khan A. Sabur was released following a general amnesty granted by the Government. He then started making various representations, the last one being on 12.6.74, but none received any favorable reply. Thereafter the petitioner-company moved this Court, and obtained this Rule. It is resisted by the Government asserting the validity of the impugned notification, on the ground that the properties in question ate abandoned property in terms of the Presidential Order No. 16 of 1972.

2. We turn the point set out above. According to the Government the properties of the Company are an abandoned property in terms of the 'Abandoned Property Order'. The petitioner says that the properties do not come within the mischief of the Order. The main controversy, therefore, center’s round the interpretation of the word 'Abandoned Property' as set out in the President's Order. There are some other subsidiary points and they will be dealt with presently.

3. From the facts set out above we get that the Company was registered in the territory now comprising Bangladesh, and on the relevant date namely 28.2.72 when the Abandoned Property Order came into operation, it was being run by a Board of Directors of the Company, as in the meantime the Life Managing Director had surrendered to the Government under the  Collaborator's Order. According to the Government, this management was done by unauthorised persons, without clearly articulating as to who were the unauthorised occupants or how, if at all, was the company run. The petitioner has unequivocally asserted that after the surrender of their Life Managing Director, the Company was run by the Board of Directors and Q. A. Rashid as the Director-in-charge. The report of the Deputy Commissioner Annexure "B" proceeds on the basis that some of the original share-holders were non-Muslims, and that the company was managed by unauthorized persons. But nothing has been elucidated or clarified as to who were the persons in unauthorized management or occupation of the properties of the Company.—There is no clear denial to the assertion of the petitioner, that it is the Board of Directors who were managing the Company and Q. A. Rashid was the Director-in-charge, Therefore on fact, we held that it was the Board of Directors of the Company who at the relevant time when running the Company. The properties of the company cannot be said to be unoccupied.

<u>4. Let us now turn to the question of law. Conceding for the moment that the property was run by unauthorised persons, could it then be said to be an Abandoned Property. This brings us to deal with the definition of "Abandoned Property" as set out in the Abandoned Property Order. It is found in Article 2 of the said President's Order and may be set out in full:</u>

<u>"2. In this order, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context :—</u>

<u>(1) 'abandoned property' means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including—</u>

<u>(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971 was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh;</u>

<u>(ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order 1972 (Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972) but does not include—(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh.</u>

<u>(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force.</u>

<u>Explanation: "Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh.</u>

<u>"Before dealing with the contention of Mr. K. Z. Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the Government, let us deal with the question as we find from the reading of the Article. The definition given is not a very clear language. The legislative authority has tried first to define 'abandoned property', then gave it an inclusive meaning, and then again excluded certain categories of properties. We will deal with the definition portion presently. Let us first refer to those properties which have been included and those excluded. Of the included properties are : (1) properties owned by any person who is a citizen of the State at war with the People's Republic of Bangladesh at any time after 25th day of March, 1971 which in short means West Pakistan, now Pakistan; (2) any property taken over under Acting President's Order No. 1/72.</u>

<u>5. The excluded properties are: (1) any property whose owner is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which in the opinion of the Government is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh; (2) any property which is in possession of the Government under any law for the time being in force.</u>

<u>6. Keeping in view the inclusive definition and exclusion, let us approach the controversial definition clause which is clans; (1). It consists of three clauses one principal clause, and two subordinate clauses. The principal clause says that abandoned property means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh. This principal clause is followed by two subordinate clauses each of which begins with a relative pronoun 'whose' or 'who'. The first clause says "whose whereabouts are not known" and the second says, 'who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property'. In our opinion the legislative authority while defining 'abandoned property' has used a complex sentence containing a principal clause, and two subordinate clauses. The two subordinate clauses are dependent on the principal clause, though they themselves are disjunctive. The principal clause denotes persons, and the subordinate clauses connote the contentions under which property of the denoted persons will become abandoned property. An explanation has been appended saying, "person who is not present in Bangladesh is to include any body of persons, or a company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of the State which was at war with the People's Republic of Bangladesh at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971." The explanation in our opinion gives a clue to the interpretation we are trying to give to the definition clause contained in sub-article (1). The legislative authority has gone on the basis of clauses, and not on the basis of words taken separately. The legislative authority has taken whole clause viz. the principal clause of sub-article (1) to for explanation. Giving its grammatical meaning, we find that 'abandoned property' will be that property whose owner, either natural or artificial person like corporation, is not present in Bangladesh. That is the first precondition, but not the whole inasmuch as the principal clause is qualified by two subordinate but alternative clauses. The first precondition of absence from Bangladesh must be added with any of the two attributes contained in the alternative subordinate clauses. The other precondition is alternative; one is whose whereabouts are not known, and the other, who has ceased to occupy or manage or supervise this property. And when both the preconditions of the principal and subordinate clauses though alternative, are present, then the property will bear answer to the definition of abandoned property. The last phrase 'manage in person' in our opinion means in case of natural person by himself, and in the case of artificial person, one who in terms of its rules of constitution is authorised to manage. We therefore find that abandoned property, will be that property whose owner is not present in Bangladesh and whose where about are either is not known, or who has ceased to occupy,' supervise or manage in person his property.</u>

<u>7. If we again turn to the principal clause, we find, that the Words 'Who is not present' requires some interpretation. The wards is our opinion mean who is voluntarily not present. It does not and cannot mean who is compelled or unable to be present; in other words when the person of his own volition, or free will is not present, but not against his volition or will. We think the conditions set out for the exclusion of property give some indication, on the construction of the sub-article. The interpretation completely harmonies the meaning of all the sub-articles. It is equally in accord with in the preamble of the Order which says that it is expedient to make provisions for the control, management and disposal of certain property abandoned by certain persons who are not present in Bangladesh, or whose whereabouts are not known, or who have ceased to occupy or supervise or manage in person their property, or who are enemy aliens. Construed thus, we find that the definition clauses affirmatively means, whose owner is not present in Bangladesh and whose whereabouts is either not known or who has ceased to manage, supervise or occupy the property; negatively, we get abandoned property does not comprehend property whose owner is a Bengalee resident in Bangladesh, albeit, the person may be natural or artificial, like Company.</u>

<u>8. So far as company is concerned its domicile is governed by the country of its incorporation. We have found that the registered office of the petitioner company is Bangladesh, and so it is a Bangali Company. We have also held that its properties and assets were run and managed by its Board of Directors. Therefore any property held by the petitioner-company domiciled in Bangladesh, is outside the ambit of the definition of abandoned property, and they are immune from the operation of the provisions of the Abandoned Property Order. The impugned notification therefore was issued without lawful authority.</u>

9. Let us now take the interpretation sought to be given by Mr. K. Z. Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney-General. He says, we are to read the three clauses in sub-article (1) distinctively, when the word 'or' has been used at the end of each clause. We are afraid, we are not permitted to do so. If it is so attempted, we will be violating the cordial rule of grammar. Instead of a complex sentence we will be substituting a compound one in that there will be three independent sentences. The other formidable difficulty will be that two subsequent clauses or sentences will be without any nominative or subject. He next says that 'who' or 'whose' will qualify 'any person' in the proceeding clause, but not the clause itself. We have already referred to the explanation, which in explaining the word 'person' given in sub-article (1) has referred to the entire clause, `person who is not present in Bangladesh.' The legislative authority by using the clause, has given sufficient indication as to how the article is to be interpreted.

<u>10. Mr. Alam's submission may be tested in another way, if we take the second exclusion. We find, it has clearly provided, that all properties whose management have been taken over under Acting President's Order No. 1 of 1972 though could be treated as abandoned property, yet shall not include those properties whose owner is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose, which in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. The exclusion is clear and significant. This distinction emphasises the point we have indicated. Not the properties of all persons living outside Bangladesh are abandoned properties, if the Government is of opinion that their stay abroad is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. We find no authority to the wide proposition of the learned Deputy Attorney-General to hold that mere non-occupation of a property by any owner resident or not in Bangladesh, will make the property abandoned. We find no merit in the contention of the learned Deputy Attorney-General.</u>

11. There is a question of Samad's holding 200 shares in the Company and no doubt Samad is a Pakistani as the petitioner in its representation to the Government has admitted him to be so. In terms of Article 8, his shares are abandoned properties. The Government under sub-article 1(b) could purchase the other shares of the Company, but has not proceeded to do so. And so neither the management of the property nor assets of the company vest in the Government nor can the Government claim to do so.

12. For the reasons we make the Rat absolute, and declare that the Notification No. Ind. M-XVI-9(12)/72/199(5) dated 1st September, 1972 issued by the Ministry of Industries Division published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary Wednesday, September 6, 1972 is without lawful authority and of no legal effect, and the Respondents are directed to hand over the possession of the property taken over by the impugned Notification to the petitioner-company. We however, make no order as to costs.

Badrul Haider Choudhury, J.- I agree.

End.

caseno: Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1716 of 2005.
lawyer:
Md Aftab Hossain, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioner. 
AKM Shahidul Huq, Advocate-on-Record ------ For Respondent Nos. 1-3.
Not represented ------ Respondent Nos. 4-19.
parties:
Government of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Md Shahabuddin and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated March 14. 2005 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2580 of 2000).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: Delay of 29 days is condoned. This petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment dated March 14, 2005 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2580 of 2000 making absolute the Rule obtained against the judgment and decree dated March 22, 2000 of the 1st Court of Sub-ordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) Kishoreganj in Other Appeal No. 139 of 1995 allowing the same upon reversing the judgment and decree dated May 20, 1995 of the Court of Assistant Judge, Kotiadi, Kishoreganj in Other Class Suit No. 28 of 1994 decreeing the same. The suit was filed seeking declaration of title in respect of the land in suit, recovery of possession upon evicting the defendants from the land in suit and demolishing the structures in the land in suit and for further declaration that the order dated April 22, 1977 passed by defendant No.3 treating the property in suit as vested property and thereupon leasing out the property in suit is illegal and void.

2. Facts, in short, are that the original owner Harihar Das entered into an agreement for sale on May 19, 1962 with Abdul Barek Bepari and upon receiving Taka 6,000 out of the total consideration money of Taka 6,500 executed an agreement for sale and made over possession, that Harihar Das having had failed to execute and register the kabala, Abdul Barek Bepari filed Other Class Suit No. 50 of 1975 for a decree for specific performance of the agreement for sale of the land, that in the suit the Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh as well as the Assistant Custodian of Vested Property were made parties. The suit was decreed and in execution of the decree Abdul Barek Bepari obtained the kabala through Court, that by a deed of exchange dated March 19, 1977 between Abdul Barek Bepari and his brother, plaintiff No. 1, the plaintiff No. 1 got the land in suit and thereupon mutated his name and paying rent and is possessing the land in assertion of title, that two rooms of the building were occupied by police personnel as monthly tenant of Harihar Das, that the said police personnel admitted ownership of Abdul Barek Bepari and paid rent as tenant to him, that in the building there were two other tenants, defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and they upon accepting Abdul Barek Bepari as landlord paid rent to him, that after getting the land by exchange the tenants accepted the plaintiff No.1 as landlord and paid rent, that defendant Nos. 7 and 8 paid rent for some time but later on, in collusion with the personnel of the vested property authority have created some forged documents and got the property enlisted as vested property, that the defendant No.7 filed three suits in the Court of Assistant Judge and one suit in the Court of Subordinate Judge, that all the suits were dismissed and thereupon the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 in collusion with the vested property officials started VP Case. No.2 of 1978-79, that the said case was contested by the plaintiffs and the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue) passed order recommending release of the property from the list of vested property and the record was sent to the Ministry of Land for final approval but the Ministry instead of passing the order of release sent back the record to the District authority for fresh consideration of the case, that while the process for releasing the property from the list of vested property was going on plaintiff No.1 transferred 2/3rd portion of the property in suit to the proforma-defendant No. 14 by the registered deed of exchange dated September 13, 1983 and the said defendant mutated his name and paid rent, that later on the order of mutation was re-called by defendant No.5. It is the case of the plaintiffs that the original owner Harihar Das had never left the erstwhile East Pakistan at material point of time and, as such, the property in suit had never assumed character of vested property and at the instance of the defendant Nos. 7 and 8 the vested property authority illegally listed the property as vested property and leased it out to the defendants.

3. The vested property authority entered appearance and filed written statement denying the material averments made in the plaint and stated, inter alia, that land in suit belonged to Harihar Das who appointed Jatindra Chandra Sarker as attorney to look after the property and to sell the property and thereupon left for India, that Attorney of Harihar Dasinducted defendant No.5 as tenant in the building and also defendant Nos. 7 and 8 and the said persons paid rent to the Attorney of Harihar Das, that Attorney of Harihar Das left for India before 1965 and had settled there, that the property left by Harihar assumed character of enemy property, later on vested property and the same vested in the Government, that Jatindra Chandra Sarker claimed title in the land in suit but he failed to substantiate his claim, that his objection against treating the property as vested property was rejected on May 20, 1969, that Jatindra Chandra Sarker left the country in 1971, that the property was in possession of the defendant Nos. 5, 7 and 8 and later on defendant Nos. 7 and 8 left the property, that the defendant No. 7 created certain papers for raising claim in the property in suit and that he in collusion with the interested quarter and behind the knowledge of the defendant No.1 upon initiating VP Case No. 199 of 1973-74 obtained lease, that defendant Nos. 5 and 8 were in possession of the land and obtained lease of the respective portion of the building, that the defendants i.e. defendant Nos. 5, 7 and 8, have become owner of the land in suit as the lessee, that plaintiffs' case of entering into an agreement by Harihar Das for sale of the property to Abdul Barek Bepari is not correct and that Harihar Das had never executed any agreement for sale and that he left erstwhile East Pakistan in 1962 and was residing permanently in India, that Abdul Barek Bepari obtained the decree in Other Class Suit No. 50 of 1975 without serving notice and upon practising fraud on the Court, that plaintiffs at no point of time got possession of the property in suit.

4. The trial Court decreed the suit declaring the right, title and possession of the plaintiffs and also declared illegal and void the order treating the property in suit as vested property. The trial Court further decreed the suit of the plaintiffs for recovery of possession upon evicting the contesting defendants.

5. The defendant No.1, Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Kishoreganj went on appeal. The appellate Court reversed the judgment of the trial Court on the finding that the plaintiffs were illegally in possession of the property and that the property assumed character of vested property. The plaintiffs moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction and obtained the Rule. The High Court Division made the Rule absolute on the finding that from the defendant's side it was not established that Abdul Barek Bepari obtained the decree for specific performance of contract without service of summons on the defendants thereof, that the judgment of the appellate Court suffers from misreading of evidence and, as such, same is not sustainable in law.

<u>6. We have heard the learned Advocate-on-Record and perused the materials in the petition for leave to appeal. It is seen from the materials on record that plaintiffs' predecessor acquired the property by the kabala executed by the Court in execution of the decree in a suit for specific performance of contract filed against Harihar Das the owner, who entered into an agreement for sale. In the said suit, Government of Bangladesh as well as the vested property authority were defendants. In execution of the decree passed in the suit for specific performance of contract the plaintiff, i.e. Abdul Barek Bepari, got the kabala. It was contended from the side of the defendants of the instant suit that the decree in the suit for specific performance of con- tract was obtained upon suppression of summons. The trial Court on consideration of the materials on record held that the defendants failed to establish their contention of obtaining decree in the suit for specific performance of contract upon suppression of summons. The trial Court also held that the property was illegally treated as vested property and the same was leased out illegally to the defendants upon evicting the plaintiffs. The appellate Court without adverting to the finding and decision of the trial Court reversed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. The High Court Division on detailed discussions of the materials on record held that the appellate Court set aside the judgment of the trial Court on misreading of the evidence and also on surmise and conjecture. The High Court Division also held that the property in suit at no point of time assumed the character of enemy property, later on vested property, since it was not established from the side of the vested property authority that the owner thereof left the erstwhile East Pakistan at any point of time.</u>

7. The learned Advocate-on-Record failed to point out any error in the judgment of the High Court Division of the kind calling for interference by this Division.

Accordingly, the petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Dr Rafiqur Rahman, Senior Advocate, instructed by Serajur Rahman, Advocate-on-Record ------ For the Petitioner. 
Not represented ------ Respondents.
parties:
Rowshan Ara Begum ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Secretary, Ministry of Works and Urban Development, Government of Bangladesh and others ------ Respondents
case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated May 15, 2005 passed by the Appellate Division in Civil Appeal No. 1 of 1999).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This petition has been filed seeking review of the judgment dated May 15, 2005 in Civil Appeal No. 1 of 1999 allowing the same. The civil appeal was filed against the judgment dated November 3, 1991 of the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 448 of 1988 making the Rule absolute. The writ petition was filed challenging the legality of the judgment dated January 3, 1988 of the Court of Settlement in Case No. 119 of 1987 (Kha-145-Tinshed Colony, Block-D) Quarter No. 169 (Holding No. 38), Tinshed Colony, Mohammadpur, Dhaka. The said case was filed challenging the listing of the property in the 'Kha' list and publishing thereof in the Bangladesh Gazette (Extra-ordinary) dated September 23, 1986. The list in respect of the property in question and the publication of the list was made as per provision of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. The Court of Settlement by its judgment dismissed the case holding that the property in question is an abandoned property within the meaning of the provision of President Order No. 16 of 1972 and the Provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 and that including of the property in question in the 'Kha' list and publication of the said list in the Bangladesh Gazette is quite legal.

2. The writ petition was filed challenging the aforementioned judgment of the Court of Settlement. The High Court Division upon making the Rule absolute declared that the property in question. is not an abandoned property and the property has been listed in the 'Kha' list without lawful authority and, as such, the same has no legal effect. The High Court Division further directed the Government to exclude the property in question from the list of abandoned property.

3. It was the case of the petitioner (Rowshan Ara Begum) before the Court of Settlement that the property in question was allotted to one Sahera Khatun, widow of late Abdul Gafur on August 24, 1957 and said Sahera Khatun orally gifted the property on April 14, 1973 to her daughter Anwari Khatun, that Sahera Khatun in confirmation of the oral gift affirmed an affidavit before the Magistrate, 1st Class, Dhaka on July 14, 1973, In the affidavit it was stated that Sahera Khatun gifted the property in presence of Amanullah Munsif, Abdul Hashim and Md Riazuddin, that Anwari Khatun on October 22, 1979 by registered deed transferred the property in question to the petitioner before the Court of Settlement, that after purchasing the property the petitioner got her name mutated in the records of the different authorities, obtained approval from the RAJUK for making construction and also obtained loan from the House Building Finance Corporation and made construction in the property in question. It was the case of the petitioner that she was in possession of the property in question and that she was surprised to see the property in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned property published in the Bangladesh Gazette as per provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985.

4. The Government contested the case before the Court of Settlement by making submissions that Sahera Khatun and her daughter Anwari Khatun during the war of liberation left the property in question without making any arrangement for its management and supervision and that after war of liberation their whereabouts were not known and that on the date of promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 whereabouts of Sahera Khatun and Anwari Khatun were not known, that the petitioner's case of making gift of the property by Sahera Khatun to her daughter Anwari Khatun on April 14, 1973 and affirming of an affidavit by Sahera Khatun in confirmation of the oral gift said to have been made by her, to her daughter Anwari Khatun are all got up story, that the claim of the petitioner that Sahera Khatun had a daughter Anwari Khatun is also a got up story, that petitioner got her name mutated in different records of the Government unauthorisedly and also upon resorting to practice which has no sanction of law, that mutation in the record of the Government was made without approval of the competent authority. The Court of Settlement dismissed the case observing, amongst others, "No oral evidence has been adduced by the petitioner that Sahera Khatun was present and her whereabouts were known after liberation at least on and from 28-2-72. The alleged oral gift has not been formally proved before this Court nor the 3 witnesses of the oral gift mentioned in the affidavit dated 14-7-73 have been examined in this case ............... In the absence of evidence to this effect it is difficult to accept the case of the petitioner that Sahera Khatun was present after liberation and that the oral gift by Sahera Khatun was genuine, rather her whereabouts were not known and oral gift was not genuine.

5. From the judgment of the Court of Settlement it appears that thee was no case of the petitioner before the Court of Settlement that the property in question was listed in the 'Kha' list without serving notice on her.

<u>6. As against the judgment of the Court of Settlement the petitioner moved the High Court Division in writ jurisdiction and obtained Rule. The petitioner before the High Court Division, amongst others, contended that the property was listed in the 'Kha' list without serving any notice. The High Court Division while making the Rule absolute observed "Unless the prerequisites as mentioned in section 5(1)(2)(sic) of the Ordinance are fulfilled, the jurisdiction of the Court of Settlement ceases to operate and the respondents are bound to prove that the properties so enlisted in the Official Gazette are abandoned properties. If this burden could be discharged by the Government then of course, it shifts or reverts to the petitioner to prove that the property is not an abandoned property............................The Court of Settlement misplaced the onus upon the petitioner to prove that the whereabouts of the original owner was not known to the government......................The fact that gift was made by Sahera Khatun in favour of her daughter Anwari Khatun having been affirmed on oath by an affidavit before the Magistrate, 1st Class, the learned Court of Settlement ought not to have challenged the same as no such challenge had been offered by the government before the Court of Settlement. The findings of the Court of Settlement having not been supported by any materials, in our view, the order is without jurisdiction. It is neither stated before the Court of Settlement nor before this Court in the affidavit that any notice has been served upon the petitioner or her vendor for surrendering the properties, the enlistment of the petitioner's property in the official Gazette is illegal and without jurisdiction ....................The enlistment of her property as an abandoned property without answering to the conditions as set forth in section 5 of the Ordinance read with PO 16 of 1972 is without any lawful authority." The High Court Division in its judgment has quoted a finding from the judgment of the Court of Settlement which reads as follows:</u>

<u>"No oral evidence has been adduced by the petitioner that Sahera Khatun was present and her whereabouts were not known after liberation at least on and from 28-2-72".</u>

7. In the aforesaid quotation the word 'not' appears to be a typing mistake, since from the judgment of the Court of Settlement, placed before us at the time of hearing of the review petition, it is seen the aforesaid portion of the judgment reads as follows:

"No oral evidence has been adduced by the petitioner that Sahera Khatun was present-and her whereabouts were known after liberation at least on and from 28-2-72."

8. In the other part of the judgment of the Court of Settlement it has been observed "In the absence of evidence to this effect it is difficult to accept the case of the petitioner that Sahera Khatun was present after liberation and that the oral gift by Sahera Khatun was genuine, rather her whereabouts were not known and oral gift was not genuine.

<u>9. The learned Counsel for the petitioner in support of the prayer for review of the judgment of this Court urged that this Court made an error apparent on the face of the record in not noticing the important fact that the property was listed without serving notice on the claimant of the property. In our judgment we addressed the aforesaid contention of the petitioner and we observed "The question of service or non-service of notice is a question of fact and determination thereof is required upon consideration of the evidence brought on record by the parties." We have observed in our judgment that before the Court of Settlement the petitioner did not take any stand or, in other words, did not make any contention as to listing of the property without serving notice and in the background thereof in our judgment we observed that the contention made as to non-service of notice in enlisting the property in question as abandoned property merits no consideration.</u>

10. The learned Counsel in support of his contention that listing of the property without serving notice as per provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 makes the list so made unsustainable in law referred to the case of Ministry of Works and others vs Helaluddin Ahmed reported in 4 MLR (AD) 140. The fact of the aforesaid case is quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case and when we drew attention of the learned Counsel to the facts of the case referred by him the learned Counsel felt difficulty to press his contention that the decision reported in the aforementioned law report has application in the facts of the instant case.

11. In the instant case while the property was listed in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned buildings and published in the Bangladesh Gazette the claimant of the property moved the Court of Settlement under section 7 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985.

<u>12. The provision of section 7 requires the claimant of the property to establish "that the building is not an abandoned property and has not been vested in the Government under the President's Order or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that Order." The Court of Settlement dismissed the petitioner's case on the finding that the petitioner failed to establish that at the material time i.e. on February 28, 1972 Sahera Khatun or, for that matter, Anwari Khatun was present in Bangladesh. This fact having not been established the Court of Settlement held that the property in question on the promulgation of PO 16 of 1972 became an abandoned property and vested in the Government. It is in PO 16 of 1972 that transfer made after the property assumed the character of abandoned property has no legal coverage. It is seen from the judgment of the Court of Settlement that no evidence was led from the side of the claimant of the property to establish the fact that Sahera Khatun or for that matter Anwari Khatun from whom the petitioner said to have purchased the property was in Bangladesh after liberation of Bangladesh and was also present on 28-2-1972. Under the law unless the claimant of the property can establish that the owner of the property from whom he/she made the purchase was present in the Bangladesh at the material time i.e. on 28-2- 1972, the claimant cannot have any relief from the Court of Settlement or, in other words, cannot have the direction from the Court of Settlement for delisting of the property from the list of abandoned property as published in the Bangladesh Gazette either in the "Ka' list or in the 'Kha' list as per provision of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. In the instant case the petitioner having not been able to establish before the Court of Settlement that the claimant of the property or for that matter her vendor Anwari Khatun were present in Bangladesh on 28-2-1972 and consequent thereupon the property having had assumed the character of abandoned Petitioners property, the listing of the property in question, even if without service of notice as per provision of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, is not material as the property because of non-service of notice for listing in the list of abandoned properties would not cease to be an abandoned property and consequent there upon the claim of title made by the petitioner in the property in question is not legally sustainable or, in other words, the petitioner cannot raise any claim of title in the property in question since said property is an abandoned property. The ground contending which review of our judgment is sought merits no consideration.</u>

Accordingly the review petition is dismissed.

End.

lawyer:
Parimal Chandra Guha ----- For the Petitioners. 
Subash Chandra Saha ----- For Opposite Party No.1.
parties:
Lalit Kumar Roy and 2 others ------ Petitioners
vs
 Krishnapada Biswas & ors ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: This Rule was obtained by the plaintiffs upon making a revision application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure against judgment and decree dated 8-7-99 passed by Additional District Judge at Bagerhat in Title Appeal No. 275 of 1995 reversing those dated 22-8-95 of the Subordinate Judge, Court No. 1 at Bagerhat passed in Title Suit No. 54 of 993 and in dismissing the suit.

2. The plaintiffs instituted the suit for partition simpliciter of the suit land measuring about 10.15 acres for a separate joint share of about 6.10 acres. The plaint case, in short, is that one Paban Mondal was the original owner in possession of the suit land. Without a son, he died leaving three daughters, namely. Boro Panchi alias Aina, Jhoharmoni and Chota Panchi alias Malati. Boro Panchi and Jhohannoni were daughters by the first wife while Chota Panchi by second wife. Boro Panchi and Jhoharmoni were each survived by a son, defendant No.1, Krishnapada Biswas and Annadacharan Haldar respectively. The plaintiffs survived Choto Panchi.

3. Under Hindu Dayabagh law of inheritance, the three daughters inherited the suit land left by Paban Mondal in limited life interest only. Then, the daughters died one after another, first Chota Panchi, followed by Jhoharmoni after independence of Bangladesh in 1971 and lastly, Boro Panchi. After the death of all the daughters, the plaintiffs along with defendant Nos. 1 and 2 inherited the suit land as reversioners in equal share.

4. The suit land was never partitioned by metes and bounds among the co-sharers. S A Khatian appears to be recorded in the names of Krishnapada, Lalit and Jhoharmoni only and there was no reason for such wrong record. Other co-sharers having declined to partition the suit land, the plaintiffs were constrained to institute the suit.

5. Defendant No. 1 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the case of the plaintiffs. His case, in brief, is that the claim of the plaintiffs is barred by the principles of res judicata, acquiescence and waiver. The suit is also barred by limitation. The plaintiffs had neither any locus standi nor any cause of action for the suit.

6. Admitting the above genealogy of the plaintiffs, the defendant contended that Paban Mondal married Sumati alias Subhadra after the death of his first and second wife. When Paban diell Sumati had a daughter, who of course could not live long. So, Paban Mondal died leaving behind, a wife Sumati, and three daughters, namely, Boro Panchi, Jhoharmoni and Choto Panchi. Under the Hindu Dayabagh School of Law, Somatic inherited the suit land as widow and possessed. While she was thus owner in possession, on 29-3-41 one Kali Charan created a fraudulent patta without any salami or consideration to grab the suit land. Sumati ultimately, got back the patta from Kalicharan through litigation up to the Court of District Judge. In the litigations to rescue the suit land, she had to take loan. To repay the loan incurred in litigation, perform the sraddha of her husband and also to maintain her, she had to transfer 10.47 acres of land including the suit land to defendant No. 1 by a registered deed of sale dated 14-5-42 and delivered possession. She also delivered the original copy of the patta to defendant No. 1 along with the sale deed.

7. While defendant No. 1 was thus owner in possession of the 'suit land, he gave 81 decimals to Nishikanta, father of the plaintiffs and 70 decimals to Jhoharmoni out of the suit land by two registered deeds of gift dated 14-2-56 and both Nishikanta and Jhoharmoni accepted the gift and took delivery of possession of their respective land. After death of Nishikanta, the plaintiffs inherited said 81 decimals only as defendant No. 2 inherited 70 decimals of the suit land from her mother, Jhoharmoni. The plaintiffs were now living in said land by erecting a homestead thereon. Defendant No. 2 died leaving four sons, Ananta, Shumanta, Akun and Bhedu who were duly substituted and were now in possession of said 70 decimals of land. Defendant No. 1 has still been possessing the rest of the land in his own right and title for more than 50 years, wherein the plaintiffs had no interest or possession .The title of the defendant No.1 in 10.47 - (0.81+0.70) 1.51 = 08.96 (approximately) acres of land has now been perfected by long and exclusive use and occupation.

8. On the pleadings, issues regarding maintainability of the suit, defect of parties Hotchpotch and the rights of the plaintiffs to partition of the suit land as co-sharers only were raised. Plaintiffs examined five witnesses while the defendant No. 1 also examined same number of witnesses. Plaintiffs' documents were marked exhibit No. 1 to 3 series while those of the defendant No. 1 as Exhibit Nos. A to E series.

9. The trial Court decreed the suit as prayed for allotting to the plaintiffs a joint share of 6.10 acres of land out of the suit land. On appeal therefrom at the instance of defendant No. 1, the Court of appeal below allowed the appeal, reversed the decree of the trial Court and dismissed the suit by impugned judgment and decree.

10. Mr PC Guha, learned Advocate for the petitioners, assails the impugned judgment and decree on various grounds. First, he submits that the trial Court has found that the defendant No. 1 failed to prove legal necessity for the transfer by Sumati vide Exhibit A dated 14-5-42 and accordingly, held that the plaintiffs are entitled to inherit the estate left by Paban Mondal as admitted reversionary along with the defendants. The Court of appeal below reversed the decree without duly reversing the findings and adverting to the reasoning’s of the trial Court for such findings, which has resulted in failure of justice.

<u>11. Elaborating, he submits that in support of legal necessity defendant No. 1 failed to adduce any evidence save and except the recitals of the deed of sale, Exhibit A. The recitals in a deed are not themselves evidence to prove the legal necessity, he submits. In support, he cites the decisions in the case of Lala Brij Lal vs Musammat Ind Kunwar; (1914) 23 Indian Cases 715, Mohammad Nuh vs Brij Behari Lal, (1924) 82 Indian Cases 5 and Promode Kumar Roy and others v Benidini Haldar and others, 21 DLR 673.</u>

12. He then submits that the trial Court having found the plaintiffs in possession of the suit land as reversioners, the Court of appeal below most illegally dismissed the suit in its entirety.

13. On the other hand, Mr Subash Chandra Saha, learned Advocate for defendant No.1 and opposite party No. 1, submits that said defendant did not dispute the possession of the plaintiffs but the possession of the plaintiffs is confined to aforesaid 81 decimals of land only, which the defendant gifted to Nishikanta, father of the plaintiffs., The plaintiffs have got no possession in any other land of the suit. Similarly, defendant No. 2 possessed 70 decimals of land out of the land, which Jhoharmoni got by way of gift from the defendant No. 1 in 1956.

14. He also submits that Nishikanta, father of the plaintiffs nor the defendant No. 2 or his predecessor-in-interest, Jhoharmoni had never challenged the alienation by Sumati vide Exhibit A. The plaintiffs also did not seek any relief either against the alienation of Sumati or for possession after the death of Sumati. After about 60 years of the alienation and death of Sumati in 1979, now they cannot challenge the alienation in the present suit as framed for partition simpliciter.

<u>15. He submits that at the time of alienation on 14-5-42, defendant No. 1 was minor and his father actually did everything on his behalf including taking delivery of possession. All the persons who witnessed the alienation were dead at the time of trial of the suit. In the circumstances, the recitals in the deed exhibit-A in respect of legal necessity for the alienation, the original registered patta Exhibit B dated 29-3-41 and the deeds of gift dated 14-5-52 Exhibit C and C1, if considered together, the legal necessity for the alienation is proved and the Court of appeal below has so found. He concludes, the judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below therefore do not call for any interference. He also cites the authorities in the case of Nanda Lal Dhur Biswas vs Jagat Kishore Acharjya, 36 Indian Cases 420, 29 DLR (SC) 137, AIR 1935 Calcutta 689 and Jagannath and others vs Sreenath and others. (1922) 59 CLJ 167.</u>

16. We have perused the record of the case and heard the learned Advocates at length. In order to appreciate the conflicting arguments, we should first see the facts, which are now concluded by the decision of the Court of appeal below and then, to find whether decision of the Court of appeal below is well founded on the facts proved and law, in the light of the authorities relied upon by the learned Advocates.

17. At the outset, the plaintiffs though did not want to recognise the existence of Sumati as the third and surviving wife of Paban Mondal but after the decision of the appellate Court, found it very difficult for them not to recognise her as the surviving widow of Paban Mondal, They only challenged the alienation by her for want of legal necessity. We also find both the trial Court as well as the appellate Court proceeded on this basis to decide the alienation by Sumati of the estate left by Paban Mondal as the surviving widow.

18. So, the genealogy now admits of no controversy. Paban Mondal was the original owner in possession of the suit land. He died leaving a wife, Sumati and three daughters, namely, Boro Panchi, Jhoharmoni and Choto Panchi. Consequently, under Dayabagh School of Hindu Law Sumati as the surviving widow inherited the estate left by Paban Mondal.

19. The nature or incidents of widow's estate and/or the rights and obligations of such widow are now well settled. At Hindu widow or a limited heir like her is not a tenant-for-life. She becomes the owner of the property left by her husband, by way of inheritance. Her rights to the estate are absolute but only subject to certain restrictions on her right to alienation, and subject to devolving of the estate upon the next heir of the last full owner upon her death. The restrictions of her power of alienation are however inseparable from her estate.

20. Alienation of the estate by her will bind the estate on proof of any of the following conditions or circumstances:

a. there was a legal necessity; or

b. the alienee after reasonable inquiry as to the necessity acted honestly in the belief that the necessity existed; or

c. the next reversionary in line consented to the alienation; or

d. it was a surrender of her whole interest in the estate in favour of the nearest reversionary.

21. We also find in section 178 of Mulla's Principles of Hindu Law, 16th edition that when any one of the above three conditions is established, the alienation may be proved of the whole or any part of the estate, but where the fourth condition is proved the alienation must be of the whole estate.

22. A widow or a limited heir like her however, cannot transfer any part of the estate inherited by her except for purposes, namely, (a) religious or, charitable and (b) other purposes amounting to legal necessity.

23. The case at hand-deals with an alienation for legal necessity. What is legal necessity is also now settled. Legal necessity as recited in the deed of sale Exhibit A was for paying off the debts incurred in payment of rent of the estate and legal costs in litigation, and also for maintenance of the widow. The purposes as stated cannot be said to be not legal necessity. The question arose, when there is no legal proof of existence of such legal necessity save and except the recitals in the deed in question, whether such recitals are sufficient to prove the existence of legal necessity.

<u>24. The nature of proof of such legal necessity, a Court of law would demand will always depend upon the facts and circumstances of a case. There cannot be any hard and fast rule formulated.</u>

<u>25. When such alienation is challenged, the burden of proof is always upon the alience. In order to sustain the alienation and bind the estate, such alience will have to prove either the existence of legal necessity or to prove that he made proper and bona fide inquiry as to the existence of the necessity and that he did everything possible to satisfy him as to the existence of the legal necessity.</u>

26. In the case before us, the alience was a minor at the time of alienation. Besides the recitals in the deed Exhibit A, he has got original registered deed of patta created by one Kali Charan, which on the pain of a case he had to return to the widow, Surnati who then delivered it to the alienee and the deeds of gift dated 14-2-56 Exhibit C and CI. We shall see how the Court of appeal below was justified to find that the alienation was proved to be for legal necessity and binds the estate left by Paban Mondal.

27. Before we further dwell upon the question of legal necessity for the alienation, we must consider the pertinent question as to whether, in the facts and circumstances of the case, the plaintiffs should be allowed to collaterally challenge the alienation by the widow in order to succeed to inherit as reversioners the estate left by Paban MondaI. We must also see whether, in the frame of the suit, the Courts below are justified to allow the plaintiffs to challenge the alienation and/or entering themselves into investigation as to the existence of any legal necessity for the alienation.

28. As stated above, the suit is for partition simpliciter. The plaintiffs have not sought for any other relief either for setting aside the alienation or for possession of the land left by Paban MondaI. It is needless to say, they cannot inherit as reversioners to the estate of Paban Mondal without setting aside the alienation by the widow vide Exhibit A dated 14-5-42.

29. We find that by an amendment, the plaintiffs amended the plaint by adding paragraph 4 (ka) therein. In the added paragraph, it is stated, inter alia, that registered deed of sale dated 14-5-42 is fraudulent, ineffective. It was created for unlawful purpose. There was no legal necessity for the alienation. Defendant No. 1's obtaining possession on the basis of the deed is false. Father of the defendant No. 1 and the widow, Sumati collusively created the deed of sale. Deeds of gift being Nos. 795 and 799 in favour of Nishi kant a and lhoharmoni were also created behind the back of the recipients under the deeds. In order to show the deed of sale dated 14-5-42 was acted upon said deeds of gift were created.

30. A case is well made out in the paragraph against the deeds, Exhibits No. A, C and CI. On such averments, the plaintiffs could have sought for appropriate relief, say, for setting aside the alienation by the widow by the deed of sale dated 14-5-42 and also the deeds of gift dated 14-2-56 and consequently, they could have sought for possession of the land after the death of the widow. But they have preferred to do none, albeit deliberately and consciously.

31. Any reversioner is entitled to institute a suit to have an alienation by a Hindu widow declared to be void except for her life i.e. for setting aside the alienation, provided he sues within a period of 12 years of the date of alienation under article 125 of the Limitation Act. Similarly, any suit by a reversioner for possession is to be instituted within same period of I imitation from the date of death of the Hindu widow under article 141 of the Limitation Act.

32. On 7-9-79 the present suit was instituted. The widow Sumita admittedly died in 1979. So, on the date of the suit any relief either for setting aside alienation or for possession already became hopelessly barred by limitation. The plaintiffs therefore, consciously and deliberately did not seek any such relief of setting aside the alienation or recovery of possession.

33. In the circumstances, when the plaintiffs did not or could not seek a relief on the ground of limitation, they cannot challenge the alienation by the widow vide Exhibit A dated 14-5-42 or the deeds of gift vide Exhibits C and CI dated 14-2-56 other way round. Here, both the Courts below fell in serious error in allowing the plaintiffs to challenge the alienation and embarking upon the investigation of existence of legal necessity without seeing the legal bar of limitation.

34. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the plaintiffs cannot be allowed to collaterally circumvent the obstacle of limitation in order to maintain the suit. It may again, be noted that Nishikanta, father of the plaintiffs or Jhoharmoni, predecessor-in-interest of defendant No. 2 or defendant No. 2 or his heirs never challenged the alienation. Rather, they accepted the gifts vide Exhibits C and CI dated 14-2-56, which is tantamount to admission of the alienation.

35. Consequence therefore, is now, that any challenge of the plaintiffs to the alienation by the widow of the suit land left by Paban Mondal vide deed of sale Exhibit A and the claim for possession of the land covered by the deed must be held to be barred by the principles of estoppel, waiver and/or acquiescence. The Court of appeal below has therefore, rightly dismissed the suit, which is wholly based upon the challenge against the aforesaid al inaction.

36. Let us now consider the validity of alienation, albeit academically. We have seen, in support of the case of legal necessity, the defendant No. 1 has adduced the deed of sale in original, Exhibit A. It is written in the deed that the widow had to sell the land for payment of rents and paying off the debts incurred in the Litigation for protecting the land left by her husband Paban Mondal and also for the maintenance of the family. Mr Guha did not say that the necessities as recited in the deed do not constitute legal necessity. It is also borne out by record that none of the persons who witnessed the alienation is now alive after about 55 years. The defendant No. 1 was also minor at the time. In such circumstances, we shall have to evaluate the recitals made in the deed, Exhibit A.

37. Recitals in the deed are, no doubt, admissible. But they are not themselves evidence of the fact of legal necessity. This is the general rule. But when a long period of time has elapsed since the sale, it is not reasonable to expect such full and detailed evidence of the circumstances giving rise to the sale, and the strict proof of existence of legal necessity. In such situation, presumptions are permissible to fill in the details, which have been obliterated by time. In the circumstances, the Court is left with no choice but to consider the recitals in the alienation in the light of other evidence on record of the existence of legal necessity. The following cases as cited at the Bar will help to understand clearly the law on legal necessity.

<u>38. (1914) 23 Indian Cases 715 Lala Brij Lal vs Musammat lnda Kunwar and others, in an appeal arising out of a suit for possession by the reversioners, from Allahabad High Court, the Privy Council held-</u>

<u>"The onus of supporting a sale by a Hindu widow is on the purchaser and there must be evidence to prove legal necessity as would bind the husband's estate. Recitals in mortgages or deeds of sale with regard to the existence of necessity for alienation are not evidence by themselves of the fact and in order to substantiate the allegation there must be some evidence aliunde."</u>

<u>39. (1924) 82 Indian Cases 5: Muhammad Nuh vs Brij Behari Lal, A Division Bench of Allahabad High Court was of the following view:</u>

<u>"There is no legal presumption of legal necessity in favour of an alienation of property by a Hindu widow.. ... . .. The value to be attached to a recital in sale deed as to the existence of legal necessity for the sale depends upon the circumstances of the case. If circumstances are such as to justify a reasonable belief that an enquiry as to the existence of necessity would have confirmed the truth of the representation made by the end or, then, when proof of actual enquiry has become impossible, the recital coupled with such circumstances would be sufficient evidence to support the deed."</u>

<u>40. In 21 DLR 673 Promode Kumar Roy and others vs Benodini Haldar and others, a suit was instituted by the reversionary for declaration of title and recovery of possession. Alienation by widow was challenged. The suit was decreed and the then High Court affirmed the findings of the trial Court that the suit was not barred by limitation and that the alienation cannot bind the estate of the husband for want of legal necessity. In disposing of the second appeal, a Single Bench was of the view: "At any rate, a transferee from such a limited owner can only succeed if he can prove that such recitals about the legal necessity was, in fact, existing or that reasonable effort was made by him for ascertaining the facts and was satisfied honestly and bona fide from enquiries and representations received in this regard."</u>

<u>41. In 36 Indian Cases 420: Nanda Lal Dhur Biswas vs Jagat Kishore Acharjya, the Privy Council held-</u>

<u>"If the deeds were challenged at the time or near the date of their execution, so that independent evidence would be available the recital would deserve but slight consideration and certainly should not be accepted as proof of facts. "</u>

<u>42. In 29 DLR (SC) 137, the question was whether or not under the Hindu Widow's Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856), a Hindu widow forfeits her right to her deceased husband's property on her remarriage. The then Supreme Court of Bangladesh affirmed the decree setting the alienation on ground of remarriage since by remarriage the widow forfeited her right to the property left by husband.</u>

<u>43. In AIR 1935 Calcutta 689, a suit was brought by the daughters of the original owner, Bhagabat, for declaration of title and recovery of possession and for partition of the suit properties. The suit was decreed in part. On appeal, the decree was varied. The question raised on the legal effect of surrender by a Hindu widow after alienation in excess of her husband's properties. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court was of the following view:</u>

<u>"For the reasons we have given we think the logical consequence of the doctrine of surrender, which means a self-effacement of the widow and amounts to a civil death and complete extinguishment of the title of the widow in her husband's estate, is that all prior alienations in excess of her powers are liable to be challenged immediately on her civil death just as they could be impeached after she had died."</u>

<u>44. In (1933) 59 CLJ 167: Jagannath and others vs Srinath and others a suit was instituted to set aside a sale of joint family property for family necessity. The Privy Council allowed the appeal, reversed the decree of the Allahabad High Court and restored the decree of the trial Court, which dismissed the suit on findings that the sale was effected for family necessities and for the payment of antecedent debts due by the original owner, Mathura and so was binding on the joint family.</u>

45. In the absence of direct evidence and on the law as considered above the recitals in the deed deserve consideration as proof of the existence of legal necessity. In support of the necessity to pay off the debt incurred through litigation, the deed of patta is also adduced and marked as exhibit B. The patta shows that an interest was created in respect of the suit land. The interest of Paban Mondal in the land would have been extinguished had the patta been not recovered. Besides, the deeds of gift to Nishikanta and Jhoharmoni Exhibit C and CI also evidence, they including father of the plaintiffs admitted the alienation as valid by accepting the gift and taking possession of their respective land. The conclusion of the Court of appeal below that the alienation by the widow, Sumati to the defendant No. 1 was for legal necessity is therefore well founded, and does not suffer from infirmity or illegality.

46. In the facts and circumstances of the case, the plaintiffs are however entitled to 81 decirnals of land only out of the suit land as defendant No.2, in his absence, his heirs, substituted defendant No. 2 (Ka) to 2 (Gha) inherited 70 decimals. As the claim of the plaintiffs in the suit being based solely against the alienation by the widow transferring entire land of 10.47 acres left by Paban Mondal to defendant No. 1 fails, and in absence of any finding that said 80 decimals of land of the plaintiffs is joint with the rest of the suit land and the plaintiffs as co-sharers are possessing their land jointly with other co-sharers, the suit cannot be saved from being dismissed.

47. In the result, the Rule is discharged without however, any order as to costs. Impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below reversing those of the trial Court in dismissing the suit are hereby upheld. Order of status quo as granted at the time of issue of the Rule on 16-8-99 is recalled and vacated.

Send down the records at once.

End.

caseno:
Appeal from Original Decree No. 146 of 2002
With
Civil Rule No. 226 (F) 2002.
lawyer:
Mir Mahfuzur Rahman with Fara Mahmuda, Advocates------- For the Appellant. 
Subrata Saha, Advocate------- For the Respondents.
parties:
Paresh Chandra Biswas------- Appellant
Vs. 
Shashan Kalimata Idol and others------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
SK Sinha J: Only point which turns upon this appeal is, whether any person interested in the Publie Religious Institution, who is said in true sense not a believer of the institution's mode of celebration of pujas is entitled to institute a suit to remove the Shebait, if it is found that the Shebait is acting against the interest of the deity's property.

2. Plaintiffs claimed that from before the settlement operation, the villagers of Gandina Hindu Community established a temple and set up the image of Sree Sree Shashan Kalimata and had been performing religious rites. In the settlement operation, the lands were recorded in the name of ex-landlord but in the remark column the "Kodaldoha Kalibari by the Hindu community" was shown as possessor. Subsequently, with a view to remove the complication that might arise in future, Abinash Chandra Ghosh and others executed a deed of Endowment on 1st September, 1947 in favour of the Sree Sree Shashan Kalimata and the local Hindu community had been performing religious rites thereon. The villagers appointed the defendant No.1 as the Shebait for the management of the properties of the deity and to perform other religious rites. During the last settlement operation, the suit lands were recorded in the name of Abinash Chandra Ghosh and others and consequent upon which the Shebait instituted Miscellaneous Case No. 338 of 1968 under section 143 (a) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The said case was allowed and the civil Court directed the Revenue Authority to record the suit lands in the name of the deity. The Shebait was not performing the religious rites regularly and he did not maintain the accounts of the deity's property and misappropriated the entire usufructs of the property. Subsequently, the plaintiffs' appointed one Santosh Kumar Chakraborty as pujari of the deity for performing religious rites. Subsequently, the defendant No. 1 removed the image of the deity from the suit lands and converted the suit property as his personal property.

3. Defendant No.1, in his written statement claimed for the dismissal of the suit by raising various pleas. His first point is that the plaintiffs have no locus standi to institute the suit as they are believor of worshipping Vishnu, who are not entitled to offer Shashan Kalipuja not to speak of appointing a Sheba it of the deity. The second point raised by the defendant is that there is no legal evidence about mismanagement and/or misappropriation of the deity's property. The third point is that since the plaintiffs and other villagers are not entitled to perform Kali puja, the suit is barred under section 15 of the Religious Endowment Act, 1863. The last point agitated by the defendant is that the suit property not being the trust property of the deity, the suit, in accordance with section 92, is not legally maintainable.

4. Plaintiffs have examined 5 witnesses in support of their claim and exhibited the khatian and the deed of endowment. On the other hand, the defendant has examined 6 witnesses and exhibited documentary evidence, as Exhibits. Ka-Da.

5.
