The learned Additional District Judge, on consideration of the evidence on record, observed that though both the parties claimed that Aboni Chandra Ghosh and others by a deed of endowment dated 1st September, 1947 established Sree Sree Kalimata but none have produced and exhibited the said deed which is shrouded with mystery. The learned Additional District Judge, however, having found sufficient evidence on record regarding mismanagement in the affairs of the Debottor property, decreed the suit in part with clear findings that the defendant has been acting against the interest of the deity.

6. The learned Additional District Judge, held that the plaintiff had been able to prove the plaint case that there had been long standing dispute between the plaintiffs and the defendant regarding the income and expenditure of the deity's property since 1972, that there is no existence of Kali Mondir in the suit lands for about 28 years, that Gonesh Chandra Karmaker, (DW 4) admitted that no bank account is maintained in the name of deity, that the defendant is not maintaining the affairs of the deity properly, that Surendra Nath Sutradhar (PW 1) is a good and ascetic type of man, that the defendant has been using the suit property as his personal property and that the suit was instituted after compliance of formalities. The learned Additional District Judge thereupon came to the conclusion that in order to protect the image of the deity and its property, a committee should be constituted from the local members of the community who would manage the affairs of the deity.

7. Mr Subrata Saha, learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondents, submits that the plaintiffs have filed the deed of endowment but inadvertently, they have not exhibited the said deed and takes us to the said deed of endowment from the record. We noticed that the plaintiffs had filed the deed of endowment in the course of trial of the suit but they did not mark it as exhibit. In this Court, they filed an application for recording additional evidence for exhibiting the deed of endowment. We have allowed the prayer and marked it as Exhibit 3.

8. Mr Mir Mahfuzur Rahman, learned Advocate, has reiterated the defendant's plea taken in the written statement and submits that the plaintiffs, being members of Sudra and Baishnab community, have no right to perform the Kalipuja; they have no right to institute the suit to remove the hereditary Shebait, who is the Brahman of Kaishta Sect. Mr Rahman argues that the deed of endowment clearly recites that the deity has been established for performing religious rites by the Kaishta sect. In this connection the learned Advocate, has taken us to a book written by Pundit Shri Syama Charan Bhattacharya regarding the procedure of performing Sree Kalipuja. The learned Advocate has placed page 117 of the said scripture wherein the procedure of medi- tation ofKalimata has been narrated. By referring to this scripture, the learned Advocate is trying to make out a case that the non believers of Shashan Kalimata have restrictions to eat meat and that the plaintiffs, being believers of worshipping Vishnu, are not touching meat and therefore, they are not entitled to perform religious rites of Shashan Kalimata. The learned Advocate has also taken us to a book "Guru Bhakti Tatta Sudha" written by Shri Jodumondan Goswami and by referring pages 136, 142 and 143, the learned Advocate wants to convince us that the Baishnaba sects are performing the seba puja of Sree Krishna, who are not legally entitled to perform Shashan Kalimata puja. The learned Advocate has also taken us to Rigved wherein the different sects of Hindu Community and their mode of performing different types of seba puja have been narrated. The substance of the argument of the learned Advocate by bringing an analogy from these religious books is that the plaintiffs have no right or locus standi to interfere with the internal management of the properties of Shashan Kalimata as they are not believers of the image of the Shashan Kalimata.

9. Since the learned Advocate has pointed out some intricate questions relating to the performance of religious rites by the believers of the deity Kali, we are inclined to deal with the subject. We would like to observe here that these theologies have no sanction of law-they may be binding upon those who believe them as theological treatise. In Tagore Law Lecture on the Hindu Law of Religious and Charitable Trust by BK Mukherjea, the author on consideration of different authorities and text books has dealt exhaustively on gifts to idol, grants for temple, to whom does the property vest after dedication, hereditary priest, legal position of Shebait, right of suit for persons other than Shebait suit by worshipper and the removal of Shebait. The Hindu Religious System is encyclopedic in its character; it is not one form of faith but a commonwealth of faiths and in it are found the different grades or strata of religious thought and culture beginning from idolatry and ending with the highest form of philosophical monism. "I do not think that any Court in India will uphold a religious trust, the object and purpose of which are to provide milk for reptiles. These practices do not form part of the Hindu religion which is founded on the Vedas, and are mostly in the nature of an excrescence due to the conduct of the Aryans with the aboriginal races of India what is, on the fact of it, sinful or immoral, cannot certainly be countenanced by any Court of law, but save and except practices like those referred above, the efficacy of religious rites and ceremonies must be determined in accordance with the ideas and beliefs that are entertained by traditional orthodox Hindus on the subject" observed by the author.

10. In the chapter of "Gifts to Idols", the author observed "a Hindu can make a valid gift of property for the worship of an idol. Under the Hindu Law an idol of a symbol of certain religious purpose is capable of being endowed with property, and it is a valid religious trust to dedicate property for perpetuating the worship of an idol. That the idol is a household or family idol and is not meant for worship by the public does not make it any less and valid object of charitable trust." The distinction which is obtained in English Law with respect to public and private charities is not to be found in the Hindu text. The idol itself is explained in West & Buhler's Hindu Law, "is looked upon as a kind of human entity, the religious services of which are allowed by the Hindu Law to be provided for in perpetuity". Trusts are generally created by Hindus for the establishment of a temple and setting up a particular deity therein, and it is regarded as quite proper to make provision for the celebration of pujas of such deities who are worshipped periodically or occasionally and of whom no permanent images are kept.

11. BK Mukharjea on relying on the PN Saraswati's TLL on endowment observed that for the purpose of perpetuating the worship of the deity, it is usual for the donor to make grants of land. Sometimes the gift of land is made to pious Brahmins, who received the Brahmottar for carrying on the worship of the idol. This generally happens in the case of public temples and this is how the priest attached to particular temples came into existence. But gifts of land are usually made to the deity itself. In this particular case as well, though the deity was established by the villagers of Gandhina, but as the lands were recorded in the name of Abinash Chandra Ghosh and others, they made a deed of endowment in favour of the deity.

12. In all types of endowment, the purpose of founder is clearly expressed in the sankalpa while the renunciation divests the founder of his rights in the property dedicated. The defendant is not the founder of the deity. The deed of Endowment, Exhibit 3, clearly provided that though the lands were recorded in the name of Shrijukta Moulvi Khurram Khan Panny and others, the shebaits of Sree Sree Kalimata were in possession of the same and with a view to remove any complication in future regarding the deity's title, the shebaits of the kalimata took pattan of the lands from the Government. The recitals in the deed clearly disclosed that the deity is a public debuttor which is being used as such for years together by the Hindu community.

13. A religious endowment which is known as Debuttor and which arises on dedication or gift of property to an idol, a Debuttor is managed and administered and it is in an ideal sense that the dedicated property vests in an idol and in the nature of things the possession and management of it is entrusted to some person as Shebait. He is the person entitled to speak on behalf of the deity on earth and is endowed with authority to deal with all its temporal affairs. In a Hindu religious endowment, the entire owner- ship of the dedicated property vests in the trustee, who holds it for the benefit of Cestui Que trust. The entire ownership of the dedicated property is transferred to the deity. It is an admitted fact that the plaintiff is the Shebait of the deity. Now the question iswhat is the status of the Shebait of a public debuttor property. It has been observed by the judicial committee in Prosonna Kumari Debya vs Golap Chand Baboo, (1875) LR 2 IA 145 "that the person so entrusted must, of necessity, be empowered to do whatever may be required for the service of the idol and for the benefit and preservation of each property, at least as great as the manager of an infant heir. If these were not so, the estate of the idol might be destroyed or wasted, and its worship discontinued for want of necessary funds to preserve and maintain them."

<u>14. BK Mukharjea also told that the exact position of a Shebait cannot be said to be altogether beyond the range of controversy, though much of the earlier theories has now been discarded. The relation of a Shebait in regard to the debuttor property is not that of a trustee to trust property under the English law. In English Law, the legal estate in the trust property vests in the trustee who holds it for the benefit of the Cestui Que trust. In a Hindu religious endowment, the entire ownership of the dedicated property is transferred to the deity or institution itself as a juristic person and the Shebait or Mahant is a mere Manager. In Vidyavarathi vs Balu Sami, LR 48IA 302 the judicial committee observed. "A trust in the sense in which the expression is used in English Law, is unknown in the Hindu system pure and simple. Hindu Piety found expression in gifts to idols and images consecrated and installed in temples, to religious institution of every count, and for all purposes considered meritorious in the Hindu social and religious system. Under the Hindu law, the image of a deity of the Hindu Pantheon is a juristic entity, vested in the capacity of receiving gifts and holding property. Religious institutions known under different names are regarded as possessing the same juristic capacity and gifts are made to their committee". Now the question is, whether an interested person or a worshipper can maintain a suit for protecting the deity's property and whether he can remove the Shebait by a suit.</u>

15. Mr Mir Mahfuzur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that in view of sections 14 and 15 of the Religion Endowment Act, 1863, the plaintiffs have no right to remove the defendant who is a hereditary Shebait. These sections read as follows:

"14. Any person or persons interested in any mosque, temple or religious establishment, or in the performance of the worship or of the service thereof, or the trusts relating thereto, may, without joining as plaintiff any of the other persons interested therein, sue before the Civil Court the trustee, manager or superintendent of such mosque, temple or religious establishment or the member of any committee appointed under this Act, for any misfeasance, breach of trust or neglect of duty, committed by such trustee, manager, superintendent or member of such committee, in respect of the trust vested in; or confided to them respectively; and the Civil Court may direct the specific performance of any act by such trustee, manager, superintendent or member of a committee, and may decree damages and costs against such trustee, manager, superintendent or member of a committee.

15. The interest required in order to entitle a person to sue under the last preceding section need not be pecuniary or a direct or immediate, interest or such an interest as would entitle the person suing to take any part in the management or superintendence of the trusts.

16. Thus, any person having a right of attendance, or having been in the habit of attending, at the performance of the worship or service of any mosque, temple or religious establishment, or of partaking in the benefit of any distribution of alms, shall be deemed to be a person interested within the meaning of the last preceding section.

17. Section 14 lays down an important provision under which any person interested in the religious establishment may institute suit against the trustees for any misfeasance and empowers the Court to direct specific performance· of act or remove the trustee. The nature of the interest entitling a person to institute such suit is described in section 15. It need not be pecuniary or immediate interest or such an interest as would entitle the person receiving it to take part in the management. Any person having a right of attendance or partaking in the benefit of any distribution for long shall be a person interested within the meaning of the section. Under section 18, such suits could be instituted only after obtaining leave from the Court. Section 18 further provides that if the Court is satisfied that the suit has been for the benefit of the trust and no party to the suit was to blame, it may direct the whole or any portion of the costs to be paid. Section 14 creates a special jurisdiction in Civil Courts for the purpose of deciding matters relating to public religious trusts and to that extent the jurisdiction is exclusive.

18. It is contended that in view of the admission of PW 1 that he is a believer of Vishnu and therefore, he cannot perform Shashan Kalipuja. PW 1 however, stated in course of cross-examination that his mother was cremated at the suit cremation ground. Mr Mir Mahfuzur Rahman, argues that this cremation of the PW 1 's mother in the suit cremation ground will not confer him any right to perform Shashan Kalipuja since he is not the believer of the said rites.

19. The Nitisara tells us "neither through colour, nor through ancestors can the spirit worthy of a Brahman be generated." Thus, according to it, caste division should not be by birth, but by capacity. Again, it says" in making official appointments work, character, and merit were to be regarded neither caste nor the family." "public opinion is more powerful than the king as the rope made of many fibres is strong enough to drag a lion." A man can rise by capacity and merit. But how is he to acquire the capacity and merit? Jawaharlal Nehru in Glimpses of World History stated: "Probably the writer of Nitisara did not consider the large number of Shudra workers as entitled to give opinion. They are hardly counted. Public opinion was perhaps, just the opinion of the upper and ruling classes." "The books however, help us to realise what the ideology or the ideas of the people were at the time, even though they may not have practised them wholly. A more frequent method of rising in the social scale was for a whole sub-caste to go up a step. New tribes were often absorbed into Hinduism at the bottom, slowly they worked themselves up." "Thus, caste was a group system based on service and functions. It was meant to be an all-inclusive order without any common dogma and allowing the fullest latitude to each group. Within its wide fold there was monogamy, polygamy and celibacy; they are all tolerated, just as other customs, beliefs and practices were tolerated. Life was to be maintained at all levels. No minority need submit to a majority, for it could always form a separate autonomous group, the only test being; it is a distinctive group large enough to function as such. Between two groups there could be any amount of variation of race, religion, colour, culture and intellectual development."

20. In "The Discovery of India' the author observed "Caste is the symbol and embodiment of this exclusiveness among the Hindus. It is sometimes said that the basic idea of caste might remain, but its subsequent harmful development and ramifications should go; that it should not depend on birth but on merit. If merit is the only criterion and opportunity is shown open to everybody, then caste loses all its present day distinguishing features and, in fact, ends. Caste has in the past not only led to the suppression of certain groups, but to a separation of theoretical and scholastic learning from craftsmanship and a divorce of philosophy from actual life and its problem. It was an aristocratic approach based on traditionalism. This outlook has to change completely, for it is wholly opposed to modern conditions and the democratic idea." There is admitted evidence that Surendra Sutradhar (PW 1) is an honest and pious man. He along with 8 other local elite communities instituted the suit for the protection of the deity's property. There is no evidence on record that the plaintiffs are not interested in endowment and therefore, they are legally entitled to institute the suit for the protection of the deity's property. DW 1 has impliedly admitted the misappropriation of the property and in view of his admission, that there is no existence of Mandir in the suit lands and that he has recorded the suit lands in his name, the plaintiffs have locus standi to maintain the suit for the protection of the deity's property.

21. In Monohar Mookerjee vs Raja Peary Mohon, 24 CWN 478, the suit was brought by an heir of the frunder upon whom the management of the Debuttor would devolve if the actual incumbent was removed for misconduct and it was held that the founder or his heir could, under the law, "sue for the enforcement of the trust, for removal of the trustees, for the appointment of a new one and may thereby secure the proper administration of the trust and its properties."

22. In B Jangi Lal vs B Panna Lal, AIR 1957 Allahabad 743, by deed of endowment Chunnu Lal dedicated some properties to the idols of Sitaramji and other deities. For the management of this endowment, he framed an elaborate scheme in the deed executed by him. According to this scheme, he was himself to be the manager of this endowment for his lifetime, and, after his death, his son Jagannath Prasad was to be its manager. The deed further provided for the appointment of a number of trustees whose duty it was to supervise the work of the manager. The office of the manager, according to the deed of endowment, was to continue in the descendants of Chunnu Lal, male or female, so long as the family did not become extinct. The suit was ultimately dismissed in which it was claimed that Panna Lal was an extravagant and careless person and he was not taking any interest in the worship of the deities. He claimed removal of the trustee. A Division Bench of the Allahabad High Court on following the Ghosh's Commentary of the Law of Endowments, 1938 observed as follows: "In case of private endowment, any person who is interested in the worship of certain idol can alone maintain a suit for declaration that certain properties are debuttor properties of his ancestral idol. Any person interested in the endowment may sue to set aside and in proper alienation of its property by the manager. An improper alienation made by the manager, being in breach of trust and in exercise of his power may be set aside by suit instituted by any of the interested persons in the endowment."

23. In Shri Mohadoba Devasthan vs Mahadba Romaji Bidkar AIR 1953 Bombay 38 it has been held:

"Where there is a testamentary guardian or a certificate guardian, nobody except such guardian could be the next friend of a minor plaintiff. But if the interests of that guardian were adverse to those of the minor, he certainly could not be appointed the next friend for the purpose of the suit. Applying that analogy so far it is possible to do so in the circumstances of the present case, no Court would appoint the manager or the Shebait who was himself a party to an unauthorised alienation, as the next friend of the image or the idol where the alienation was being challenged. The next friend would, of necessity, be some person other than the manager or the Shebait of the image or the idol, and what better person could ever be found than the person next in order of succession of the shebaitship? In the case before us, Waman Chimnaji Waghule was the person who was alleged to have unauthorisedly alienated some of the suit properties. He could certainly not be appointed the next friend of the plaintiff for the purpose of instituting and prosecuting this suit. Keshav Waman Waghule, the son of original defendant 3, was the next vahivatdar after Waman Chimnaji Waghule. It was therefore, in the fitness of things that he acted as the next friend of the plaintiff in the matter of the institution and prosecution of this suit."

24. In Sri Iswar Radha Kanta Jew Thakur vs Gopinath Das, AIR 1960 741 it was observed as follows:

"Suit No. 980 of 1954 instituted by Rajen Sen in the name of the deity has been challenged, on the ground that Rajen Sen had no authority in law to institute the suit. According to Hindu Law, shebait represents the deity and he alone is competent to institute a suit in the name of the deity. In exceptional circumstances, however, where the shebait does not, or by his own act deprives himself of the power of representing of deity, a third party is competent to institute a suit in the name of the deity to protect the debuttor property. Dr Das contends that such a party must be a member of the family or a worshipper and that a total stranger, in law, is not competent to institute a suit in the name of the deity. I do not, however, consider this to be the correct view in law. A worshipper or a member of the family has, no doubt, his own right to institute a suit to protect his right to worship and for that purpose to protect the debuttor property. That is, however, a suit by the member of the family or worshipper in his personal capacity and not a suit by the deity. The deity has also a right of its own to have a suit instituted by a next friend. As I understand the law, the person entitled to act as next friend is not limited to the members of the family or worshipper. Anybody can act as such next friend, but the law requires that anybody other than shebait instituting a suit in the name of the deity must be appointed as such, by an order of the Court. That is the law as recognised by this Court".

25. In Bishwnath vs Thakur Radha Balladhji, AIR 1967 SC 1044 it was observed:

"The question is, can such a person represent the idol when the Shebait acts adversely to its interest and fails to take action to safeguard its interest. On principle we do not see any jurisdiction for denying such a right to the worshipper. An idol is in the position of a minor and when the person representing it leaves it in a lurch, a person interested in the worship of the idol can certainly be clothed with an ad hoc power of representation to protect its interest. It is a pragmatic, yet a legal solution to a difficult situation. Should it be held that a Shebait, who transferred the property, can only bring a suit for recovery? In most of the cases it will be an indirect approval of the dereliction of the shebait's duty, for, more often than not, he will not admit his default and take steps to recover the property, apart from other technical pleas that may be open to the transferee in a suit. Should it be held that a worshipper can file only a suit for the removal of a Shebait and for the appointment of another in order to enable him to take steps to recover the property, such a procedure will be rather prolonged and a complicated one and the interest of the idol may irreparably suffer? That is why decisions have permitted a worshipper in such circumstances to represent the idol and to recover the property for the idol."

26. In Peary Mohan Mukerji vs Manohar Mukerji ILR 48 Calcutta 1019 (PC) (this case was decided from the decision in 24 CWN 478, this suit was instituted by the present first respondent to obtain the removal of the appellant from the office of Shebait of certain debuttor property, to set aside a purchase of part of that property, namely a four fifths share of lot Bahirgora, and for the appointment of a receiver. The plaintiffs alleged that the Shebait misconducted in the Debuttor property. The suit was dismissed by the trial Court. On appeal, the judgment of the trial Court was reversed by the High Court. The views of the High Court have been referred earlier. Their Lordships of the judicial committee maintained the judgment of the High Court observing as follows:

"In a case of this description, if the purchase was allowed, precisely the same mischiefs would result as have been apprehended by eminent judges in cases of purchases of trust properties by trustees for sale. Indeed, the mischief might be of a more aggravated character, less likely to be discovered than rectified, as, unless the Shebait was removed, it might be impossible to determine the impropriety of the transaction and the injury inflicted thereby on the debuttor estate. If the contrary view prevailed, it is not inconceivable that an unscrupulous Shebait, anxious to seize a particular portion of the debuttor estate for his personal use, might, notwithstanding ample funds at his disposal, be encouraged to borrow money in the character of Shebait, allow a decree to be passed against him, acquiesce in the consequent execution sale, and ultimately, purchase the property in his private capacity."

27. It has been held in the case of Jagannatha vs Seenu, ILR 42 Mad 618 that even a hereditary priest can be removed if he is guilty of misconduct, and it is within the competence of a Civil Court to determine whether misconduct has been proved or not.

28. There are unanimous views regarding the removal of a Shebait by any interested person either a worshipper or a member of donor's family if the Shebait has misconducted himself in the management of the debuttor property or if he has misappropriated the property for his personal use and the mischief might be aggravated and less likely to be rectified. The deity has also a right of its own to have a suit instituted by a next friend and anybody can act as next friend and if mischief is done by the Shebait, such mischief would be aggravated unless the Shebait is removed. The unscrupulous Shebait would be encouraged to convert the entire Debuttor property to his personal use. Now the question is, whether there is sufficient evidence in support of the plaintiff's claim of mismanagement and/or misappropriation of the deity's property by the defendant appellant. The deed of endowment clearly indicated that before the execution of the deed on 1st September, 1947, the Hindu community had been performing Kalipuja in the suit lands and the deed was executed with a view to remove future complications. This shows that there was image of the deity in the suit property from before 1947.

29. DW 1 admitted in course of cross-examination that the suit lands were wrongly recorded and that the record was prepared in his name. Exhibit-Ga shows that the suit lands have been recorded in the name of plaintiff Sree Sree Ma Kalimata Thakurani. The learned Advocate has drawn our attention to a khatian from the record which shows that after the suit lands have been recorded in the name of the deity, the appellant has got his name recorded as the exclusive owner in pursuance of the judgment passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 338 of 1968. DW 1 himself has admitted that he has recorded the suit lands in his own name by deleting the name of Sree Shashan Kalimata. The consistent case is that there was a Kali Mondir in the suit lands. DW 1 also admitted that Abinash Babu constructed a Mondir on the suit lands and established the image of the idol and thereafter performed seba puja therein. He further admitted that he also performed the seba puja there and that there is no existence of the Mondir. According to him, the plaintiffs have removed the Mondir in 1985. The plaintiffs' claim is that the defendant-appellant has removed the image of the idol to his house and removed the Mondir from the suit lands for grabbing the suit lands as his personal property.

30. DW 2 also admitted that there was existence of Mondir in the suit lands. In course of cross-examination, he stated that he did not see the performing Kalipuja by the defendant-appellant after the liberation of Bangladesh and that the defendant whimsically maintains the income and expenditure of the deity's property. DW 3, in course of cross-examination, also admitted that there is no existence of Kali-Mondir in the suit lands and that he did not see any Mondir in the suit lands for the last about 28 years. He further admitted that the defendant sometimes performed seba puja of the Kalimata by him and sometimes through other thakurs. DW 5 also admitted in course of cross- examination that there is no existence of any Mondir. There. is therefore, admitted evidence on record that there was a Mondir and the image of the Kalimata in the suit land and the defendant- appellant had removed the Mondir and the image of the idol. The purpose for which the lands were endowed were not utilised and the properties were used for personal purpose of the defendant. The defendant-appellant has got the lands recorded in his own name. These facts manifestly proved that the defendant-appellant has mismanaged and misappropriated the property of the deity.

31. Mr Mir Mahfuzur Rahman, the learned Advocate, submits that the suit property not being a public trust, the plaintiffs cannot bring the suit in. accordance with section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure. As observed above, a Debuttor property would fall in the category of religious and charitable trust, although in true sense it would not fall within the meaning of "trust" under the English concept. Section 92 provides that suits Wider this section can be filed by Attorney-General or any other person having an interest in the trust with the leave of the Court, because the main purpose of this provision is to give protection to the public trust of a charitable or religious nature from being subjected to harassment by suits being filed against them. It does not impose a general embargo on filing of a suit in a Civil Court but only attracts that the suits of the nature mentioned in sub-section (1) of section 92 shall not be instituted in a Civil Court except in conformity with the provisions set out there. This section applies to public trust and provides that a suit against a trustee for the relief mentioned in the section could be instituted only in the manner provided therein. Where members of the public as persons interested in the endowment to enforce the right of the idol as against the trustee and claimed reliefs mentioned in the section, the suit must be brought in conformity with that section and a suit under the general law is barred.

32. In all cases of such nature, the suits are being instituted by the prospective Shebait, the worshippers or persons interested in the endowment in their own names. It cannot be denied that a worshipper or a prospective Shebait or a next friend has an interest of his own quite apart from that of a deity and his right to worship and the maintenance of the object of worship. A Shebait, who is guilty of misconduct or abuse of his possession as a trustee can be removed by the Court in a proper judicial proceeding. It has been observed by the judicial committee in Gulgari Lal vs Etah, 35 CWN 699, that "the standard of rectitude and accuracy expected from every trustee of charitable fund is of the highest, and that standard must, in all circumstances, be maintained by the Court if the safety of property held upon such trust is not to be imperiled throughout British India." It would be sufficient ground if the Shebait by his conduct places himself in such a position which makes it impossible for him to discharge faithfully the duties of his office, is a sufficient reason for determination by a Court for the removal of a Shebait. There are cases that where a Shebait has acted with gross impropriety or breach of trust, he is liable to be removed from the office even if no actual misappropriation had resulted and the deity had not suffered loss. These views are taken in the case of Nirmal Chandra Banerjee vs Jyoti Prasad" 45 CWN 709. It has been observed.

"A Shebait is certainly a person interested in the endowment, and if he can institute a suit to bring back to the debuttor any property of the idol which was illegally alienated by his co- Shebait, there is no good reason, in my opinion, why he cannot, in the same capacity, maintain a suit in the interests of the endowment itself for removal of a Shebait from his office on the ground of misappropriation of the deity's money and for recovery of the money that might be illegally retained by the latter."

33.	 Mukherjea, J observed:

"In my opinion, nothing turns upon the fact that in the case of a property dedicated to an idol, the juristic person is the deity himself in whom the property is vested and the Shebait is a mere manager or custodian of the idol. In the case of a mutt also the proprietary right vests in the institution and not in the Mohunt. As was pointed out by the Judicial Committee in the case of Vidya Varathi Thirtha vs Balusami (II) the idea of a trust in the English sense of the word was unknown in Hindu law. Hindu piety found expression in gifts to images consecrated or installed in temples or to religious institutions, by whatever name they might be called. In the case of a temple, it is the idol which is the juristic person, while in mutts the juristic person is the institution itself. Neither the mohunt nor the Shebait is a trustee in the English sense and has property conveyed to, or vested in, him, but in almost every case he has some personal interest in the endowment which depends on the usage or terms of the grant. It is the presence of this personal interest in the trust property which makes the rule of English law relating to appointments of new trustees, when a trustee becomes a lunatic, inapplicable to a Mohunt or a Shebait in India."

34. The learned Additional District Judge, on a proper appreciation of the evidence on record, rightly observed that there was no existence of the Mondir, that the defendant did not maintain any account of the debuttor property; that he did not make any attempt for construction of the Mondir on the suit lands and that there is no proper committee for the management of the debuttor property. We find the learned Additional District Judge is perfectly justified in coming to such conclusions which are based on proper appreciation of the evidence on record. We find no substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the appellant.

The points agitated by the learned Advocate for the appellant are devoid of substance. This appeal merits no consideration.

35. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs. The connected Rule is discharged.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: The precise reference to this Full Bench is as follows:

"Having regard to the gravity and importance of the issues raised in the writ petition, including that of destruction of basic structure of the Constitution, we are of the opinion that the Full Bench, if constituted, should decide all issues raised in the writ petition, and particularly the issue where the Act 1 of 1996 has caused amendment in the provisions of Articles 48(3) and 56 of the Constitution requiring assent thereto through referendum as contemplated by 142 (1A), (1B) and (1C) of the Constitution."

2. The Full Bench itself was constituted in the following circumstances.

3. This Rule in the present writ petition (Writ Petition No. 4112 of 1999) was obtained by the petitioner on 25-1-2000 as under:

"Let a Rule Nisi be issued upon the respondents calling upon them to show cause as to why the impugned Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1996 (Act No. 1 of 1996) (Annexure "A", "A 1" to the petition) should not be declared to be ultra vires of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and of no legal effect and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this court may seem fit and proper."

4. It is stated in the petition that the petitioner is a practicing Advocate of the Supreme Court Bar and it is his sacred duty as a citizen to safeguard and defend the Constitution and to maintain its supremacy as the embodiment of the will of the people of Bangladesh. The petitioner is also the Secretary General of the Association for Democratic and Constitution Advancement of Bangladesh (ADCAB) which has been working for the people's awareness to guard against the violation of the Constitution and the rule of law. The petitioner seeks to impugne the Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1996 (Act No. 1 of 1996) (hereinafter referred to as 'the impugned Act) as being ultra vires of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh which was passed by the 6th Parliament of Bangladesh introducing in the Constitution the concept of non-representative government violating the basic and fundamental concept of democracy and also in violation of the mandatory provisions of Article 142(1A) of the Constitution. Although the said Act was passed by the Parliament in disregard of its being unconstitutional the President assented to it on 28th March, 1996 without referring the question to a referendum as required under Article 142(1A) of the Constitution to ascertain and assess the opinion of the people as to whether the impugned Act in the form of Bill should be assented to inasmuch as the impugned Act amended Articles 48 and 56 of the Constitution.

5. Originally the present writ petition was filed impleading Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law and Parliamentary Affairs; Secretary, Jatiya Sangsad and the Chief Election Commissioner. After the issuance of the Rule, one Mr Amanullah Kabir was added as respondent No. 5 as an intervener. Thereafter, the General Secretary, Bangladesh Awami League and the Secretary General of Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) were added as respondent Nos. 6 and 7 respectively. Respondent Nos. 1-5 and 6 contested the Rule by filing affidavit-in-opposition separately.

6. The respondent No. 1 by filing affidavit-in- opposition denied the statements contained in the writ petition that the impugned Act by incorporating Articles 58A, 58B, 58C, 58D and 58E by way of amendment to the Constitution introduced the concept of non-party Caretaker Government in the Constitution which was violative of the basic and fundamental structure of the Constitution i.e. the democracy and the democratic system of government as enshrined in the Constitution. It is contended in its affidavit-in-opposition that in view of the bitter experience of the people in the past few elections held in the country, particularly in Magura Pourashava by-election held in 1994, the people, specially belonging to the opposition political parties and also the people at large, were of the view that there cannot be any free and fair election by the government comprised of persons belonging to a political party inasmuch as the political party in the government at the relevant time invariably used the government machinery in a bid to influence the election result affecting the fairness of the election. In order to do away with this malaise all political parties including the BNP in the government reached a consensus that the general election to the Parliament must be held by a non-party caretaker Government installed for a very temporary period. The non-party caretaker Government was perceived merely to hold the general election to the Parliament and not to take any policy decision unless it was indispensably necessary. Thus the concept of non- party caretaker Government was incorporated in the Constitution by necessary amendment and since the impugned Act did not amend Articles 48 and 56 of the Constitution there was no necessity of holding a referendum as contemplated under clause (1A) to Article 142. It is further contended that even if it is assumed for the sake of argument that the impugned Act has amended the provisions of Articles 48 and 56 of the Constitution there was no necessity of holding a referendum inasmuch as the provisions of clause (1A) to Article 142 for holding a referendum are ultra vires the Constitution as this clause was not introduced in the Constitution by an Act of Parliament but by a Martial Law Proclamation in 1978 by a Martial Law Administrator.

7. The respondent Nos. 5 and 6 by filing separate affidavits-in-opposition contended on similar terms stating that the Parliament passed the impugned Act amending the Constitution providing for a non-party caretaker government for a limited period for the purpose of holding free, fair, independent and peaceful general election to the Parliament in order to have a government formed of true representatives of the people. Further, it is contended that the amendment to the Constitution in question incorporating the concept of the non-party caretaker government is not destructive of the concept of the democratic government, rather it helps consolidate and institutionalize the democracy in Bangladesh. Concept of a neutral caretaker government as desired by the people is a government which will be solely and exclusively committed to the empowerment of the electorates free from fear and pressure of the muscle and money power so that they can freely choose the government they want.

8. The impugned Act (Act No. I of 1996) was first challenged by one Syed Mashiur Rahman by filing Writ Petition No. 1729 of 1996. A Division Bench comprising Mr Justice Md Mozammel Haque and Mr. Justice MA Matin summarily rejected the writ petition without issuing any Rule mainly on the ground that the provision of the impugned Act did not fall within the definition of alteration, substitution or repeal of any provision of the Constitution and, as such, it was not an amendment as contemplated under Article 142 of the Constitution. Their Lordships summarily rejected the writ petition in the following language:

"Since the provisions of the 13th Amendment Act, as it appears to us, do not come within definitions of alteration, substitution or repeal of any provision of the Constitution and since for temporary measures some provisions of the Constitution will remain ineffective, we do not find any substance in the submission of the petitioner that Article 56 of the Constitution had been, in fact, amended by the 13th Amendment Act. It appears that those provisions were made only for a limited period for 90 days before holding general election after dissolution of the Parliament. We find that no unconstitutional action was taken by the legislature and, as such, we do not find any reason to interfere with the 13th Amendment Act. We do not find any merit in the application. It is summarily rejected."

9. Later, the petitioner before us also challenged the impugned Act and the present Rule was issued in the terms already stated hereinbefore. Eventually, the said Rule came up for hearing before another Division Bench of the High Court Division comprising Mr Justice Shah Abu Nayeem Mominur Rahman and Mr Justice Md Abdul Awal. Their Lordships having heard the Advocates for the petitioner and also Mr Fida M Kamal, Additional Attorney-General for the respondent No. 1 and Mr M Amirul Islam for respondent No. 6 passed an order on 21-7-2003 stating that since their Lordships could not agree with the order passed in the case of Syed Muhammad Mashiur Rahman (WP No. 1729 of 1996), reported in 1997 BLD 55, on the validity of the impugned Act recommended the matter to the Hon'ble Chief Justice for a reference to a decision by a Full Bench as required under Rule 1 of Chapter 7 of the High Court Rules. It appears that their Lordships while expressing their views on the point whether the impugned Act, in fact, amended Articles 48 and 56 of the Constitution refrained from considering whether the impugned Act was violative of any basic structure of the Constitution.

10. Hence, keeping in view the conflicting views taken by two Benches of this Division on the point that the impugned Act was an amendment to the Constitution and the scope and extent of the reference recommended by their Lordships, the learned Chief Justice constituted this Full Bench by order dated 16-6-2004 to resolve the issues.

11. At the hearing of the Rule, Mr MI Faruqui, the learned Advocate appeared for the petitioner. On the other hand, the learned Attorney-General appeared for the respondent No.1, Mr AbduI Razzaque appeared for the added respondent No.5 and Mr M Amirul Islam appeared for the respondent No.6. In course of hearing of the matter, it was considered necessary to have assistance on the points involved in the matter and accordingly, Mr Rafique-ul-Huq and Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocates, were called upon to appear as Amici Curiae to assist the court to resolve the issues involved.

12. Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, having taken us through the writ petition, affidavits-in-opposition, affidavit-in reply together with annexures thereto and also having placed the historical perspective warranting the amendment to the Constitution by the impugned Act, canvassed the following points:

(a) Since the impugned Act by enacting Articles 58A, 58B, 58C, 58D and 58E has destroyed democracy and since the democracy is a basic structure of our Constitution the impugned Act is void and unconstitutional.

(b) The impugned Act having amended Articles 48 and 56 of the Constitution was liable to be sent for referendum as envisaged in Article 142(1A) of the Constitution but it was not done. Hence the impugned Act is unconstitutional and void.

(c) Article 58C(3) having amended Article 99 providing for the retired Judge and the retired Chief Justice of the Supreme Court to become the Adviser and the Chief Adviser to the non-party Caretaker Government respectively has in effect impaired the independence of judiciary inasmuch as such position tends to make him act in a manner subservient to the Government.

13. The learned Attorney-General Mr Hasan Ariff, Mr M Amirul Islam and Mr Abdur Razzaque opposing the above contentions of Mr Farooqui, advanced similar arguments upholding the constitutionality of the impugned Act providing for the non-party caretaker government in the Constitution. The learned Attorney-General while elaborating his points argued that the entire nation acting through their elected representatives expressed their uniform demand for holding, general election to the Parliament by non-party caretaker government, He enumerated and elaborated the events which led the political parties to come to a consensus for holding the general election to the Parliament and submitted that the concept of non-party caretaker government to function for a limited period of 90 days was evolved and incorporated in the Constitution for holding free, fair, independent and peaceful election and this was indispensable for consolidating and institutionalizing the democracy in the country and not to destroy the same, Accordingly, the impugned Act was passed by the 6th Parliament. According to the learned Attorney-General, this non-party caretaker government concept was and still is considered as an indispensable mechanism for holding free, fair and meaningful election in order to form a government by the true representatives of the people, Hence this concept of non-party caretaker government is far from being destructive of the democracy as one of the fundamental structures of the Constitution, The learned Attorney-General further submitted that although Articles 58A to 58E have been added to the Constitution as an amendment thereto but they cannot be taken to have amended Articles 48 and 56 requiring the impugned Act to be sent for referendum as envisaged in clause (1A) of Article 142.

14. These apart, the learned Attorney-General also argued the point of locus standi of the petitioner to file the instant writ petition. He has also argued the principle of res judicata submitting that the present writ petition is not maintainable on the ground that similar point was also raised and decided by a Division Bench in the case of Syed Muhammad Mashiur Rahman vs President of Bangladesh, 1997 BLD 55.

15. The learned Attorney-General also argued with reference to a few Articles of the Constitution, which are still there but remain inoperative during non-party caretaker government, that even prior to the non-party caretaker government concept introduced in the Constitution by the impugned Act there was a caretaker government system in the Constitution and in that the Prime Minister was allowed to run the Government on the dissolution of the Parliament till the general election to the Parliament was held and the Parliament was constituted although he (the Prime Minister) ceased to be an elected representative on the dissolution of the Parliament. In other words, prior to the non- party caretaker government concept introduced in the Constitution under the original constitutional dispensation, the Prime Minister was permitted in the Constitution to run the government including the holding of the general election to the Parliament after the Parliament was dissolved or stood dissolved making it a caretaker government. Learned Attorney-General tried to emphasise that in practice it was not possible to have an elected government during the interregnum to hold the general election to the Parliament. But nonetheless, this type of caretaker government was not considered as a neutral caretaker government for holding a free and fair election, inasmuch as the experience showed that such caretaker government indulged in influencing the election result in favour of the political party it belonged to by using the government machinery. Hence instead of such caretaker government the concept of non-party caretaker government comprised of non-partisan and disinterested persons was introduced in the Constitution for holding free, fair and independent election.

16. Mr M Amirul Islam, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondent No.6, also argued along the same lines and supported the constitutionality of the impugned Act. He also, in brief, traced the background of the popular demand of the people which led to the introduction of the aforesaid mechanism in the Constitution for obtaining free, fair and independent election to the Parliament. He also tenaciously argued to show that in the presently prevailing condition in the country where conflicting, violent and partisan views of the political parties were galore the non-party caretaker government was the only need of the hour to realise the long cherished demand and aspirations of the people of the country to have a truly representative government through fair and impartial election. Mr Islam, however, argued one step further and suggested that the concept of non-party caretaker government might not be any longer considered as a foolproof mechanism and it might be required to be replaced by an even more efficacious and effective system for holding a fair, peaceful and independent election to the Parliament provided a consensus is again reached in this regard by the people's representatives. He in this context, suggested that the nation might even think of a National Government as an alternative beneficial system to non-party caretaker government Mr Islam however, submitted that since the impugned Act did not directly amend the Preamble and Articles 8, 48 and 56 of the Constitution there was no requirement for the impugned Act to be sent for a referendum as required under Article 142(I A) of the Constitution. The impugned Act is therefore, valid and constitutional.

17. Mr Abdur Razzaque, the learned Counsel, argued that the impugned Act having added Articles 58A, 58B, 58C, 580 and 58D to the Constitution cannot be considered to have amended the Constitution. He also argued that the impugned Act could not be considered destructive of democracy or any other-basic feature of the Constitution and, as such, it should not be considered unconstitutional. Mr Razzaque also advanced the same line of argument as that of the learned Attorney-General that the Constitution provided for a caretaker government before the non-party caretaker government system was introduced in the Constitution by the impugned Act in that the Prime Minister was to continue in the government to hold the general election to the Parliament till another Parliament was constituted although he lost his representative character after the Parliament was dissolved. But since it did not yield the desired result the non-party caretaker government was introduced by the impugned Act in the Constitution to have a free, fair and independent election which was a sine qua non for the democracy. In this connection, he also mentioned that even in the Indian Constitution there is also a system of caretaker government which runs the government during the interregnum and holds the general election to the Parliament and such system has not been considered or held undemocratic in India.

18. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq and Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, appointed as the Amici Curiae by the court, also painstakingly argued expressing the same view as expressed by the learned Attorney- General that the impugned Act not having directly amended the Preamble, Articles 8, 48 and 56 of the Constitution was not required to be sent for referendum and the impugned Act was therefore, valid and constitutional.

19. Mr Huq also syllogistically argued echoing the concern of Mr Amirul Islam that Article 58C(3) and amendment of Article 99(1) by section 5 of the impugned Act having provided for the retired Judge and the retired Chief Justice respectively to become the Adviser and the Chief Adviser of the non-party caretaker government have affected and impaired the independence of the judiciary. He therefore, suggested that the representatives of the people should put their heads together again to find a suitable mechanism for obtaining free, fair and independent election without involving the Judge and the Chief Justice in the process in particular.

20. In view of the stand taken by the petitioner and the respondents and the points raised and argued on their behalf by their lawyers including the Amici Curiae to assist the court the following points fell for our consideration.

(1) Whether the incorporation of Articles 58A to 58E in the Constitution by virtue of the impugned Act can be considered as an amendment to the Preamble, Articles 8, 48 and 56 of the Constitution or at' least to Articles 48 and 56 requiring approval thereof of the people by means of the referendum before the assent of the President as contemplated under Clause (1A) of Article 142.

(2) Whether the impugned Act having brought about the above amendment is destructive of the democracy which is one of the fundamental structures of the Constitution.

(3) Whether the amendment of Article 142 by adding clauses (1A), (1B) and (1C) there to by the Second Proclamation (Fifteenth Amendment) Order, 1978 can be said to be a valid constitutional amendment.

21. Before we proceed to consider the above points, it is advisable to advert to and decide two preliminary points raised by the learned Attorney- General touching, the maintainability of the writ petition namely, (a) locus standi of the petitioner to file the writ petition and (b) whether the writ petition is hit by the principle of res judicata.

22. The petitioner is described in the writ petition as a practicing Advocate of the Supreme Court and a conscious citizen and since it is the sacred duty of every citizen of the country to safeguard and defend the Constitution and its supremacy he filed this writ petition challenging the impugned Act for a declaration that the impugned Act is destructive of democracy which is one of the basic features of the Constitution. He also asserted, in order to justify his standing in filing this. writ petition, that he was the Secretary General of the Association for Democratic and Constitutional Advancement of Bangladesh (ADCAB) and in that capacity also he brought this action under the constitutional jurisdiction of this court, inasmuch as the said Association had been working for the people's awareness to guard against the violation of the Constitution and for developing the rule of law. The petitioner by bringing this action, in our view, has sought for a determination as to whether the impugned Act was destructive of one of the basic features of the Constitution, namely, the democracy. He has also sought for a declaration whether section 5 of the impugned Act by amending Article 99(h) of the Constitution by adding the words" or the office of Chief Adviser or Adviser" has impaired the independence of the judiciary enabling the immediately retired Chief Justice to become the Chief Adviser and a retired judge of the Supreme Court to become an Adviser to the caretaker Government under Chapter 11A of the Constitution. This aspect, in our view, has aroused and created sufficient interest and concern in the petitioner and other citizens and the petitioner also shares this common interest and concern with others. This gives the petitioner necessary standing or locus standi to file the writ petition in view of the principles laid down in the cases of KM Rahman vs Bangladesh, 26 DLR (AD) 44, Dr Mohiuddin Farooque vs Bangladesh, 49 DLR (AD) 1 and also the case of ETV Ltd vs BTRC, 54 DLR (AD) 130.

23. The learned Attorney-General also contended, with some force, that since similar points were also urged for consideration before a Division Bench of the High Court Division in the case of Syed Muhammad Mashiur Rahman vs Bangladesh, 1997 BLD 55 and their Lordship passed the judgment rejecting the writ petition summarily, the present writ petition is not maintainable being hit by the principle of res judicata.

24. We have already stated above in some detail that in the said judgment it was held that the provisions of the impugned Act did not amend Articles 48 and 56 of the Constitution as the provisions of the said Articles were temporarily made ineffective. But however, we have already stated hereinbefore that the present Rule involves more points than that discussed and considered by their Lordships in the judgment of the aforesaid case and these points are required to be considered in the present judgment as all of them involve substantial questions of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution.

<u>25. The principle of res judicata is nowhere mentioned in the Constitution. But the principle of res judicata as found in the Civil Procedure Code is also applicable to a writ petition involving dispute of civil nature and the principle should not, however, be applied in a writ matter in terms of the Code of Civil Procedure but in substance. One of the important ingredients of res judicata is that the matter must be directly and substantially in issue between the same party or between the parties under whom they or any of them claim. A decision given in a writ petition between the same parties on an issue or issues operates as a res judicata and no fresh writ petition on that point is maintainable. The cases of Md Yakub vs Chief Settlement Commissioner, PLD 1965 SC 254 = 17 DLR (SC) 105 and the case of Asoke Kumar vs National Insurance, AIR 1998 SC 2046 may be cited in this connection. In the previous case Syed Muhammad Mashiur Rahman was the petitioner and in the present case M Saleem Ullah is the petitioner and there is no mutual representative character between them. The cases cited in this regard by the learned Attorney-General, namely, AIR 1968 SC 1196, AIR 1986 SC 391 and AIR 1993 SC 2422 are not relevant and applicable in the fact and circumstances of the present case. This point is accordingly, held in favour of the petitioner.</u>

26. This now takes us to the main points to see whether the impugned Act incorporating Articles 58A, 58B, 58C, 58D and 58D to the Constitution by way of addition thereto can be said to be an amendment under Article 142 of the Constitution. If the reply is in the affirmative, the question arises whether such amendment in effect is ultra vires of the Constitution being destructive of one of the fundamental features of the Constitution namely, the democracy. We have already noted that the impugned Act has created a new Chapter being Chapter 11A in the Constitution under the heading "Non-party Caretaker Government" and this Chapter is comprised of Articles 58B, 58C, 58D and 58E. Article 58A is also a creation of the impugned Act and is placed as the last Article of Chapter 11.

27. Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, seriously contends that the impugned Act having incorporated in the Constitution the concept of the non-party caretaker Government by adding Chapter IIA to the Constitution has amended Articles 48 and 56 by implication as the operation of these two Articles has been made inoperative for a period of 90 days during which the non-party caretaker government will have the rein of the government and hold the general election to the Parliament. The impugned Act while in the form of Bill, it is argued, was therefore liable to be referred by the President to a referendum as envisaged under clause (1A) to Article 142 but it was not done. Hence, the impugned Act is invalid and unconstitutional. It is further contended by Mr Farooqui that the essence of this argument is that because of the incorporation of the concept of non-party caretaker government in the Constitution an unelected non-representative government has been allowed to govern the country even though for a short period of 90 days and this scheme is therefore destructive of the democracy which is a fundamental feature of the Constitution. Hence, the impugned Act is also ultra vires of the Constitution.

28. Mr Farooqui by referring to page 170 of Construction of Statute by Crawford and also by referring to pages 180 and 181 of Black's Law Dictionary submits that the word amendment means to bring about some change or modification, deletion or addition in the constitutional provision in order to improve or change for the better by removing the defect or faults. We find that the word amendment has also been considered and discussed in the case of Anwar Hossain Choudhury vs Bangladesh, BLD 1989 (Special Issue). Mr Justice Badrul Haider Choudhury in the said case attempted to define the word amendment in the following language.

"The term "amendment" implies such an addition or change within the lines of the original instrument as will effect an improvement or better carry out the purpose for which it was formed "(para 192)

29. Mr Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed in paragraph 378 of the judgment in the above case has observed in this connection as under:

"Amendment of the Constitution means change or alteration for improvement or to make it effective or meaningful and not its elimination or abrogation. Amendment is subject to the retention of the basic structures. The Court therefore has power to undo an amendment if it transgresses its limit and alters a basic structure' of the Constitution."

<u>30. Article 142, as it stands now, has empowered the Parliament to effect any amendment to the Constitutional provision by way of addition, alteration, substitution or repeal by Act of Parliament provided the Bill for such amendment expressly states in its long title as to which provision of the Constitution it would amend. Such Bill is thereafter sent to the President for assent if it is passed by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of members of the Parliament Further clause (1A) to Article 142 requires that if any such Bill is passed which seeks to amend the Preamble at any provision of Articles 8, 48 or 56 or Article 142, the same must be referred to a referendum for ascertainment whether the Bill should or should not be assented to by the President. The learned Attorney-General read the impugned Act to us and submitted that the long title thereof did not in any manner state that the impugned Act amended the Preamble or any of those Articles. Hence, according to him, there was no necessity in the present case for referring the impugned Act for referendum. The impugned Act is intra vires of the Constitution, it is submitted.</u>

31. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq, as a manifestation of his serious and hard work, produced the photo copies of the entire proceedings of the Parliament showing the discussions and deliberations that were made by the Hon'ble Members of the Parliament during the passage of the concerned Bill and submitted that there was no indication that by the said Bill the Preamble and or any of the said Articles were amended. We have also carefully examined the said parliamentary proceedings and it appears that neither the long title of the concerned Bill nor the Parliamentary proceedings concerning the Bill disclosed that the impugned Act in effect amended the Preamble and or any of those Articles requiring reference of the Bill to referendum. We have also examined the impugned Act keeping the arguments advanced at the Bar including that of the Amici Curiae in mind and we have no hesitation to hold that the impugned Act has not amended the Preamble and or any of the Articles Of the Constitution mentioned above requiring reference of the said Bill to referendum.

<u>32. Now it is to be seen, as seriously argued by Mr MI Farooqui, whether the Articles namely, Articles 58B, 58C, and 58E incorporated in the Constitution by the impugned Act have amended the Preamble and the Articles 8, 48 and 56 by implication and even if it has done so, whether that could be regarded as an amendment. It is reiterated that, according to Mr Farooqui, amendment of any provision can even be made by implication. We respectfully disagree with the contention advanced by Mr Farooqui in this connection and hold that no amendment of any provision of law or Constitution can be made or effected by implication or as of consequence. The amendment mainly effected in any provision of law is for achieving something better in order to accomplish the desired result. Amendment of any legal or constitutional provision has therefore to be made by way of addition, substitution or repeal of any provision of law or Constitution directly, and expressly and not by implication or as of consequence and it must not be also for a limited period, If we examine Article 58E in this perspective we find that the operation" of Articles 48(3), 141A(l) and 141(C)(1) of the Constitution has been rendered - ineffectual or suspended for a limited period. In our view, the operation of Article 48(3) can at best be said to have been suspended for a limited period and, as such, it cannot be said that Article 58E has amended Article 48.)</u>

33. We would now consider the next point, whether the impugned Act by incorporating Articles 58B to 58E in the Constitution and also by amending Article 99(1) by virtue of section 5 thereof has destroyed or in any way affected the basic feature of the Constitution namely, the democracy and or the independence of the judiciary. In this regard, we recall the agitation and popular demand of the people of Bangladesh to develop and provide for some device or scheme by amending the Constitution to secure a free, fair, independent and peaceful general election to the Parliament so that the elected representatives of the people had true representative character. In this background of the plethora of agitation and movement, a consensus was reached among the elected representatives of the people regardless of their political affiliation. As a result, the 6th Parliament passed the impugned Act introducing non-party caretaker government mechanism in the Constitution with a view to realising the aforesaid goal and the country through this newly added constitutional device has successfully held three consecutive general elections to the Parliament which have been widely acclaimed both at home and abroad as free, fair and independent elections.

34. A careful study of the Preamble shows that both democracy and the independence of judiciary are also the basic features of the Constitution. As a necessary corollary, free and fair election are also considered to be the basic features of our Constitution. Mr Justice Shahabuddin Ahmed in his judgment in the case of Anwar Hossain Chowdhury vs Bangladesh 1989 BLD (Special Issue) in para 377 held that the democracy and independence of judiciary are basic features of our Constitution. The Indian Supreme Court in the case of Sreemati Indira Gandhi vs Raj Narayan AIR 1975 SC 2299 also held that free and fair election was also one of the basic features of the Indian Constitution. Since democracy is a basic feature of our Constitution it is not very far to see that free and fair election being an inextricable part of the democracy is also a basic feature of our Constitution. This position is also unequivocally shared and supported by the learned. Counsels representing the respondents and also by the Amici Curiae that the impugned Act was passed to strengthen, consolidate and institutionalize the democracy in Bangladesh.

35. The learned Attorney-General, in an apparent reinforcement of the argument in support of the non-party caretaker government, submitted that even; before the amendment of the Constitution in question our Constitution also provided for a caretaker government system in that the Prime Minister was to run the government for a limited period and hold the general election to the Parliament after the Parliament was dissolved or it stood dissolved and in support of this contention he referred to Articles 57(2) and 58(4) and submitted that in view the Article 58A, as incorporated by virtue of the impugned Act, the operation of Articles 57(2) and 58(4) providing for such caretaker government; remains suspended when the non-party caretaker government under Chapter 11A is formed. Because the original concept of caretaker government run by the Prime Minister could not ensure free and fair election to the Parliament. Mr Rafiqul-ul-Huq also tacitly argued by referring to Article 48(5) of the Pakistan Constitution that in Pakistan also there is a concept of a caretaker government system which holds the election to the National Assembly within the period of ninety days after the National Assembly is dissolved by the President. Mr Razzaque also supported this position and argued that as per the constitutional scheme in India the Prime Minister of India at the instance of the President continues to run the government for the interregnum and holds the election to the Parliament.

36. We therefore, find that both Mr Rafique-ul- Huq and Mr Razzaque have in effect supported the learned Attorney-General in his view that both in India and in Pakistan there has been a constitutional device to hold the general election to the Parliament or the National Assembly by a non-representative caretaker- government after the Parliament or National Assembly is dissolved. According to them, similar constitutional provisions are also there in our Constitution. But since such scheme was not found to suit the genius of the people of our country there was an outcry for a non-party caretaker government to hold the general election of the Parliament to ensure free, fair and independent election. We find force in this contention. People of Bangladesh suffered bitter experience in relation to holding of election to the Parliament by the previous caretaker government system. Fair, independent and impartial election was not possible for the reason that although the Prime Minister used to run the government during the interregnum and held the general election to the Parliament but the election was not free and fair inasmuch as the government men and machinery were used by such government to influence the election result in favour of the political party to which the Prime Minister belonged. This was the major factor necessitating the passing of the impugned Act for en grafting the non-party caretaker government system in the Constitution in 1996 by amending the Constitution.

37. Careful examination of the Preamble and Article 8 of the Constitution shows that democracy is a basic feature of the Constitution. In Election Commission, in Re Special Reference No.1 of 2002, (2002) 8 SCC 237, (Gujarat Assembly Election Matter) Mr Justice VN Khare observed that "democracy" is a part of the basic structure of the Indian Constitution and the said observation was made in the following language:

"It is no doubt true that democracy is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution and periodical free and fair election is the substratum of democracy. If there is no free and fair periodic election, it is the end of democracy" and the same was recognised in MS Gill vs Chief Election Comm., (1978) 1 SCC 405: AIR 1978 SC 851 as under:

12. A free and fair election based on universal adult franchise is the basic, the regulatory procedures vis-a-vis the repositories of functions and the distribution of legislative, executive and judicative roles in the total scheme, directed towards the holding of free elections, are the specifics. The super authority is the Election Commission the kingpin is the Returning Officer, the minions are the presiding officers in the polling stations and the electoral engineering is in conformity with the elaborate legislative provisions."

38. In the same reference, Arijit Pasayat, J also observed that free, fair and periodic elections are part of the basic structure of the Constitution of India and "Democracy" and "free and fair" election are inseparable twins. Arijit Pasayat, J further observed in this regard as under.

"Free, fair and periodic elections are part of the basic structure of the Constitution of India (in short, "the Constitution"). In a democracy, the little man-voter has overwhelming importance and cannot be hijacked from the course of free and fair elections.

108. "Democracy" and "free and fair election" are inseparable twins. There is almost an in severable umbilical cord joining them. The little man's ballot and not the bullet of those who want to capture power (starting with booth-capturing) is the heartbeat of democracy. Path of the little man to the polling booth should be free and unhindered, and his freedom to elect a candidate of his choice is the foundation of a free and fair election.

109. The message relates to the pervasive philosophy of democratic elections which Sir Winston Churchill vivified in matchless words;

"At the bottom of all tributes paid to democracy is the little man, walking into a little booth, with a little pencil, making a little cross on a little bit of paper-s-no amount of rhetoric or voluminous discussion can possibly diminish the overwhelming importance of the point."

39. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq argued that even if the impugned Act is considered to have amended the Preamble, Articles 8, 48 and 56 of the Constitution, the impugned Act is not required to be tested on the touchstone as provided under Clause (1A) of Article 142 meaning reference of the same to referendum inasmuch as, according to him, this clause having been incorporated in the Constitution by amending Article 142 through unconstitutional means, meaning the Martial Law Proclamation the said clause (1A) must be taken to be void and non-est. We regret we cannot subscribe to this view of Mr Huq. Clause (1A) apart, there are other provisions in the Constitution which have been also incorporated in the Constitution through unconstitutional means i.e. the Second Proclamation, (Fifteenth Amendment) Order 1978 (Second Proclamation Order No. IV of 1978) and these amendments have been ratified under Paragraph 18 to the Fourth Schedule and Article 150 of the Constitution. This amendment is therefore, considered as valid and part of the Constitution. We accordingly, hold that unless this amendment (namely, Clause (1A), is declared void by a Court of law the same should be held to be valid. Consequently, if any amendment is found to have amended the Preamble, Articles 8, 48 and 56 of the Constitution, the amending Bill must be referred for referendum before it is assented to by the President.

40. Mr Farooqui has also argued that Article 99 has been amended by section 5 of the impugned Act providing for the retired Judges and retired Chief Justice to hold the office of Adviser and the Chief Adviser, as the case may be, and this has impaired the independence of the judiciary and since independence of the judiciary is also a basic feature of the Constitution the said amendment must also be held to be unconstitutional. We have noticed that the non-party caretaker government system has been incorporated in the Constitution by the impugned Act with the main objective to hold free, fair and peaceful general election to the Parliament and by amending Article 99 retired Judges and the retired Chief Justices have been made eligible to hold such office in the non-party caretaker government. It is widely known and appreciated that the Judges and the Chief Justices of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh are not only most learned persons but also by virtue of their training and holding of such high office they are normally considered to have attained and acquired the status and image of upright, qualified, impartial and independent persons in the contemporary times. The legislature therefore, in its wisdom, preferred them as persons of high moral and impartial character and dignity and high caliber and most capable for discharging the powers and functions as Adviser and the Chief Adviser in the non-party caretaker government. We therefore, do not find any reason or justification to question, suspect or undermine the wisdom of the legislature in this regard.

41. Mr M Amirul Islam as well as Mr Rafique- ul-Huq submitted that some other suitable and appropriate person or persons may be found out by the representatives of the people for the said office in lieu of the retired Judges or the Chief Justices of the Supreme Court. This however, attracts no comment from us. No system should be taken to be a fool-proof one. The people's representatives in the Parliament must always try and find out even a better system to ensure free, fair and peaceful election to the Parliament. It is therefore, up to the Parliament in future to bring any amendment to the Constitution to achieve this end for consolidating and institutionalising the democracy in the country.
