But till then, since we find the impugned Act valid and constitutional, the present constitutional dispensation i.e. the Non-party Caretaker Government system for holding free, fair and peaceful election to the Parliament, must be retained.

42. The comparative study of the election laws in the countries of the Sub-continent shows that the Election Commission of Bangladesh is sufficiently strong and independent in matters of its operation and decision making. It has financial autonomy which is all the more important for discharging its functions independently. Care and caution must however, be exercised in appointing the Chief Election Commissioner and other Commissioners so that persons of high morality, integrity uprightness and sagacity are invariably chosen for the said office. On top of this, the Chief Election Commissioner, as of necessity, must, in addition thereto, be a person knowledgeable in law and its administration. We nonetheless, deem it profitable to recommend a few points by way of electoral reform as under

1.	The role of pre-poll enquiry committee be strengthened with power to take immediate action.

2.	Amendment in penal provisions may be made for making the punishments for different offences practicable and commensurate with the offence committed.

3.	The Code of Conduct for the candidates should be avoided.

4.	Review powers should be given to the Election Commission for fair conduct of election.

5.	Contempt provision which was made earlier should be restored.

6.	Activities of the summary trial Courts should be strengthened.

7.	The Election Commission must monitor and ensure that the Police should exercise its power given in Article 87 A of the Representation of the People Order, 1972 and punishment should be provided for any non-compliance.

8.	Registration of political parties with the Election Commission should be made compulsory. There should be provision that the political parties must submit their statement of accounts regularly to the Election Commission.

9.	Section 5(2) of the Representation of the People Order, 1972 should be amended to include the word "and the law enforcing agency" after the word "Government" in the first line to make the service of the Defence Services of Bangladesh and other law enforcing agencies available for holding fair and peaceful election, if it is considered expedient and necessary in a given situation.

10. Voters should be provided with their identity card for their use at the time of casting vote at any polling centre or polling booth. Necessary provision in this regard be incorporated by amending the relevant law.

Although Mr Amirul Islam, while arguing for the respondent No.6, Bangladesh Awami League, has supported the incorporation of the non-party caretaker government mechanism in the Constitution for the purpose of free, fair and independent general election to the Parliament by amending the Constitution but he has at the same time expressed his anxiety that the non-party caretaker government may not anymore be accepted as a mechanism for a foolproof election to the Parliament. He has, therefore, argued that it is also now necessary and expedient to think about some electoral reforms to achieve the desired goal. In this context, we are persuaded to observe that there cannot be any holistic approach to the solution of the alleged problem. The status of the Election Commission and the electoral system in Bangladesh, as already indicated above, is by far sound and efficacious. The only important factor that needs to be dispassionately looked at and considered is to ensure that the persons in authority and the leaders of the political parties must have real and clear conception of democracy and its values and norms. This can only be achieved not by mere theorising of the same but by initiating its practice and true culture and religiously practicing the same at all levels in the national life and the body polity. There has unfortunately, been charade of democracy in the Government as well as in the political parties in Bangladesh and this is more due to lack of clear conception, appropriate culture of democracy and perception of its norms and values in the political parties. As a result, the political behavior of a section of political parties has become so perverse, erratic and incompatible with any acceptable norms and standard requisite for due growth and sustenance of democracy to the benefit of the people of Bangladesh who fought and achieved liberation and independence of Bangladesh at an enormously high price which has no parallel in the contemporary history. Medias, specially the printing media, have a formidable, gigantic, powerful and valuable role to play in this regard in educating the people at large, persons in authority, political leaders and activists about the real culture and practice of democracy to make the parliamentary democracy a success. The important requisite in this regard is to ensure objective journalism.

43. Democracy, which was uncompromisingly fought for and achieved by the people of Bangladesh in 1990, much after the war of liberation and independence, by throwing aside the yoke of the autocratic rule, is a form of government of representative democracy in which the powers of the majority are exercised within the constitutional framework which is known as liberal or constitutional parliamentary democracy. Such democracy requires to be nourished sustained and consolidated through right culture, instillation and inculcation of certain democratic norms and values in the persons in authority and the government as well as in the political parties. The important and overriding democratic values and principles lie in the exhibition of tolerance and respect for the views of others embraced with indivisible allegiance, loyalty and patriotism for the country. Polities of confrontation and violence being anathema to real democratic culture, values, norms and practice must be shunned at any cost. If these are achieved, free, fair and independent election will not anymore be a distant goal. Many developed countries in the world and also some developing countries in the sub- continent have achieved this goal to an appreciable extent through the traditional constitutional mechanism in lieu of non-party caretaker Government system.

44. The democratic and political culture is yet another important and indispensable factor in establishing democratic society and good governance in the country. Every democratic political party should not only be committed but must also be seen to be committed to cherish and practice sound and healthy democratic and political culture. Regrettably, there has been a degeneration of democratic and political culture due to mobilisation of funds through undesirable and disdained private financing. This pursuit of private finance is aimed at mobilising political parties and electoral activities. And this makes both the political parties and leaders hostage to special interest groups. Political leaders are thus held hostage to these special interest groups and this, in turn, compels the leaders to make corrupt decision and protect and patronise crimes in the society. Consequentially, various democratic and important institutions in the country are increasingly becoming weak and are thus not in a position to 'perform their desired and expected role to the utter despair and despondency of the citizenry. This calls for drastic measures by enacting law for electoral reforms or otherwise to eliminate this political symbiosis of the politicians, businessmen and bureaucrats creating collusive relationship among themselves as this has infected the country's democratic political system .Because such system of political financing, by its nature, is destructive of transparency and accountability. Accordingly, the political institutions are gradually becoming dysfunctional. There is yet another agonising factor. Major opposition political parties unilaterally impose dogma and more often resort to violent means for its implementation as popular and mass demand creating undue political unrest retarding the desired and expected growth of trade, commerce, economy and also the education in the country. This proclivity of the political parties has to be averted in the interest of bolstering democratic and healthy political culture in the body polity for general welfare and well-being of the people.

<u>45. In this background of whatever has been stated above we hold the following:</u>

<u>(1) The writ petition is maintainable.</u>

<u>(2) The Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1996 (Act No.1 of 1996) is valid and constitutional.</u>

<u>(3) The Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1996 has not amended the Preamble, Articles 8, 48 and 56 of the Constitution and it was therefore, not required to be referred to referendum.</u>

<u>(4) The Constitution (Thirteenth Amendment) Act, 1996 has not affected or destroyed any basic structure or feature of the Constitution, particularly the democracy and independence of the Judiciary.</u>

<u>(5) Clauses (1A), (1B) and (1C) to Article 142 of the Constitution are valid and consequently, any amendment to the Preamble and Articles 8, 48 and 56 of the Constitution must observe the formalities provided in clauses (1A), (1B) and (1C) to Article 142 of the Constitution. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.</u>

46. In conclusion, we record our deep appreciation of the valuable assistance rendered by the learned Attorney-General and the learned Advocates including the amici curiae.

47. Mr MI Farooqui, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, prays for a certificate under Article 103 of the Constitution for preferring appeal before the Appellate Division. We find that the present case involves a substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution. Certificate in this regard is accordingly granted.

A copy of this judgment be sent to the office of the Prime Minister, Speaker of the Parliament, Ministry of Law, Chief Election Commissioner and the Secretary to the Election Commission forthwith.

Md Awlad Ali J: I have the advantage of going through the judgment delivered by my learned brother Mr Justice Md Joynal Abedin, although I concur with the main decision given by him but I venture to express my own views in a brief manner on the main issue i.e. the invalidity or unconstitutionality of the 13th Amendment of the Constitution, namely, Act 1 of 1996, passed by the 6th Parliament.

50. Relevant facts, background of the reference have been elaborately discussed in the main judgment. Writ Petition No. 1729 of 1996 challenging the vires of the 13th Amendment of the Constitution was summarily rejected by a Division Bench of this Court by judgment dated 25-7-96 reported in 1997 BLD 55 holding that by 13th Amendment of the Constitution the legislature intended to keep certain provisions of the Constitution ineffective for a limited period and after that period those provisions will automatically revive and the provisions of the 13th Amendment do not come within the definition of addition, alteration, substitution or repeal of any provision of the Constitution. Thereafter, the present petitioner Mr M Saleem Ullah, one of the learned Advocates, of the Supreme Court Bar Association, again challenged the 13th Amendment of the Constitution in 2000 and a Rule Nisi was issued upon the respondents calling upon them to show cause as to why the Constitution 13th Amendment Act (Act No. 1 of 1996) should not be declared to be ultra vires of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. The main contention raised by the petitioner is that the impugned Act which was passed by the Parliament introduced new concept of non-representative Caretaker Government violating the basic concept of democracy, the fundamental structure of the Constitution and also in violation of the mandatory provisions of Article 142(1A) of the Constitution, for by the impugned Act 1 of 1996 the provisions of Articles 48 and 56 have been amended but before the bill was assented to by the President it has not been put to a referendum, the question whether the bill should or should not be assented to as provided by Article 142(1A) of the Constitution and therefore, the said Act did not get any validity in the eye of law and according to the provision of the Constitution. After hearing the contending parties another Division Bench of this Court disagreed with the decision in the case of Syed Muhammad Mashiur Rahman vs President of Bangladesh and others in WP No. 1729 of 1996 but without deciding the issue of violation as to or destruction of basic structure of the Constitution and referred the matter to the Hon'ble Chief Justice. We are now called upon to decide the questions raised in the writ petition, particularly the issue whether the Act 1 of 1996 his caused amendment to the provision of Articles 48(3) and 56 of the Constitution requiring assent thereto by the President through referendum as contemplated under Article 142(1A) of the Constitution. Contentions raised and detailed submissions made by the learned Counsel for the petitioner Mr MI Farooqui, Mr AFM Hasan Ariff, the learned Attorney-General representing the Republic, Mr M Amirul Islam, Mr Abdur Razzak representing the respondent Nos. 6 and 5 have been recorded by my learned brother in the judgment. Besides, two learned Amici curiae Mr Rafique-ul- Huq and Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan expressed their valued opinion by way of submission.

51. Main contention of Mr MI Farooqui is that by 13th amendment the Parliament have incorporated some new Articles under Chapter IIA of the Constitution introducing a non-party caretaker government which have in effect amended the provisions of Article 8, 48 and 56 of the Constitution and the bill for such amendment should not have been assented to by the President without referring it to the referendum. Therefore, the Act I of 1996 passed by the 6th Parliament is unconstitutional. His further contention is that 'the 13th Amendment has destroyed the basic structure of the Constitution namely, the democracy, as the elected government is replaced by a non-elected and unrepresentative Government although for a temporary period. His further contention is that by that amendment the independence of the judiciary has been impaired.

52. Now the question firstly to be determined as to whether the 13th Amendment has amended Articles 8, 48(3) and 56 of the Constitution and thereby destroyed the democracy which is the fundamental and basic structure of the Constitution. If those Articles have not been amended by Act 1 of 1996 then there cannot be or shall not be any valid reason or constitutional obligation to refer it to referendum under Article 142(IA) of the Constitution.

53. Before discussing the legislative power of Parliament as respect of amendment of the provisions of the Constitution as provided under Article 142 of the Constitution, let me see what is the meaning of the term amendment. Although it has already been described in the judgment given by my learned brother but I like to quote it here for further elucidation of the issue in question. In Black's Law Dictionary amend means to improve, to change for the better by removing of defects-Amendment means to change or modify for the better, to alter by modification or addition. Article 142 of the Constitution is as under:

"142. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in this Constitution-

(a) any provision thereof may be amended by way of addition, alteration, substitution or repeal by Act of Parliament. Provided that-

(i) no Bill for such amendment shall be allowed to proceed unless the long title thereof expressly states that it will amend a provision of the Constitution;

(ii) no such Bill shall be presented to the President for assent unless it is passed by the votes of not less than two-thirds of the total number of members of Parliament;

(b) when a bill passed as aforesaid is presented to the President for his assent he shall, within the period of seven days after the Bill is presented to him, assent to the Bill, and if he fails so to do he shall be deemed to have assented to it on the expiration of that period.

(1A) Notwithstanding anything contained in clause (1), when a Bill, passed. as aforesaid, which provides for the amendment of the Preamble or any provisions of Articles 8, 48 or 56 or this Article, is presented to the President for assent, the President, shall, within the period of seven days after the Bill is presented to him, cause to be referred to a referendum the question whether the Bill should or should not be assented to. It appears that the provision of the Constitution may be amended by way of addition, alteration, substitution or repeal by Act of Parliament. The Parliament by Act 1 of 1996 has added or introduced a new Chapter, namely, Chapter 1A, in the Constitution under heading Non-party Caretaker Government containing Articles 58B to 58E. Why this addition was necessary? In the proceedings of the Parliament which has been placed before us by the learned amici curiae Mr Rafique-ul Huq, and in the discussion on the 13th Amendment Bill in the Parliament it has been said by the then Law Minister that:

নির্বাচন কমিশনকে সাহাহ্য ও সহায়তা করার জন্য এবং সংবিধানে অর্পিত যে ক্ষমতা প্রয়োগ করে দায়িত্ব পালনের জন্য একটি নির্দলীয় ও তত্ত্বাবধায়ক সরকার. non-party Caretaker Government গঠন নিয়ে আলোচনা করতে হচ্ছে। আজকে সরকার নির্বাচন চালাচ্ছে। প্রশ্ন যখন উঠেছে আমরা বিশেষভাবে মনে করছি যে, জনসমক্ষে একটি নির্দলীয় তত্ত্বাবধায়ক সরকার একান্ত প্রয়োজন।”

Necessity for forming non-party caretaker Government was felt in the Parliament and by the votes of two-third majority the bill was passed. Chapter IIA non-party caretaker Government has been introduced by way of addition by Act I of 1996 with Articles 58A and 58B-58E as temporary measure for limited period, that is for 90 days only, for holding election to the Parliament. How far the said articles have in effect amended the provisions of Articles 8, 48 and 56 of the Constitution. If it is held that those Articles or some provisions of those Articles have been amended then the question of referendum would arise.

54. In the original Constitution of 1972 in Article 142 there has been no provision for referendum. The provision for referendum as incorporated in Clause (1A) of Article 142 was inserted by the Second Proclamation (5th Amendment) Order, 1978 (Second Proclamation Order No. IV of 1978). Therefore, the provision for referendum was basically made not by an Act of Parliament but by some external agency' and extraneous authority like Martial Law Proclamation although the Parliament ratified the said provision by the Constitution (Fifth Amendment) Act 1979 which is now part of the Constitution. One of the four pillars or main fundamental principles of state policy of the Constitution, namely, Secularism, was deleted by the Proclamation Order No. 1 of 1977 which is called the Proclamation (Amendment) Order, 1977. By the same Proclamation Socialism, another pillar, was given different attribution meaning economic and social justice. Such change or destruction of the basic structures of the Constitution has been ratified by the Constitution (Fifth Amendment) Act 1979. Nobody challenged that amendment.

55. Four fundamental principles of state policy, otherwise called the four pillars of the Constitution, were enunciated in original Article 8 of the Constitution of 1972, viz, Nationalism, Socialism, Democracy and Secularism. Those are the four pillars and main fundamental principles of the Constitution and the principles which are derived from them are also known as fundamental principles of state policy and basic structure and feature of the Constitution. Article 8 as incorporated in the original Constitution of 1972 in Part-Il was as follows:

"8.(1) The principles of Nationalism, Socialism, Democracy and Secularism together with the principles derived from them as set out in this part, shall constitute the fundamental principles of state policy."

56. The principles derived from the four main principles as were set out shall also constitute the fundamental principles. Article II in the present form incorporated in Part-Il is as follows:

"11. The Republic shall be a democracy in which fundamental human rights and freedoms and 'respect for the dignity and worth of the human person shall be guaranteed and in which effective participation by the people through their elected representatives in administration at all levels shall be ensured."

Article 11 speaks about democracy and human rights. Democracy as one of main pillars is there in Article 8, and human rights which is called the fundamental human rights as declared and adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 10 December, 1948 are incorporated in Part-III of our Constitution under heading Fundamental Rights. Since the fundamental human rights are derived from Article 8 the entire Part-Ill of the Constitution under heading Fundamental Rights comes within the meaning of basic structure or basic feature of the Constitution. I have already stated that one of the four pillars, namely, secularism, was deleted and socialism was changed by giving a meaning thereof by proclamation of Martial Law Order and that has now become a part of the Constitution by Act of Parliament and there has been no challenge of that on the ground of unconstitutionality.

Article 65 of the Constitution reads as under:

"65(1) There shall be a Parliament for Bangladesh (to be known as the House of the Nation) in which subject to the provisions of this Constitution, shall be vested the legislative powers of the Republic.

In destroying two main features or pillars of the Constitution the legislative powers of the Parliament under Article 65 have not been exercised. The House of the Nation only ratified the Acts done under the Martial Law Proclamation.

57. 13th Amendment as enacted by the Parliament is the product of political stress and crisis. Major political parties and also the small parties struggled for a system where all citizens, may he be an indigent under-privileged and a citizen having enough wealth and power, will have the equal opportunity to exercise his voting power to elect representatives of his or their own choice in the election of the Parliament. What was experienced by the political parties and citizens of the country is that intimidation, coercion, undue influence perpetrated by the party in power hampered the normal process of election, the freedom of the citizen to express their will by ballot papers which ultimately gave a death blow to democracy, the basic feature of the Constitution. The popular demand through long political stress and crisis was ultimately accepted and conceded to by the party in power representing the people of vast multitude and that led to the Parliament to legislate the enactment, namely, the 13th Amendment Act. Theoretically also, it is based on the general will of the people as the people's demand or popular demand was accepted and people agreed to adopt and practice the system as envisaged in the 13th Amendment. No segment of people opposed it. It was enacted to consolidate democracy. It was introduced in the Constitution to strengthen the democratic process, to achieve better democracy, so the impugned Act is in aid of democracy not in derogation of democracy as enshrined in the Constitution. If after dissolution of Parliament general election to Parliament is held under the party Government or in the system that existed in the Constitution the voting power may be monopolised by a sectional interest or interests at the expense of the rest of the citizens.

58. Win in the election of particular candidate or party by foul means viz, by manipulation, coercion, intimidation and exerting undue influence upon the Government machineries is a defeat of democracy, destruction of democracy which is the fundamental structure of the Constitution for which our martyrs shed their blood with aspiration that they will get a society free from all kinds of exploitation and their fundamental right will be ensured. In the preamble of the Constitution it has been recited that the people of Bangladesh having proclaimed independence and through a historic war for national independence pledged that it shall be a fundamental aim of the state to realise the democratic process of a socialist society, free from exploitation, a society in which the rule of law, fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice, political, economic and social, will be secured for all citizens.

59. Constitution is an identifiable document embodying selection of the most important rules about the Government of the country. All norms or rules may not be or cannot be incorporated even in the modem written Constitution. For practical convenience the people of the country or political parties representing all citizens may agree to a type of non-party caretaker Government as contemplated in Act 1 of 1996, for holding free, fair and impartial election through an independent Election Commission as provided in Part-VII of the Constitution even without amending the provisions of the Constitution.

60. If we trace back to the democracy of City State of Greece-there the whole body of citizens formed the assembly which was vested the supreme authority. Freedom and rule of law were the two aspects of the City State. The Athenians called "no man their master." Then comes the question of general will or will of the people as propagated by' Jean Jacques Rousseau in his Social Contract. The general will of the application of human freedom to political institution. The legislator is the engineer who invents the machine, the prince merely the mechanic who sets it up and makes it go. In a modem state in a nation of any size this principle has now been firmly established for choosing a certain number of agents or representatives who are numerous enough to speak for the whole people and few enough to meet at one place. The first essential of a democratic constitution is that the entire people must be represented in the legislature by their nominee to be elected periodically by them. The object being that the popular will should be reflected in the legislature. The same political concept is enunciated in Article 7 of our Constitution which says all powers in the republic belong to the people and the Constitution is the solemn expression of the will of the people. Before the 13th Amendment Act was passed when the struggle for achievement of non-party caretaker government was going on, the right thinking people of the country the intellectuals, the journalists, lawyers, educationists, other professionals, the civil society as a whole-supported the idea of non-party Caretaker Government because it was for the sake of democracy. If we really believe in democracy and want to practice democracy then what is the harm if certain provisions as laid down in Articles 48(3), 56 and 57(3) of the Constitution are suspended or kept in abeyance for a period of three months. Because the people wanted a system where democratic norms for free and fair election would be adhered to. Mr Attorney-General, at the very outset of his submission, quoted the age-old saying of President Abraham Lincoln of the United States: 'democracy is of the people, for the people and by the people.'

61. Now let me see how 13th Amendment has amended the provision of Articles 48(3) and 56 and also 57(3) as contended by the learned Counsel for the petitioner and whether the 13th Amendment has really amended certain provision of those Articles and Article 8. Article 48 is in the following terms.

"48. (1) There shall be a President of Bangladesh who shall be elected by Members of Parliament in accordance with law.

(2) The President shall, as Head of State, take precedence over all other persons in the State, and shall exercise the power and perform the duties conferred and imposed on him by this Constitution and by any other law.

(3) In the exercise of all his functions, save only that of appointing the Prime Minister pursuant to clause (3) of Article 56 and' the Chief Justice pursuant to clause (1) of Article 95, the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister."

Provided that the question whether any, and if so what, advice has been tendered by the Prime Minister to the President shall not be enquired into in any Court.

It has been contended pointing out clause (3) of Article 48 of the Constitution that during the period of non-party caretaker Government the provision that the President shall in the exercise of all his functions save appointment of Prime Minister and the Chief Justice act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister who is elected democratically by the people will be completely negated, when chapter IIA will come into operation the advisory function of the Prime Minister, which is the constitutional dispensation, will no longer exist even for a limited period affecting the democratic method of governance and principle of democracy.

Article 56 is as follows:

"56. (1) There shall be a Prime Minister, and such other Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers as may be determined by the Prime Minister.

(2) The appointments of the Prime Minister and other Ministers and of the Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers shall be made by the President.

Provided that no less than nine-tenths of their number shall be appointed from among members of Parliament and not more than one- tenth of their number may be chosen from among persons qualified for election as members of Parliament.

(3) The President shall appoint as Prime Minister the member of Parliament who appears to him to command the support of the majority of the members of Parliament.

(4) If occasion arises for making any appointment under clause (2) or clause (3) between a dissolution of Parliament and the next following general election of members of Parliament, the persons who were such members immediately before the dissolution shall be regarded for the purpose of this clause as continuing to be such members.

Mr Farooqui has, on Articles 56 and 57 of the Constitution, emphatically argued that by the 13th Amendment Act the democratically elected Prime Minister, who is elected representative of the people and who is supposed to hold the office until his successor enters upon the office as per clause (3) of Article 57, will cease to function and the whole cabinet will be replaced by a non-elected body namely, the caretaker government, which is against the concept of democracy, the fundamental feature of the Constitution. Further, he has specifically referred to clause (4) of Article 56 and argued that between a dissolution of parliament and the next following general election of members of parliament the members immediately before dissolution shall have the right to continue to be such members but because of the 13th Amendment such members who are elected by the people will lose their membership much ahead of time schedule which is also against the Constitutional dispensation so far as it relates to the rights of the elected members. Argument has been put forward pointing out clause (3) of Article 57 of the Constitution which was obviously not the subject of reference.

62. Article 57 provides that the office of Prime Minister shall become vacant if he resigns from office, if he ceases to become member of Parliament, if the Prime Minister ceases to retain the support of a majority of the members of Parliament he shall advise the President to dissolve the Parliament and the President shall dissolve the Parliament if no other member commands the support of the majority.

Clause (3) says that nothing in this Article shall disqualify the Prime Minister for holding office until his successor has entered upon office.

Mr Farooqui, therefore, has argued that even if the office of Prime Minister falls vacant for the aforesaid reason but the Prime Minister could continue to hold office until his/her successor has entered upon office. Thus, the formation of nonparty caretaker Government under Act I of 1996 shall impede the democratic process and he argues that Article 58B has in effect amended the provision of clause (3) of Article 57.

63. Now let me see what is the trial and test of amendment of any provision of law or provision of the Constitution. One of the tests is that when a particular provision of law or the Constitution is amended by way of addition, alteration or substitution that amended portion shall have its stability and permanence, and until that amended provision is further amended that will remain there in the Statute and the Constitution. To remove the amended provision further amendment by Act of Parliament is required. Provisions of Articles 48(3), 56 and 57(3) will be there in the Constitution only those provisions will be suspended and will remain ineffective during the operation of Articles 58B-58E as introduced by the impugned amendment for a limited period. 13th Amendment has neither added any new provisions to those Articles nor altered the existing provisions thereof; it will merely keep certain provision ineffective for a limited period. The Chapter IIA under heading Non-party Caretaker Government containing Articles 58B to Article 58E as inserted in a constitutional mechanism and under that mechanism some provision of the aforesaid Articles will be suspended and will again come into operation after the general election to the Parliament is held and new elected government enters upon the office. 13th Amendment as respect caretaker Government itself will remain completely ineffective and all other provisions of the Constitution will be in full force and operation after the formation of the elected government. And under the mechanism the process of suspension and operation will be going on until the 13th Amendment is deleted from the Constitution. The 13th Amendment is an apparatus set in the body of the Constitution and that apparatus during the period of 90 days will regulate certain provisions of the Constitution i.e. it will keep certain provision ineffective and after general election and constitution of a new Parliament the apparatus itself will become inoperative and the Articles contained in Chapter IIA will remain as dead articles until the dissolution of Parliament for the purpose of holding general election. 13th Amendment introducing non- party caretaker Government is a peculiar and novel political contrivance, and it is an unprecedented legislation in our legislative history since the framing of our Constitution. It is the outcome of the consensus of the political parties now accepted by the people of the country. It is a system where the little man of Churchill, as quoted in the passage, paragraph 109 in the matter Special Reference No. 1 of 2002 (Gujarat Assembly Election Matter) reported in (2002) 8 SCC 23, J feels secure to go out of his home freely to the polling booth and can have the ballot paper to cross on it or to seal it according to his choice and what was the prime object of the impugned legislation enacted by the Parliament.

64. Now comes the question, whether the 13th Amendment has impaired the independence of judiciary, axiomatically, independence of Judiciary is one of the basic features of our Constitution. To make it independent in truest sense and also in the subordinate courts level provision has been laid down under Article 22 of the Constitution.

Article 22 is as follows:

"22. The State shall ensure the separation of the judiciary from the executive organs of the State."

In line with the above principle and spirit of the Constitution the Hon'ble Supreme Court, Appellate Division gave twelve directives in the case of Secretary, Ministry of Finance vs Md Masdar Hossain and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) 82. The directives are yet to be implemented.

65. In the scheme of the impugned legislation it is well thought out plan which is based on the political consensus that a retired Chief Justice shall hold the office of Chief Adviser and in case of non availability of such person alternatives are, mentioned there in the relevant articles. The relevant portion of Article 58C is quoted below.

"58C(3) The President shall appoint as Chief Adviser the person who among the retired Chief Justices of Bangladesh retired last and who is qualified to be appointed as an Adviser under this Article;

Provided that if such retired Chief Justice is not available or is not willing to hold the office of Chief Adviser, the President shall appoint as Chief Adviser the person who among the retired Chief Justices of Bangladesh retired next before the last retired Chief Justice.

(4) If no retired Chief Justice is available or willing to hold the office of Chief Adviser, the President shall appoint as Chief Adviser the person who among the retired Judges of the Appellate Division retired last and who is qualified to be appointed as an Adviser under this Article.

Provided that if such retired Judge is not available or is not willing to hold' the office of Chief Adviser, the President shall appoint as Chief Adviser the person who among the retired Judges of the Appellate Division retired next before the last such retired Judge.

(5) If no retired Judge of the Appellate Division is available or willing to hold the office of Chief Adviser, the President shall after consultation as far as practicable with the major political parties, appoint the Chief Adviser from among citizens of Bangladesh who are qualified to be appointed as Advisers under this Article."

Keeping the above provision in view, the words or the office of Chief Adviser or Adviser were inserted in Article 99 of the Constitution by Act 1 of 1996. I have already stated that the whole legislation which is under challenge is the outcome of the consensus of the political parties. Then that was enacted by the representatives of the people. It is the highest expectation and supreme confidence of the people and also it is the constitutionally provided ethos that a retired Chief Justice or a retired Judge of the Appellate Division having held such highly exalted position under oath must reaffirm the people's faith in them and they are supposed to be most impartial and independent persons to hold the office of Chief Adviser. A Judge becomes independent when he is impartial. In the panel the persons who were regarded as impartial and independent personality Chief Justice was put in the first place in the formation of non-party caretaker Government. A retired Chief Justice after his retirement going out of his office is not likely to influence the judiciary in any manner. Argument has been advanced that this position is an allurement and the Chief Justice also for some reason may be influenced by the highest executive and become partisan in running the administration of caretaker Government. Firstly, my consideration would be that ecclesiastically, the Chief Justice or any Judge of the Appellate Division is far from any misgivings and they are free and should be free from any temptation. Egalitarian point of view is that the command and source of power of a Judge of such high profile is the will of the people and that is why trust was reposed upon them. Besides, under Article 118 of the Constitution it is provided that there shall be an Election Commission and the Election Commission shall be independent in the exercise of its functions. The non-party caretaker government in exercise of the executive functions of the Republic shall assist the Election Commission to hold the free and fair election. The Election Commission must be made more powerful and independent by making appropriate legislation. If it is innate in any retired Chief Justice or any Judge as mentioned above and if for any reason the prospective Chief Adviser feels that he has any bias towards a particular political party for which he may wish a particular political party to win the election in that case he should not accept the office of Chief Adviser of the non-party caretaker Government because such bias or leaning will frustrate the will of the people and the concept of caretaker Government. Mr Amirul Islam, in his submission, suggested that there should be certain reformation and development in the system and in the panel some other persons may also be included according to the consensus of the political parties so that in case of controversy about the appointment, the non- party caretaker Government may be headed not by the retired Chief Justice but by any other independent, impartial and non-partisan personality. That can again be done according to the consensus of the major political parties as indicated in clause (5) of Article 58C.

66. Mr Rafique-ul-Huq,the learned Amicus Curiae, has expressed his opinion on clause (1 A) of Article 142 of the Constitution and he said that insertion of clause CIA) in Article 142 is a fraud upon the Constitution. Therefore, insertion of such provision in Article 142 of the Constitution although is not void but voidable. The issue whether Clause (1A) of Article 142 is void or voidable cannot be determined in this reference.

67. About the destruction of the basic structure of the Constitution, I have already observed that in original Article 8 of the Constitution of 1972 under heading 'Fundamental principles of State Policy' there were four pillars of the Constitution, nationalism, socialism, democracy and secularism Article 8, as it stands now, reads thus:

"The principles of absolute trust and faith in the Almighty Allah, nationalism, democracy and socialism meaning economic and social justice, together with the principles derived from them as set out in this Part, shall constitute the fundamental principles of state policy."

<u>68. By Martial Law Proclamation (Amendment) Order, 1977 Proclamation Order No. 1 of 1977, one of the pillars of the Constitution, namely, secularism, was deleted and socialism although was not deleted but that was given a different connotation meaning economic and social justice and that deletion of one of four pillars of the Constitution and alteration of another one were not done by the legislative act as envisaged under Articles 65 and Article 142 of the Constitution. By the Martial Law Proclamation one of the main pillars of the Constitution was destroyed and such destruction of basic pillar' or the basic structure by Martial Law Proclamation was done by the Second Proclamation (Fifth Amendment) Order, 1978 (Second Proclamation Order No. IV of 1978) and that proclamation order or orders was ratified and confirmed by the Constitution (Fifth Amendment) Act 1979 and that was made part of the Constitution, Clause (1A) came in the same way and that was inserted in Article 142 of the Constitution by the Act of Parliament by amendment by way of ratification. The insertion was basically not the legislative act, because the legislative power is vested in the Parliament to be known as the house of nation, But the Parliament had no power under Article 142 of the Constitution to change the basic structures. The principle expounded in Constitution 8th Amendment case, Anwar Hossain vs Bangladesh is that the structural pillars or basic structures of the Constitution established by the framers of the Constitution cannot be altered by the simple exercise of amending power. Nobody has up till now challenged such destruction of the basic features of the Constitution. This Court cannot amend the provisions of the Constitution. The unconstitutionality of legislative enactment or changing of main pillars or basic structure by Parliament can only be struck down if it is challenged by any citizen of the country. In the 5th Amendment Act, 1979 in the fourth schedule after paragraph 17 paragraph 18 was added under the title Ratification and Confirmation of Proclamations and all Proclamations, Proclamation Orders, Martial Law Regulations, Martial Law Orders and other laws made during the period between the 15th August, 1975, and the 9th April, 1979 (both days inclusive), all amendments, additions, modifications, sub- situations and omissions made in this Constitution during the said period by any such Proclamation, etc were ratified.</u>

<u>69. With the ratification and confirmation the constitutional amendment including amendment of Article 8 of the Constitution was done by the Martial Law Proclamation and that was ratified by Acts of Parliament. Whether the Parliament had such authority to ratify the constitutional amendment made by Martial Law Authority changing the basic pillars of the Constitution will be decided by the citizens of the country, by the future generation. But the legislature constituted by the people's representatives can again, by way of amendment, restore the basic pillars of the Constitution according to the provision of the Constitution. In the case of Mr AYBl Siddiqui and another vs Mr Abdur Rahim Khan and others reported in 2001 BLD 75 it was contended that the Parliament is not authorised to ratify the law which is not enacted according to the provision of the Constitution and consequently, the Parliament is not authorised to ratify the laws made under the Proclamation of Martial Law. In support of the proposition, reliance was placed in the case of Miss Asma Jilani vs Government of Punjab and another reported in PLD 1972(SC) 139 where Hamoodur Rahman CJ observed that person who destroys the national legal order in an illegitimate manner cannot be regarded as a valid source of law making. May be that on account of his holding the coercive apparatus of the state the people and the court are silenced temporarily, but let it be laid down firmly that the order which usurper imposed will remain illegal and courts will not recognise its rule and act upon them as de jure.</u>

<u>It was further observed that in a democratic polity when a country is run and governed by the Constitution only the constitutional authority can make legislation and the Martial Law Authority cannot be the valid source of legislation.</u>

70. The Parliament has the plenary power to alter, amend or repeal the law as projected in paragraph 18 of the said Fourth Schedule which has destroyed the basic structure of the Constitution and the laws which are inconsistent with Article 7 of the Constitution.

In view of the above discussion as I have already concurred with the decision given by my learned brother on the main issue, I do not find that the 13th Amendment has amended any provision of the Constitution and, as such, Act I of 1996 was not required to be referred to a referendum as contemplated in clause (1 A) of Article 142 of the Constitution.

Mirza Hussain Haider J: While agreeing with the decision already arrived at by my brothers in this matter, I would like to add a few words of my own.

72. Since the relevant facts and background of this reference have already been discussed in the main judgment and since all the contentions of the learned Advocates for the parties, including the two learned amici curiae, have been carefully considered by my learned brothers, it is not necessary to repeat the same.

73. The Bill placed before the 6th Parliament incorporated Article 58 (A) in Chapter II and a new Chapter, namely, Chapter IIA embodying Article 58B to 58E, under the heading "Non-party Caretaker Government" in the Constitution of Bangladesh. By the said incorporation some of the Articles of the Constitution have been made ineffective during the tenure of the non-party care-taker Government. The bill which was unanimously passed is commonly known as the Thirteenth Amendment.

74. The main contention of Mr Farooqui, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, is that the Thirteenth Amendment (13th Amendment) has affected other Articles including Articles 48, 56, 99 and also the Preamble of the Constitution, which refers to "Democracy" as one of the fundamental principles of the Constitution. Thus being a basic feature of the Constitution it cannot be amended. As such, the failure to comply with the procedure prescribed in Article 142(1A) has rendered the said amendment ultra vires the Constitution.

75. On the other hand, the learned Advocates appearing on behalf of the respondents in one voice contended that the 13th Amendment has not amended the provisions mentioned in Article 142(1A); rather, it has made some Articles ineffective for a certain period. According to them, in view of its temporal nature and for a particular purpose, it is not an amendment for which the procedure prescribed in Article 142(1A) could be attracted. The two amici curiae, Mr Rafiq-ul-Hoque and Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, also expressed their valued opinion supporting the amendment.

76. The learned Advocates for the respondents further submitted that the amendment has not affected any basic structure/feature of the Constitution. According to them, "democracy", which is claimed to be one of the basic features of the Constitution has not been amended; on the contrary, its process and practice has been strengthened by the amendment in question.

77. Upon hearing the learned Advocates appearing for their respective parties, we are impelled to examine first what 'Democracy', in fact, is. Abraham Lincoln said 'democracy meant the government of the people, by the people and for the people'. Justice Matthew said 'democracy means the rule of majority'. Sir Ivor Jennings’s understanding of democracy is 'the vesting of the political power in free and fair election.' Thus, democracy and free and fair election are inseparable twins. Upon considering the above notions, it can be said that 'Democracy' is the rule of majority elected by the people upon exercising their voting rights in a free and fair election for the betterment of the people. Undoubtedly, election is the process by which the majority can be determined. A pre-condition to achieving that goal is the free and fair exercise of the "people's will". Democracy becomes meaningful only when a man, no matter how small his power is, can cast his "vote" "freely" in a "fair election". What is crucial is to enable the small man to come to the polling center, enter the small room and exercise his right of franchise by putting a mark in the ballot paper freely without any influence or pressure. The question is, whether the all-important person, i.e. the said small man, "the voter", can exercise his constitutional right freely and fairly without any inducement, fear, influence or under any compelling circumstances. If he cannot, then the whole process of the 'rule of majority' becomes meaningless. Thus, to practice democracy and to give it an institutional shape, it is imperative that periodic, free and fair elections are conducted. In the absence of free, fair and periodic election democracy becomes meaningless.

78. In the case of Gujarat Assembly Election Matter, (Special Reference No. 1 of 2002 (8 SCC (2002) 237}, Justice Pasayat, while delivering the judgment observed that “elections conducted at regular, prescribed intervals is essential to democracy as envisaged in the Constitution. So is the need to protect and sustain the purity of the electoral process. That may take within it the quality, efficacy and adequacy of the machinery for resolution of electoral disputes'. Thus, free, fair, impartial and periodic election may constitute a basic structure of the Constitution. All these are needed for expressing a voter's right of choice, freely in a fair election.

79. In this respect we are to look back and see the history of democracy as practiced in our country. After the British Rule, India was divided into two parts on the basis of religion of the majority people. Accordingly, India and Pakistan were created in 1947. Both the countries, subsequently, framed their own constitutions and in their own way they started practicing democracy. India continued with the parliamentary system of democracy but Pakistan experienced different forms of government, including supra constitutional power like Martial Law government, on various occasions. However, after the emergence of Bangladesh as a sovereign state, the then constituent assembly enacted, adopted and gave a Constitution on the 4th day of November, 1972 which is baptised by the blood of the martyrs. The said Constitution promised economic and social justice in a society wherein rule of law, fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice were assured. It has further given a guideline as to how a government is to be formed by the people's representatives elected in a free and fair election. Subsequently, with the passage of time the process of free and fair election suffered numerous setbacks and obstructions on various occasions for various reasons. However, against one of such governments, which came to power in an unconstitutional way through an undemocratic process, country-wide popular upsurge began for overthrowing the same and for giving democracy an institutional shape in its true meaning. The then President was compelled to tender resignation in the face of the said mass upsurge in 1990.

80. It is evident from history that the people of this country never compromised for the cause of establishing their rights. They never hesitated to render extreme sacrifice on occasions, whether it was for the cause of language, independence or democracy. After the historic success in 1990, the people, irrespective of their religion, class, political affiliation or profession under the banner of the then three main political alliances made an ardent call to the then Chief Justice of Bangladesh to hold the reins of a neutral and impartial government as its head for running an impartial office to establish a democratic government through a free, fair and impartial election to the Parliament. With the whole purpose of restoring democracy, for giving it an institutional shape through free and fair election, the then Chief Justice of Bangladesh' in response to the people's call assumed the office of the President of the country for running an interim Government for holding a free, fair election of the Parliament. Accordingly, general election was held in 1991 under the said non-party caretaker government peacefully. The concept proved successful. Subsequently, the party securing majority seats in the parliament formed the government pursuant to the free, fair and impartial election held on 27-2- 1991 under the non-party interim government, and was in office for almost its full term of 5 (five) years for the first time in the history of the country.

81. Thereafter, certain incidents, as described in the writ petition, prompted the nation to consider afresh the concept of holding election under a non- party caretaker government, which would never influence the election or its result and accordingly, proposals were made by the civil society to amend the Constitution. The Magura by-election and its aftermath followed by mass resignation of all the opposition party members of the 5th Parliament and the consequent holding of the 6'h parliamentary election on 15-2-1996 under the supervision of the party in power, Which was boycotted by all the political parties, proved that free, fair and impartial election cannot be held under the supervision of the ruling party because of their abuse of power and use of money and muscle. Conspiracy rigging and intimidation was resorted to on a massive scale to win a seat in the Parliament which resulted in the common people losing their interest and confidence in the electoral process. Such election became questionable for the reasons of unnecessary and excessive use of muscle, money and power against which country-wide agitation and violence erupted which almost paralysed the country. The political parties understood that without free, fair and impartial election the actual verdict of the people is impossible to be established. Under such situation the people of the country through their elected representatives in the parliament came up with an acceptable solution of holding election under the supervision of impartial caretaker government-and accordingly, the 13th Amendment Bill was placed in the 6th Parliament for incorporating the provision of "Non-party Caretaker Government in the Constitution for holding free, fair and impartial election for the members in the parliament. Side by side, the other political parties continued agitating for a caretaker government outside the Parliament. Representations were also made' to the President to form a caretaker government forthwith. They also continued their mass movement to pull down the government elected in February 1996. Upon placing the 13th Amendment Bill in the Parliament the then members of parliament held long and continuous debates on the said bill and ultimately, passed the same on 25-3-1996 and the 13th Amendment became a part of the Constitution.

82. On 30-6-1996 the 6th Parliament was dissolved and, according to the new provision of the Constitution the President invited the immediate retired Chief Justice of the country to be sworn in as the Chief Adviser, the head of the "non-party caretaker Government" which apparently brought an end to the two-year-long political crisis and a deadlock in the country. The political parties withdrew all their programmers of non-cooperation movement on the formation of the non-party caretaker Government and expressed their solidarity and readiness to join the election under the new system. So long the idea and attitude of grabbing or retaining power by anti-democratic means like mob, muscle, money and power were impeding the process of free, fair and impartial election, which is a sine qua non of Democracy, and the term Democracy remained a far-fetched and elusive object, like a twinkling star on the horizon.

83. From the above it appears that the crisis of creating congenial atmosphere in holding free and fair election was created by the political parties and the political parties have themselves come forward with the solution for overcoming the same through the constitutional process of "non-party caretaker Government." With such amendment, free-will of the people for exercising their fundamental right of casting vote in the general election, has contributed to the establishment of democracy in its true meaning. As such, the people of Bangladesh with such amendment came up with a popular slogan আমার ভোট আমি দিব যাকে খুশি তাকে দিব।  I Thus It appears that the people have accepted the concept of non-party caretaker Government" which has given the real meaning to the term "Democracy" and the democratic process as a whole. The crisis thus created in the political arena in practicing democracy, has been solved. Consequently two general elections namely 7th and 8th general elections, for the Parliament have been held under the new system and the democratic government elected by the people on exercising their rights freely, fairly and impartially has been running the country for their full terms.

<u>84. Sir lvor Jennings rightly said that in democracy political power rests in free elections. Thus for the sake of practicing democracy necessary amendments can be made in the Constitution in the case of Kesavananda Bharati vs State of Kerala reported in (1973) 4 SCC 225, by majority view democracy has been treated as a basic feature of the Constitution. Justice Jaganmohan Reddy explicitly considered parliamentary democracy as part of the basic structure. Former Chief Justice of India Justice Subba Rao reiterated the saying "responsible government through parliamentary executive is part of the Constitution." More recently in the case of PV Narasimha Rao vs State reported in (1998) 4 SCC 626, 673 para 47 Justice SC Agrawal, observed that . 'parliamentary democracy is a part of the basic structure of the Constitution which cannot be altered. But improvement of the system alone is 'permissible.' Thus, the concept of basic structure of the Constitution being an imprecise and elastic concept was kept open by several jurists. So, even if democracy is' taken as a basic structure of the Constitution the 13th Amendment cannot be said to be ultra vires since improvement, which is permissible, has been brought in the' system. We are to realise even at this distance of time how to work successfully with the democratic process making minimal changes necessary in the provisions relating to election. In Golaknath vs State of Punjab reported in (1967) 2 SCR 762 (918) Justice RS Bachawat observed "A static system of law is the worst tyranny that any Constitution can impose upon a country. An unamend able Constitution means that all reforms and progress are at a standstill." If democracy accepted as a basic structure of the Constitution, then free and fair election is also a part of it. Without free and fair election democracy can never be practiced in its true sense. So, it can rightly be said that free and fair election is an essential postulate of democracy and one of the fundamental aims of our society enshrined in the Preamble of the Constitution. It appears that the 13th Amendment has actually strengthened and improved the system of holding free, fair and impartial elections by which the people can exercise their fundamental rights freely in electing the government. Thus, it cannot be said to have affected the basic feature of the Constitution.</u>

85. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned amicus curiae and Mr M Amirul Islam the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 6 categorically submitted that "Article 142(1)( a )(i) of the Constitution provides "No Bill for such amendment shall be allowed to proceed unless the long title thereof expressly states that it will amend a provision of the Constitution." The long title of the 13th Amendment does not show that it has affected any of the basic structures of the Constitution or any other provision, namely, Articles 8, 48 or 56 or the Preamble as contemplated in Article 142(1A), Article 142(lA) clearly says that for amendment of the Preamble or Articles 8,48 or 56 of the Constitution a referendum is required, Neither the long title nor the amendment itself shows that there is any breach of the provision of Article 142 as a whole. Previously, Article 142(1A) contained that in the event of any amendment made in Articles 8, 48, 56, 58, 80, 92A or 142 and the Preamble, the President would be required to refer the bill for referendum. But Articles 58, 80 and 92A have been omitted from Article 142(1A) by the 12th Amendment Act 1991. It is the common view of the jurists that every word of a constitutional instrument must be given effect to; no word, as a general rule, should be rendered meaningless or inoperative. So, the present provision of Article 142 must be followed strictly. Thus, it appears that unless amendment is brought in the Preamble or in Articles 8, 48, 56 or 142 itself by mentioning the same in the long title, there is no necessity of referring the bill for referendum. In the present case, there being no mention of any of those provisions in the long title, the provision of referendum as in Article 142(1A) cannot be attracted.

86. The concept of interim Caretaker government is inherent in our Constitution and in most of the countries where democracy is in practice, particularly in the sub-continent when the parliament is dissolved and till the next parliament is formed the concept of Caretaker Government is provided for in the Constitution. Mr Abdur Razzaque, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondent No.5, in this regard took us through several provisions of the Indian Constitution wherein the Prime Minister or the Chief Minister is called upon to form the interim Government for a limited period when the Parliament is dissolved. Similar provisions exist in the Pakistan Constitution. Upon reading Articles 50(1), 56(3)(4), 57(2)(3), 58(3)(4), 65(2), 72(2)(3) (4) and 141(1A) of our Constitution what is derived is that the outgoing Prime Minister who lost his/her character as an elected representative immediately with the dissolution of the parliament continues to hold office along with the members of the outgoing cabinet till the successor i.e. the next elected government, enters upon the office by the next election. Such continuation being for a temporary period is in the shape of interim care-taker government, notwithstanding the fact that the outgoing Prime Minister and the cabinet lose their character as the people's representatives but they continue to retain their affiliation with their party. Moreover, they are also eligible to participate in the ensuing election. So, holding of an election impartially, free from influence or power under a partisan government becomes a remote proposition. It has been stated earlier that since the political parties fond it difficult to hold free and fair election under the supervision of the partisan government, they came out with the solution of forming a 'non- party Caretaker Government' to ensure impartiality and eliminate partisanship in holding the same freely and fairly, by the 13th Amendment for the purpose of strengthening democracy, its process and practice. Otherwise, the whole democratic process and/or the system would be destroyed.

87. Again, upon perusing the amendment it appears that by incorporating Article 58(E), Article 48(3) has been kept ineffective during the period of 90 days of the "non-party Caretaker Government" i.e. with the entrance of the newly elected government into its office Article 48(3) automatically becomes effective. Similar is the case in respect of Articles 56(4) and 57(3). Thus by no means it can be said that the Preamble or Articles 8, 48 or 56 have been amended by the 13th Amendment for which Article 142(1A) can be attracted as claimed by Mr Farooqui. Article 142 gives power to amend any provision by way of addition, alteration, substitution or repeal which are merely modes of amendment. Amendment means a change in some of the provisions of a statute in whole or in part or something being added to or taken from it or is in some way changed or altered in order to make the provision amended more meaningful and effective. In the present case, the system of interim caretaker government being already provided in the Constitution, the 13th Amendment has brought positive changes in the said existing system for holding free, fair and impartial elections for the Parliament. When the Constitution is amended it is the result of political consensus of the people agreeing on certain points through their elected representatives. A Constitution is meant to be permanent but as all changing situations cannot be anticipated or envisaged, amendments may be necessary to adapt to future developments; provisions are thus made in the Constitution itself to respond to the dynamics of the changing circumstances. When a legislature, which is creature of the Constitution, is given the power of amendment, it is a power given not to subvert the Constitution, but to make it suitable to the changing situations. .The background of the 13th Amendment clearly shows that the same was required under the changed circumstances for giving a complete meaning of democracy and also for making the existing provisions of interim caretaker government meaningful and more effective.

88. Mr Bhuiyan rightly submitted that Chapter II and IIA are alternative to each other. One will exist in the absence of the other. When one operates the other remains suspended. The concept of suspension of certain Articles of the Constitution including the enforcement of fundamental rights, has already been provided explicitly in the Constitution itself under certain situation, as in Article 141 Band C of Chapter IXA of the Constitution. So, keeping certain provision ineffective or suspended for a particular period, for the sake of the others and thereby allowing the people to exercise their fundamental rights of electing the democratic government freely and fairly cannot be termed as unconstitutional. The functions of the non-party caretaker Government as envisaged in Article 58D of Chapter IIA, are two- fold (I) to discharge its functions as an interim government and to perform the routine functions of such government and, except in case of necessity of discharging of such functions, it shall not make any policy decision and (II) to render all possible aid and assistance that may be required to hold the general election of the Parliament peacefully, fairly and impartially; which has been proved to be futile and not possible under the partisan interim government described under Articles 57(3) and 58(4). The whole purpose of the 13th Amendment is to give the people a Constitutional safeguard for exercising their right of franchise freely without any application of force, inducement, duress or threat in selecting the people who will form the government for the next term.

89. On Article 99 of the Constitution Mr Rafiq-ul-Hoque and Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the two learned amici curiae, expressed their valued opinion. According to Mr Bhuiyan, by inserting the words "or the office of the Chief Adviser" in the said Article it cannot be said that the office of the Chief Justice or the independence of the judiciary as a whole has been put into question. He contends that no such question can arise because the Chief Justice after his retirement from the said office would become the Chief Adviser provided he is available or willing to hold the said post. Original Article 99 did not contain any provision for retired judges to plead before any Court or hold any office of profit in the service of the Republic not being a judicial or quasi-judicial office. By the 2nd Proclamation (15th Amendment) Order 1978 the retired judges of the High Court Division were allowed to plead before the Appellate Division and the retired judges of the Supreme Court were allowed to hold office of profit in the service of the Republic. Mr Farooqui's submission that by amending Article 99 through 13th Amendment "the judges are being allured' is thus not tenable since it was the earlier amendments which had allowed the retired judges to hold office of profit, not the 13th Amendment. By merely adding the words, or the office of Chief Adviser or Adviser" in Article 99 it cannot be said that the 13th Amendment has brought about an allurement for the judges or interference in the independence of the judiciary.

90. Mr Rafiq-ul-Haque, opined that the Chief Justice, while in his office, cannot be allured nor can be appointed as Chief Adviser, the question of such appointment arises only when he retires from that office. It is the office of the Chief Justice upon whom faith and trust of the people rests. Thus, a person having held the position of Chief Justice he is ideally suited for the independent, impartial and trustworthy office of the Chief Adviser of the impartial non-party caretaker Government and has thus been selected for holding the said office. In this, connection Mr Rafiq-ul Haque produced before us the copies of the text of the Debate on 13th Amendment Bill in the Parliament wherein it has been categorically emphasised by all the members present that 'the judicial system of the country and the judiciary is always impartial and the judiciary is performing its duty impartially. As such, an impartial non-party car-taker Government can only be headed by a person who had been heading the impartial judiciary, the Chief Justice of the country, upon whom the people have full trust and confidence'. The same view is also reflected in Appendix XIV (Act 24 of 1991) of the Constitution itself wherein an ardent call to the then Chief Justice of Bangladesh was made by all, regardless of their political affiliation, belief and leanings, to take and hold the reins of a neutral and impartial government formed for the purpose of holding a free, fair and impartial election to the Parliament. So, the words "trust", "faith" and "confidence" is always carried by the Judiciary, the office of the Chief Justice and the person holding such office.

91. Legal tradition concerning the vital role of maintaining the independence of judicial officers and assuring their capacity effectively to fulfill their duties which they assume upon their appointment rests upon the persons themselves who are appointed as judges. In situations which involve interpretation of law or giving a clear finding as to any Constitutional interpretation or for avoiding Constitutional deadlock, the Judiciary emerges as the most powerful wing of the State relative to the legislature or the executive.

92. In the case of Supreme Court Advocates- on-Record Association vs Union of India [4 SCC (1993)] 441 the Supreme Court of India mandated the Chief Justice to involve at least two of his senior-most colleagues in the process of selecting the candidates for appointment as judges. In Special Reference No.1 of 1998 [7 SCC (1998) 739] the Court opined that the Chief Justice of India should associate at least four of his senior colleagues instead of two in the matter of appointment of Judges. Thus, it appears that the appointment of Judges is of vital importance for maintaining the independence of judicial officers and assuring their capacity effectively to fulfill the duties. Justice SP Bharucha, while addressing the Advocate-General's Conference in May, 1999 observed, "Accumulation of unlimited power is one thing and exercising it with circumspection and self-restraint is an altogether different thing. Unless the dam is strong, the reservoir cannot retain water. We need extremely capable, honest and independent judges, nay statesmen, to handle this enormous power of judicial review in the interests of the people". Thus, while appointing judges in the higher judiciary it should be kept in mind the importance and gravity of the said high post and expectation of the nation. After a person is appointed a judge and takes oath to serve as such he/she progresses through a process of evolution over a period of time and eventually is moulded to be the person capable of holding any office or handing any situation requiring the highest standard of impartiality and integrity. Taking into consideration the above position in our neighbouring country, the appointment of judges in our country also should be made from amongst the most capable candidates irrespective of affiliation, caste, creed or gender and, in that process, the advice of the Chief Justice should be sought for in the manner as stated above since he is the person who knows best about the capability of the candidates.

93. However, the Parliament by its absolute majority having passed the amendment in question with full consent of all the political parties and appointment of the former Chief Justice as the head of the non-party Caretaker Government as the first option, the people through their representatives in the Parliament have expressed and reiterated their trust, faith and confidence in the judiciary as well as in the high post of Chief Justice as the symbol of fairness and impartiality. The device is created by the legislature and if any question is raised at all, it would be the duty of the legislature to come up with a different and better device to select or appoint an appropriate person in the key post of the Chief Adviser. Moreover, the 13th Amendment being already found to be Constitutional a part of it cannot be looked into separately.

94. The Election Commission created under the Constitution is a high constitutional authority charged with the duty of ensuring free, fair and impartial election and the purity of the electoral process. To effectuate the constitutional objective and purpose it is to draw upon all incidental and ancillary powers for holding free and fair election. Developments may also be made in this sector for its proper functioning depending on the required necessity. But man-made situation intended to defer or obstruct holding of free and fair election should be sternly dealt with. It seems that the process under which democracy was in practice in this country, free, fair and impartial election became a far cry for the people. Because of the situations prevailing in the electoral process and massive use of power, muscle and money, incorporation of the new chapter by the 13th Amendment was necessitated for holding election freely and fairly under the 'Non-party Caretaker Government'. It is a common saying "where law ends, tyranny begins". If the people cannot trust or keep faith on the partisan government or on the system in holding free, fair and impartial election then obviously an alternative is to be looked for. Benjamin Disraeli said, "That all power is trust-that we are accountable for its exercise; that from the people and for the people, all springs, and all must exist." Thus, it was found necessary to incorporate provisions for non-party Caretaker Government in our Constitution, which, in my opinion, is not unconstitutional.

For the reasons and discussions made hereinabove I hold that since none of the Articles mentioned in Article 142(1A) of the Constitution has been amended; since "Democracy", if it is called a basic structure of the Constitution, has not been affected, rather the same has been strengthened; and since by inserting certain words in Article 99 the independence of judiciary has not been affected, the 13th Amendment Act (Act No. I of 1996) was not required to be referred to referendum nor it is ultra vires the Constitution. With these insights I fully concur with the decision already arrived at in this reference.

End.
