Vs.
Chairman, First Court of Settlement and another -------- Respondents.
full_judgment:
SM Ziaul Karim J: By this Rule Nisi, the petitioner has challenged the legality and propriety of the judgment and order dated 29-5-1997 (Annexure-A), passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka, in Case No. 40 of 1995, excluding the holding No. 1-D/3-31, Mirpur, Dhaka, from the 'Ka' list of the abandoned properties.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule are that the petitioner is the People's Republic of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works. The Ministry deals, amongst others, with the management and control of the abandoned properties. The petitioner included the house No. 1-D/3-31, Mirpur, Dhaka, (hereinafter referred as case property), in the "Ka" list of abandoned properties, published in Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary, dated 23rd September, 1986, against serial No. 403. The case property is an abandoned property within the meaning of Article 2 of President's Order No. 16 of 1972. The Government controls and manages the case property by allotment to DN holder M Waziullah by issuing demand note to him. Subsequently, the case property was sold by the Government to him at a consideration of Taka 1,33,907 by a registered sale dated 19-12-1989. The claimant respondent No. 2, is not the son of the original lessee, Esamul. Therefore, the property was rightly declared as abandoned property.

3. The respondent No. 2, contested the case before the Court of Settlement, contending, inter alia, that the case property was leased out to Esamul by a registered lease deed dated 11-8-1961. He was a1through in possession of the case property. He died on 19-10-1974 leaving behind 4 sons and 3 daughters as heirs. Subsequently, the miscreants dispossessed the lessee Esamul by force, one year after independence in 1971. He approached to the different authorities for its restoration but with no effect. He along with his brothers and sisters are the nationals of Bangladesh as their father was. The case property is not an abandoned property. The Government wrongly included the same in the "Ka" list of the abandoned buildings. Thereafter, he filed the case No. 40 of 1995 in the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka, for releasing the case property, from the list of abandoned properties.

4. Eventually, after hearing the Court of Settlement by the judgment and order dated 29-5-1997, allowed the case and excluded the property from the list of abandoned properties holding, inter alia, that the Government could not show as to how the case property came under the control and management of the Government. There is no evidence in the Government file that the Government took over possession after complying with the mandatory provisions of Article 7 of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972. Therefore, the case property is not an abandoned property.

5. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid Judgment and order, the Government, as petitioner, preferred this Writ petition and obtained the present Rule.

6. Mr Md Jafar Imam, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, supports the Rule and submits that the original owner of the case property was not present in Bangladesh and whose whereabouts were not known after President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into operation. So, the property was rightly enlisted as abandoned property by operation of law. The learned Counsel adds that the Court of Settlement most erroneously shifted the onus upon the Government to prove that the case property is an abandoned property. In support of his contention the learned Counsel refers the case of Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works vs Md Jalil reported in 48 DLR (AD) 10 wherein it is held:

"The onus is on the claimants of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant."

7. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the concerned authorities rightly included the case property as abandoned property after President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into operation.

8. No one appears for the respondent No. 1.

9. Mr Syed Haider Ali, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 2, without filing any affidavit-in-opposition, opposes the Rule and submits, that the case property was leased out to the father of the respondent No. 2 by registered lease deed dated 11-8-1961 and since then he was in possession. His father died on 19-1-1974. After one year of the independence some miscreants dispossessed them from the case property, thereby the Government enlisted the same as abandoned property and listed in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the Government without any basis enlisted the property as abandoned property.

10. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels, we have gone through the writ petition as well as the other materials on record and given our anxious consideration to their submissions.

11. Now, the question which calls for our consideration is, whether, the Court of Settlement rightly excluded the case property from the list of abandoned properties.

12.  Admittedly, Esamul was the original lessee of the case property as per allotment order dated 12- 5-1961. Subsequently, deed of lease was registered in favour of him on 11-8-1961. It appears that after coming into force of Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972 i.e. President's Order No. 16 of 1972, the Government treated this property as abandoned property as defined in Article 2 of the said Order and the case property was listed as abandoned property in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings published ill the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary, dated September 23, 1986 against Serial No. 403.

13. The respondent No.2 claims that the case property was leased out to his father Esamul by a registered lease deed dated 11-8-1961. His father died leaving behind 4 sons and 3 daughters including him as heirs and they are Bangladeshi Nationals but Government wrongly enlisted the case property as abandoned property. The Government (herein petitioner) disowned such facts.

14. We find from record that the Court of Settlement in its judgment and order dated 29-5- 1997  (Ann(Annexure-A) categorically held that Esamul, the original lessee, died in Bangladesh leaving behind 4 sons and 3 daughters including respondent No.2 as heirs, who filed the case on behalf of the others.

15. It further appears to us that the Court of Settlement wrongly held that the Government failed to show as to how the case property came under its control and management.

16. This view of the Court of Settlement is absolutely erroneous, inasmuch as the Court of Settlement shifted from the cardinal question of facts, as to the whereabouts of Esamul after President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into operation on 16-2-1972. Moreover, the Court of Settlement shifted the onus upon the Government to prove that the case property is an abandoned property. It has been well settled that the duty upon the person, who claims that the property is not an abandoned property, to show that at the relevant time i.e. when President's Order No. 16 of 1972 came into force, the owner of the property was in Bangladesh and in possession of the property.

<u>17. On careful consideration of the materials on record we hold that the Court of Settlement, in our opinion, started with a wrong premise holding that the presumption of correctness of the entries in the Gazette Notification does not absolve the Government from denying the facts alleged by the claimant or from disclosing the basis of treating the property as abandoned property when it is disputed. Section 5(2) of the Ordinance clearly provides that the list published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned properties and have vested in the Government, as such. section 7 says that a person claiming any right or interest in any such building may make an application to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the building from such list, etc. on the ground that the building is not an abandoned building and has not vested in the Government under President's Order No. 16 of 1972 or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that Order. The onus, therefore, is squarely on the claimant of the building to prove that the building is not an abandoned property. The Government has no obligation either to deny the facts alleged by the claimant or to disclose the basis of treating the property as abandoned property merely because the same is disputed by the claimant.</u>

18. In the case of Rahima Begum liS Court of Settlement reported in 1997 BLD (AD) 118 = 2 ELC (AD) 108 wherein it is held:

"Once a building is in the list of abandoned properties it is conclusive evidence that the building in question is an abandoned property where the owner either was not present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were not known or he ceased to manage or occupy the property at the time when PO 16 of 1972 was promulgated on 16-2-1972. This presumption is, of course, a rebuttable one. It is for the claimant to show that the original owner was present in Bangladesh or his whereabouts were known or he did not cease to occupy or manage the property in question at the relevant time. Since the notification in the official gazette carries a presumption that the building in question is an abandoned property, it is exempt from any legal process be it an auction sale by the Government itself or through Court."

19. This view also receives support in the case of Sadharan Binia Corporation vs First Court of Settlement reported in 2007 BLD (AD) 21.

20. Having regard to the facts, the submissions advanced by the learned Counsel for the petitioner prevails and appears to have a good deal of force.

21. In view of the discussions made above and the preponderant Judicial views emerging out of the authorities referred to above, we are of the view that the judgment and order of the Court of Settlement dated 29-5-1997 (Annexure-A) suffers from legal infirmity which calls for interference by this Court. Thus the Rule having merit succeeds.

22. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any' order as to cost. The impugned judgment and order dated 29-5-1997 (Annexure-A) passed by the First Court of Settlement, Dhaka, is hereby declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

23. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

Send down the record to the concerned Court.

End.

lawyer:

parties:
Padma Type Foundry Karmachari Samabaya Sarnity Ltd ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works & another ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Above Rule Nisi was issued asking the respondents to show cause as to why impugned order dated 2-11-2000 passed by the 1st Court of Settlement at Segun Bagicha at Dhaka in Case No. 105 of 1997 rejecting the prayer of the petitioner for exclusion of the property in question from the kha list of the Abandoned Buildings, Annexure-B to the writ petition.

2. Petitioner is stated to be a limited company registered under the Co-operative Societies Act, 1940 having Certificate of Registration No. 928 of 1974.

3. The case of the petitioner, in short, is that it purchased the case property comprising holding Nos. 30, 33/1, and 34/1, Jogi Nagar at Dhaka at a public auction held on 9-2-76 by the Tax Recovery Officer under rule 55 of the Income Tax/Sales Tax Recovery Rules, 1969. The sale was on 15-3-76 confirmed and made absolute. A sale certificate was also issued to the petitioner vide Memo No. 571/5-76 dated 18-3-76 and on 17-3-76 possession of said property was delivered to the petitioner.

4. On 14-8-86 the petitioner made an application under section 7 of the Abandoned Building (Supplementary Provision) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. LIV of 1985), in short, the rdinance, for exclusion of the said property from the Khalist of Abandoned Buildings published under section 5 of the Ordinance in the official Gazette. The government contested the case without filing any written objection to the application. In support of the application, one Biswas Nasim Ahmed was examined as PW 1 as the then president of the petitioner Samity.

5. Upon consideration of the application and materials on record, the Court of Settlement came to a finding that the auction sale of the case property in 1976 for arrears of taxes was unauthorised and without jurisdiction since the property acquired the character of the abandoned property before 15th November, 1975 when the certificate case was initiated. It further held that in view of articles 6 and 14 of the Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order No. 16 of 1972, (President's Order No. 16 of 1972) hereinafter referred to as PO No. 16 of 1972, the petitioner hopelessly failed to prove its case and, as such, was not entitled to the relief as prayed for.

6. Mr Khan Saifur Rahman, learned Counsel for the petitioner, took us through PO No. 16 of 1972 with particular reference to articles 4, 7 and 14 and submitted that no notice under Article 7 was ever served upon anyone in possession of the case property and the petitioner purchased the case property in execution of a certificate sale held by the Income Tax Authority in 1976 and possessed the property since then lawfully and, as such, the Court of Settlement fell in serious error in not excluding the case property from the Khalist of Abandoned Buildings.

7. Regarding service of a notice dated 5-12-84 upon the petitioner, he submitted that the case property was never declared or treated as abandoned property before 24-11-84 and possession of the case property by the petitioner on the basis of the sale certificate dated 18-3-76 must be held to be lawful and the Court of Settlement has go no manner of authority to override the auction sale and delivery of possession of the case property.

8. Respondent No. 1 appeared and filed an affidavit-in-opposition denying the case of the petitioner. In the affidavit, it is stated that the case property was lawfully enlisted in Kha list following the procedure. Before such enlistment, a notice under article 7(3) of PO No. 16 of 1972 was served upon the petitioner in Form No. 10 vide Memo dated 5-12-84 being service No. 889 as per rule 3(8) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (taking over possession) Rules, 1972. Upon receipt of said notice, the petitioner on 27-12-1984 made an application before the Hon'ble Minister of the Ministry of Housing for cancellation of the said notice.

9. The petitioner also filed an affidavit-in-reply. In such reply, it is claimed that before 5-12-84 the case property was not relatable to PO No. 16 of 1972. It is also reiterated that acquisition of the case property by auction purchase and delivery of possession would not be hit by such notice dated 5-12-84.

10. Mr Md Zafar Imam, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, submitted that admittedly the case property included in the Khalist of the Abandoned Building under section 5 of the Ordinance and before exclusion of such property from the said list, the petitioner was required to prove first that the case property was not abandoned property and did not vest in the government under PO No. 16 of 1972 and secondly, the petitioner got same right or interest in the case property that was not affected by PO No. 16 of 1972. In support of the impugned order, he cited a number of cases, namely, Bangladesh vs Chairman, Court of Settlement 1997 BLD (AD) 301 = 50 DLR (AD) 93; Secretary, Ministry of Works and Urban Development vs Rowshan Ara Begum 57 DLR (AD) 167 and Bangladesh vs Ashrab Ali 2 MLR (AD) 96.

11. In the circumstances and in view of the submissions of learned Advocates, only issue which is facing us is, whether the Court of Settlement was justified and well founded in rejecting the application of the petitioner for exclusion of the case property from Khalist of the Abandoned Building by impugned order.

12. It appears from the deposition of PW 1 Biswas Nasim Ahmed (Annexure-A to the writ petition) recorded on 6-9-2000 that Madina and Sons was the owner in possession of the case property. Before auction, no notice was served upon them but they were verbally and repeatedly asked. Madina Khatun is a non-Bengali. After the liberation war, she left the country. He however, denied that before the liberation war Madina Khatun left, the country and the case property was rightly enlisted as abandoned property.

13. Upon such evidence and the materials on record, the Court of settlement found that owner of the case property was a non-Bengali and citizen of Pakistan. During the liberation war she left the country. Consequently, the case property was enlisted as abandoned property under PO No. 16 of 1972.

14. The Court of Settlement further found that the tax recovery officer sold the case property in auction in certificate Case No. 84/187/75-76 dated 15-11-75. Certificate case was initiated in 1975 for recovery of arrear income tax for the period from 1965-1976. On the materials of the tax recovery proceeding, it could not find any record as to whether Madina Khatun was an income tax payee. On consideration of articles 6 and 14 of PO No. 16 of 1972, it held that the case property already vested  in the government as the owner Madina Khatun left the country during liberation war and initiation of certificate proceeding and sale of the abandoned property were all illegal, unauthorised and without jurisdiction.

<u>15. Facts which are not disputed are that Madina Khatun, who was the owner of the case property, was a non-Bengali and citizen of Pakistan and was not present in Bangladesh, whose whereabouts were not known and ceased to occupy, supervise and manage the case property. Upon such broader facts, the case property acquired the character of abandoned property within the meaning of article 2(1) of PO No. 16 of 1972. Once the case property acquired the character of abandoned property on the commencement of PO No. 16 of 1972, it vested in the government under article 4 of said PO No. 16 of 1972 by operation of law. No further order or action was necessary. After such property vested in the government article 14 of said PO No. 16 of 1972 became operative at once with the consequence, such property was exempted from all legal process, including seizure, distress, ejectment, attachment or sale by any officer of a Court or any other authority, etc.</u>

16. In the circumstance, the notice for surrender of possession of the case property that was served on 5-12-84 on the petitioner cannot be said to be invalid in law. The petitioner also on 27-12-84 made an application to the Ministry concerned for cancellation of such notice. Moreover, the petitioner practically took no step in the case to prove under section 5 of the Ordinance that the case property was not abandoned property and had not vested in government or that it got any other rights independent of those of the original owner, Madina Khatun in the case property. The proceedings taken for arrears by the Income Tax Authority and ultimate sale of the case property in execution of a certificate for such arrears and delivery of possession were all therefore correctly held to be not sanctioned by law and, as such, without jurisdiction.

17. For the reasons aforesaid, we find the impugned order rejecting the prayer of the petitioner for exclusion of the case property from the Khalist of the Abandoned Buildings does not suffer from any illegality or irregularity calling for any interference by this Division.

18. In the result, the Rule is discharged with cost.

19. The order of stay granted on 15-7-01 is hereby recalled and vacated.

Communicate at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Abdur Rashid J: Above Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Supreme Judicial Commission Ordinance, 2008 (Ordinance No. VI of 2008) hereinafter referred to as the Ordinance should not be declared to be void being ultra vires of Articles 7, 22, 94,111 and 112 of the Constitution.

2. The Hon’ble Chief Justice by his order dated 18-6-08 constituted this Bench for hearing and disposal of the Rule. On 30-6-2008 when the Rule came up for hearing/ we issued a notice as contemplated under Order XXVIIA of the Code of Civil Procedure to the Attorney-General to appear and assist the Court in the interpretation of relevant provisions of the Constitution for Appointment of Judges in the Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

3. We also requested Senior Advocates Mr Shafique Ahmed, the President of the Supreme Court Bar Association, Mr TH Khan, Dr Kamal Hossain, Mr Rafiqul Huq, Khandaker Mahbubuddin Ahmad, Mr Mahmudul Islam, Ajmalul Hossain, QC to assist the Court as Amicus Curiae. Mr M Amirul-Islam with Dr Shahdeen Malik appeared for the petitioner.

4. Mr Fida M Kamal, Attorney-General did not appear. Mr Salauddin Ahmed, Additional Attorney-General (as he then was) with Muhammad Zafar Imam, Assistant Attorney-General and Monjur Alam, Assistant Attorney-General appeared for the respondent No. 1 Bangladesh. Mr Shafique Ahmed, Mr TH Khan, Mr Rafiqul Huq and Mr Ajmalul Hossain appeared as Amicus Curiae. Mr Abdul Matin Khasru, Mr MK Rahman and Mr Syed Ahmed Raja also volunteered to assist the Court and made their learned submissions. Dr Kamal Hossain and Khondaker Mahbubuddin Ahmad did not appear with intimation while Mr Mahmudul Islam declined to receive the notice of request issued by the Court.

5. The petitioner is stated to be an Advocate of the Supreme Court and made the writ petition in public interest to uphold the supremacy of the Constitution for ensuring the independence and separation of the judiciary from other organs of the State. He challenged the constitutionality of the Ordinance.

6. The premises upon which, the writ petition was made, in short, are that the separation and independence of the judiciary from the executive and legislative organs have been the cornerstone of the fundamental principles of State policy as enshrined in Article 22 of the Constitution. The Constitution in number of articles such as Article 94(4) and 116A mandates the independence of judiciary. Independence of judiciary and supremacy are further consolidated by the Constitution in Article 111 by providing that the law declared by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh is binding on all Courts subordinate to it and that Article 112 mandates that the executive and judicial authority of the State shall act in aid of the Supreme Court.

7. The idea of separation and independence of the judiciary was elaborated by the Appellate Division in now famous case of the Secretary, Ministry of Finance vs Masdar Hossain 52 DLR (AD) 82 in which the Appellate Division issued 12 directives for ensuring complete and full separation and independence of the judiciary from the executive and legislative organs of the State and such separation and independence have now been effective from November 1, 2007 in the subordinate judiciary of the country.

8. There are at least three cardinal aspects of the independence of judiciary which are (a) process of appointment of judges is not subject to control or influence by or of other organs of the State, (b) the tenure, discipline and removals are internal matters for the judiciary and (c) judgment can be delivered without fear and favour.

9. The Constitution has clearly set down through the provisions of the Supreme Judicial Council, the procedure for removal of the judges of the Supreme Court but the procedure for appointment has been dealt within broader terms and manner in Articles 94, 95, 97 and 98 of the Constitution.

10. The Ordinance was published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary on Sunday, March 16, 2008 providing matters for appointment of judges in both the Appellate Division and the High Court Division of the Supreme Court. It has provided for Constitution of a Supreme Judicial Commission, hereinafter referred to as the Commission, for selection and recommendation of names to the President of the Republic for appointment as additional judges, and judges of the High Court Division and judges of Appellate Division of the Supreme Court.

11. Section 3 of the Ordinance stipulates, the Commission will consist of nine members with the Chief Justice as Chairman and the Minister of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, two senior most Judges of the Appellate Division, Attorney-General, two members of Parliament nominated by the Leader of the House and Leader of the Opposition in Parliament and the President of the Supreme Court Bar Association. By an amendment, namely, the Supreme Judicial Commission (Amendment) Ordinance, 2008 sub-section (2) of section 3 of the Ordinance is substituted and after such amendment the Commission will now consist of the Chief Justice as chairman, and the Minister of Law, three senior most judges of the Appellate Division, two senior most judges of the High Court Division, Attorney-General and the President of the Supreme Court Bar Association as members.

12. Chairman of the Commission, that is the Chief Justice, shall convene the meeting of the Commission if he is requested to do so for selection and recommendation of the names by the appropriate authority, that is the Ministry, Division or Department upon which the responsibility rests by the Rules of Business, 1996, for forwarding the recommendation of the Commission to the President, which, in other words, mean that the meeting of the Commission and whether it should recommend names for appointment as judges is to be determined by the Government through its Ministry.

13. Under section 4(4) of the Ordinance five members out of nine members shall constitute quorum of the meeting and a decision to recommend names for appointment can be taken by a majority of the members present which, in other words, mean that the names for appointment may be selected and forwarded by a decision supported by three members only of the Commission in a meeting attended by five members only.

14. Section 6 provides that the Ministry of Law will forward names to the Commission for selection and recommendation for appointment as additional judges and judges of the High Court Division and judges of the Appellate Division. Said Ministry will send a minimum of three and a maximum of five names for each vacancy. The Commission shall select and recommend under section 5(2) two names for each vacancy. The Commission will consider the suitability of the candidates by taking into account their performance, ability, honesty and reputation.

15. Under section 9 it is provided that the President shall generally appoint judges of the Supreme Court in accordance with the recommendation of the Commission. If the President disagrees with the recommendation of the Commission, he would send said recommendation to the Commission for reconsideration. After receipt of any such request from the President for reconsideration, the Commission shall speedily reconsider and send its reconsidered recommendation or early recommendation for reasons recorded to the President. If the President wants to reject the recommendation of the Commission, he could finally reject the recommendation of the Commission for reasons recorded in writing.

16. Under section 10, notwithstanding anything contrary in the Ordinance, the Commission shall not be required to recommend two names from amongst the additional judges appointed under Article 98 for confirmation and/or appointment as judge under Article 95 of the Constitution, in that case it would not be required to recommend two names against every vacancy. In case of confirmation of additional judges in the High Court Division as permanent judges, the recommendation of the Commission would be necessary. The Commission shall consider overall suitability along with skills, seniority, professional integrity and reputation as additional judges of the High Court Division in case of recommendation for appointment as permanent judges of the High Court Division from amongst the additional judges of the High Court Division and the Commission shall abstain from recommending any additional judge for appointment as permanent judge, if he is found to be unfit in its consideration. The general rules of the Ordinance shall mutatis mutandis apply in case of recommendation for appointment of any person directly as a judge of the High Court Division or the Appellate Division.

17. It was also submitted that the Ordinance has completely overturned the constitutional mandates and independence and separation of the judiciary, and almost all the sections of the Ordinance are inconsistent with the canons of the independence and separation of the judiciary. Three members of the commission are below in rank and status than those of the judges of the Supreme Court. Their inclusion in the Commission is not only violate of the elementary principle and fairness but also is contrary to the established principle that the members of a selection body should be higher in rank and status than the persons to be selected and hence, such composition is void.

<u>18. By making the provisions for forwarding names for recommendation of the Commission by the Ministry of Law, the Ordinance has clearly made the judiciary subservient to said Ministry as the Chief Justice has been deprived of its prerogative and mandate of selecting names for appointment of judges, a prerogative and authority long recognised by our constitutional convention and tradition. The Ordinance by entrusting the Ministry of Law with the task of initial selection of names clearly negates all notions of the independence of judiciary and, as such, is void and ultra vires the Constitution.</u>

19. Requirement of convening meeting of the Commission, if requested to do so by so-called appropriate authority for selection of names, the Chief Justice hair clearly been made subservient to said appropriate authority which is a flagrant violation of the constitutional separation and supremacy of the Supreme Court. Provision for assessment of qualification, ability, honesty and reputation of the judges in case of selection for appointment as judges of the Appellate Division by a Commission consisting of three members who are not judges, undermines, negates and diminishes the role, prestige and standing of judges of the High Court Division by subjecting them to the scrutiny of others, which is tantamount to destroying the scheme of separation of organs of the state, which is central to the independence of the judiciary and, as such, ultra vires the Constitution. The procedure for selection and recommendation of names on the basis of a decision by majority, the office of the Chief Justice in the scheme of the Constitution would greatly be compromised when the Chief Justice will find himself in the minority. The provision providing for absolute authority of the President to reject the recommendation of the Commission is clearly intended to establish the supremacy of the executive over the judiciary and undermine the independence of the judiciary. By giving the power to the President to totally disregard the recommendation of the Commission, the Ordinance, in fact, challenged the decision of the Appellate Division in the Masdar Hossain case that the opinion of the Judiciary would have supremacy over the Executive.

20. Respondent Bangladesh appeared and filed an affidavit-in-opposition sworn on 8-6-08 and supplementary affidavit-in-opposition sworn on 15-7-08. In the affidavit, it is asserted that the Ordinance is not inconsistent with the independence or separation of the judiciary but aimed at fair and sound appointment to the posts of the Supreme Court judges from amongst the qualified persons on the basis of objective satisfaction and not depending on subjective satisfaction of the executive organ of the State. In order to prevent politically motivated choice which happened in recent past and in order to invite the actual qualified person for appointment to the post of the Supreme Court the Ordinance was promulgated by the President to safeguard the public interest.

21. The commission is a mere recommending authority and not an appointing authority of the judges of the Supreme Court. The Rules of Business 1996 provides that the Ministry of Law has to initiate the file relating to appointment of judges to be placed before the President through the Prime, Minister/Chief Adviser. Under 48(3) of the Constitution, the President shall act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister. Only an exception has been made in case of appointment of the Prime Minister and Chief Justice under Article 56(3) and 95(1) respectively of the Constitution. The President shall act depending on the subjective satisfaction of the executive head of the Government (Prime Minister/Chief Adviser).

22. For that reason, the criteria for appointment of judges of the Supreme Court were severely criticised and questioned. Accordingly, to mitigate this pain for the first time a check and balance has been introduced in promulgating the Ordinance. The Ordinance has empowered the President to accept and reject the names recommended by the Commission, even if, having concurrence with the Prime Minister/Chief Adviser. The composition of the Commission was questioned and criticised, and showing respect to the public opinion, an amendment of the Ordinance was approved by the Cabinet on 1-6-08 which would be promulgated very soon.

23. After amendment of the Ordinance, the members of the Commission are closely associated with the affairs of the Supreme Court being judges and practicing lawyers of the Supreme Court. They are appropriate persons for recommending the names of the qualified and dignified persons for appointment. The influence of the executive organ is totally excluded and a check and balance has been introduced to prevent the unfettered and uncontrolled power of the executive branch of the Government, which was being exercised before introduction of this Ordinance. Inclusion of the members in the Commission from other organs of the state is not outside the purview of the constitutional scheme because each organ of the state is mutually intra-dependent with the other.

24. For example, item No. 50 of Schedule IV of the Rules of Business framed by the President provides that the matters relating to appointment and resignation of the judges of the Supreme Court must be dealt with by the Ministry of Law. The Supreme Court or the President himself cannot directly deal with this matter going outside the channel of the Ministry of Law as an executive branch of the State violating said Rules of Business. Moreover, serial No. 30, item No. 14 of Schedule I of the Rules of Business (allocation of business) provides that the matters relating to the administration of justice be dealt with by the Ministry of Law.

25. From this legal point of view, the Ministry of Law has to render secretarial assistance to the office of the President as well as to the Supreme Court in case of appointment of judges. There is no hard and first rule that the persons who are below in rank and position may not be able to be members of the Commission for recommending the names of the judges of the Supreme Court for appointment.

26. After amendment of the Ordinance, members of the Commission may not be treated as below in rank and status. Rules of Business has laid down the provision that the proposal relating to appointment of judges needs to be initiated through the Ministry of Law and such an appointment is completed by the President on the basis of recommendation made by the Prime Minister/Chief Adviser. This is the set legal norms which are being practiced till today and has become a tradition in our jurisdiction. The system may not be treated as opposed to the independence and undermining the dignity and prestige of the judiciary because the judiciary itself is not independent organ to appoint its judges. In so many administrative matters, it has to work closely with the Ministry of Law, which is an executive branch of the Government.

27. Convening the meeting of the Commission by the Ministry of Law does not necessarily make the Chief Justice, Chairman of the Commission subservient to the Ministry of Law rather the role of the Ministry of Law in this context may be considered as extending the secretarial assistance to the commission, keeping consistency with the Rules of Business for appointment of judges of the Supreme Court as well as administration of justice. The Supreme Court being the apex judicial organ of the State is not empowered within our constitutional framework to appoint its own judges at its own initiative, rather the Constitution has laid down special provision for appointment of judges by the President following the Rules of Business (?).

28. In this case, the Supreme Court has no independent mechanism to appoint its judges without the assistance of the executive organ office State which, in fact, is an indispensable requirement of the Constitution. By the Ordinance, no supremacy of the executive has been established over the judiciary rather a check and balance has been ensured in the appointment of judges and unfair as well as politically motivated exercise of power in this respect has been, curtailed to a great extent introducing fair and equal treatment for all eligible incumbents to be elevated as judges of the Supreme Court. Without the Ordinance, it was quite impracticable and impossible to rule out the parochial group interest of the political authority for appointment of the judges in the Supreme Court. The Ordinance is now only an effective instrument to materialise the supremacy of the judges of the Supreme Court for appointment of its own judges and in this way the spirit of the Masdar Hossain case can be upheld.

29. In the supplementary affidavit, it is stated that proclamation of emergency on.11 January, 2007 and subsequent assumption of the State power by the present Caretaker Government and all incidental executive and legislative actions taken during this Government are obviously to meet the emergent situations. Whether any such emergency existed or exists are all political questions. All Ordinances promulgated by the President during this caretaker Government are presumed to be made and promulgated in exercise of the power conferred by Article 93 read with article 58E of the Constitution. Because the President is not debarred to take and execute any legislative policy under Article 93 and in view of Article 58E of the Constitution during the Caretaker Government, though under Article 58D of the Constitution the Council of Advisers of the Caretaker Government suffers from some limitation to formulate any policy decision except for necessity. But no such legal barrier exists in the Constitution for the President to formulate legislative policy. Legislative policy of the Caretaker Government depends on the predominant authority of the President and does not depend on the advice of the Council of Advisers, whose advice may be accepted or rejected by the President in view of Article 58E of the Constitution. Therefore, making and promulgating air Ordinance is an exclusive inherent legislative power of the President during caretaker Government when Parliament is or stands dissolved.

30. Appointment of judges of the Supreme Court is alleged to have been politicised in recent past, which has been severely questioned and criticised. For instance, controversy arose as to the genuineness of LLB: certificate of a former High Court Division Judge. Later on that very judge Mr Faisal Mahmud Fayzee tendered resignation. Similarly, former President of the Supreme Court Bar Association, Mr Rokanuddin Mahmud raised allegations of malpractice against a former sitting judge of the High Court Division (Mr Md Shahidur Rahman) in connection with bail matter who had to face the Supreme Judicial Council. Non-confirmation of some judges of the Supreme Court for political consideration as claimed is now pending before the High Court Division. Finally, the statement of Chief Justice Mr Ruhul Amin while addressing a Bar Association meeting may be quoted, which is to the effect that বিচারক নিয়োগে ভুলের কারণে মহাপ্রলয় ঘটে গেছে।, which was widely circulated in the national media. There are sufficient admitted evidences and circumstances, which satisfied the President who thought it expedient to take immediate action by making and promulgating an Ordinance for fair and impartial appointment of judges of the Supreme Court holding effective consultation (recommendation) with the Commission headed by the Chief Justice to protect the integrity of the Apex judiciary.

31. Considering the present system, an alternative mechanism be devised, which will ensure that competent and efficient personnel are appointed to safeguard the independence/integrity of the higher judiciary. Otherwise, the inevitable effect of which is that upper judiciary may lose the confidence of the citizen. Therefore, it is essential to man the higher judiciary with the personnel of highest caliber, character and integrity through a better selection procedure.

32. The power of the President to make law is co-extensive with the power of Parliament. Therefore, power of the President to make and promulgate Ordinances depends on the subjective satisfaction of the, President. And such satisfaction of the President regarding existence of the circumstances requiring immediate action cannot be questioned in Court [Ahsanullah vs Bangladesh 44 DLR 179]. The power of making Ordinance as a legislative power cannot be struck down on the ground of mala fide or want of application of mind in promulgating the Ordinance [ Venlcata Reddy vs Andhra Pradesh: AIR 1985 SC 724; Nagraj vs Andhra Pradesh: AIR 1985 SC 551). Therefore, when an Ordinance is challenged on the ground of absence of emergency, the Court may start with a presumption of the existence of emergency as the executive’s assertion of the existence of emergency should be given due and proper weight. Every casual and passing challenge to the existence of the necessary circumstances cannot be entertained [A K Roy vs India.AIR 1982 SC 710, 725]

33. The process of making and promulgating an Ordinance is developed as a policy on behalf of the President by the Cabinet/Council of Advisers in pursuance of Rules of Business as a normal practice. So, the President being satisfied in view of Article 58E and Article 93 of the Constitution promulgates an Ordinance. Here formulating a legislative policy decision is a predominant role played by the President himself being satisfied to that effect and not at the instance of the Council of Advisers (who is a recommending body and whose recommendation is not binding as per Article of 58E of the Constitution). Therefore, during the Caretaker Government in view of Article 58E the President has got the pre-dominant role as well as independent wisdom in making an Ordinance. Accordingly, Ordinance making power depends on the subjective satisfaction of the President during the period of Caretaker Government and the objective criteria of which is to be determined by the forthcoming Parlament, which may approve or disapprove the same.

34. It was also submitted that the impugned Ordinance is no where conflicting with the Constitution in terms of independence of judiciary rather it is supplementary and complementary to the principles of effective consultation with the Chief Justice in case of appointment of judges of the Supreme Court. The principle of consultation with the Chief Justice which was omitted by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975 is in fact reintroduced by the Ordinance. Such an Ordinance ensuring recommendation (consultation) by the Commission headed by the Chief Justice is absolutely necessary for independence of judiciary which is a basic feature of our Constitution. In the absence of such an Ordinance, there was no constitutional and legal requirement of consultation with the Chief Justice for appointment of the judges and there was an allegation of denial of consultation with the Chief Justice in this regard. Since no such uninterrupted and continuously observed constitutional convention has developed regarding consultation with the Chief Justice this Ordinance will help grow a constitutional convention in this area.

35. In England, a Judicial Appointment Commission has been established under section 61 of the Constitution Reforms Act, 2005. The Judicial Appointment Commission constitutes supplemental to the unwritten British Constitution. In our context, the Commission constitutes supplemental to our written Constitution to uphold independence and fair appointment of judges of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh.

36. Article 147 of the Constitution provides that terms and conditions of persons holding constitutional posts such as the judges of the Supreme Court may be determined by law along with remuneration and privileges. Qualification and other terms and condition of service of the judges of the Supreme Court may be determined by law under Article 95 as well as Article 147 of the Constitution. For election of the President a separate law, namely, the President Election Act, 1991 was enacted. Similarly, a separate law, namely, Parliament (Reserved Women Seat) Election Act, 2004 has been enacted for election of women members of Parliament for 45 reserved seats. Apart from this for election of members of Parliament separate law, namely, the Representation of the People Order, 1972 is prevailing in Bangladesh. From that legal point of view, the Ordinance as introduced for selection and recommendation of the Judges of the Supreme Court is not unconstitutional. Because, the other terms and conditions of service including the process of selection and recruitment of persons holding constitutional posts (such as Supreme Court judges) may be determined by law in view of Article 147 of the Constitution as preappointment conditions and selection procedure are also treated as conditions of service.

37. It also relied upon the observation of Mr Bhagawati J in the Judges’ Transfer Case [AIR 1982 SC 149] that “There must be collegiums to make recommendation to the President, in regard to the appointment of a Supreme Court Judge. The recommending authority should be broader based and there should be consultation with wider interests. If the collegiums is composed of persons who are  expected to have knowledge of the persons who may be fit for appointment on the Bench and have qualities required for appointment and this last requirement is absolutely essential, it would go a long away in securing the right kind of judges, who would be truly independent and who would invest the judicial process with significance and meaning for the deprived and exploited sections of our society.”

It was submitted that before introduction of the Ordinance, there was no such express, apparent, transparent and effective provision of consultation with the Chief Justice by the President as the consultative process was taken way by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975. The Ordinance provides for effectively, transparent as well as accountable provisions of such consultation by the President with the Chief Justice and others forming the Commission (a collegium consisting of six judges of the Supreme Court and three others very closely related to the Supreme Court being lawyers of the Supreme Court Bar Association).

38. By the Ordinance, the exercise of absolute constitutional power of the President has been thought to be developed in consultative process with the Commission and there is nothing unconstitutional with such practice. The fundamental principle of constitutional jurisprudence is that no law or provision of law shall be declared void unless found to be inconsistent with the Constitution. In the instant case not a single provision of the Ordinance is conflicting with or ultra vires the Constitution in terms of appointment of judges of the Supreme Court, rather. It is supplementary and complementary to the Constitution relating to independence of the judiciary.

39. Mr M Amir-ul-Islam and Dr Shahdeen Malik, for the petitioner, challenged the authority of the President in making the Ordinance during the period of the caretaker administration in the absence of Parliament. They submitted that in view of Articles 58D and 58E and in the context of Article 55 of the Constitution, the Caretaker Government has got no power to make any policy decision like the one of making an Ordinance.

40. They submitted that in view of the basic features of the Constitution, independence and separation of the judiciary, the President has got no power to make any Ordinance altering or changing such basic feature and/or structure of the Constitution. The Caretaker Government must be involved only to assist and aid the Election Commission for holding free and fair election of the members of Parliament as early as possible and to hand over power to the newly elected government.

41. Mr Islam submitted that the Bar was surprised seeing the Ordinance, which just fell from heaven. No body the Law Commission, the Bar Association, the Attorney-General or judiciary was taken into confidence or consulted before making such an important Ordinance prescribing a mode of selection and recommendation of persons for appointment of judges in the Supreme Court, , which directly concerns the independence of the judiciary. Caretaker Government has got no power to advise for making such an Ordinance and the President acted beyond his constitutional power in making such Ordinance.

42. Dr Shahdeen Malik submitted that the process envisaged by the Ordinance is subversive of the independence of the judiciary with a view to consolidate the control of the executive. Objective, tenor and intention as disclosed in the Ordinance are to establish the authority of the executive over the Supreme Court through a law. There was no necessity for such an Ordinance for making appointment of judges at the moment. Unlike Article 115, the Constitution could not conceive of any law empowering the President to make a law prescribing a mode of selection and recommendation of persons for appointment of judges in the Supreme Court. The Ordinance is completely against the spirit of the Constitution.

43. Mr Salahuddin Ahmed, Additional Attorney-General, submitted that the Ordinance was made for selection and recommendation of the names in the process of consultation with the Chief Justice for appointment of judges to the Supreme Court with the advice of the Prime Minister, and such process is complemented and supplemented by the Ordinance. By introducing the Ordinance, effect is given to the constitutional convention of consultation. Constitutional provision cannot be changed but constitutional convention could be changed by law. He however does not dispense the concept of primacy of Chief Justice. But in the matter of consultation and recommendation in order to perfect such consultation, the Ordinance was made which must be taken a step in the right direction to secure independence of the judiciary. The old system of appointment of judges of the Supreme Court was cloaked with secrecy devoid of any transparency and the Ordinance had made the process fully transparent.

44. He submitted that the power of the President in making the Ordinance is coextensive with that of the Parliament. Lastly, he challenged the intention of the petitioner in obtaining the Rule, which must be for collateral purpose.

45. Mr Shafique Ahmed submitted that there was long agitation and debate continuing over non-appointment and appointment of judges by the last elected administration. If the Ordinance is the result of that, it must be said that it violates Article 95 read with Article 48(3) of the Constitution. President has no authority to make such Ordinance during the Caretaker Government.

46. He submitted that the scheme devised by the Ordinance is to impose total control of the executive over the judiciary. The Bar was never consulted nor was taken into confidence before promulgation of the Ordinance. The Ordinance does not address the anxiety of the Bar nor does it safe-guard the transparency in the appointment of the judges. If the opinion of the Chief Justice is formed after consultation with senior most judges of both the High Court Division and the Appellate Division and senior members of the Bar Association and the Attorney-General for recommendation of any person as a judge of the Supreme Court that will make the consultation effective and transparent. The executive must come out openly to accept and act upon such recommendation for which no law is necessary at the present.

47. He submitted that various provisions of the Ordinance, particularly sections 5, 6 and 9 are inconsistent with the consultative process as developed in India, Pakistan and elsewhere and therefore, violates the Constitution. The Ordinance would not serve any purpose of such effective consultative process.

48. Mr TH Khan, learned Senior Advocate, submitted that introduction of the caretaker government was made in the Constitution as a stopgap arrangement, for holding free and fair election and functions of the caretaker administration must be confined to routine day-to-day works of the Government in addition to their main function to assist and aid the Election Commission. Promulgation of Ordinance during such caretaker administration is futile exercise and made in excess of the jurisdiction. The Chief Justice cannot head any such Commission since the Chief Justice has got no place in Articles 95 and 98 of the Constitution. Power of the Chief Justice is first required to be restored by amendment of the Constitution, which could only be done by Parliament.

49. Mr. Rafiqul Hoque submitted that the approach in making the Ordinance for providing a mechanism for appointment of judges may be good but the Caretaker Government has got no authority to make any policy decision. Nor they could make any Ordinance not related to the holding of election of the members of Parliament.

50. He submitted that Ordinance making power of the President is very limited in the absence of Parliament. Article 93 imposes various limitations for making an Ordinance. Life of an Ordinance is only one month. The present Caretaker Government has made number of Ordinances, which the coming Parliament would not even be able to read them during the period of one month. He also referred to the system and/or process for appointment of judges in South Korea, South Africa, Sri Lanka and Singapore.

51. Lastly, he submitted that the provision for consultation with the Chief Justice omitted by the Constitution (Fourth Amendment) Act, 1975 was restored by the Second Proclamation (Seventh Amendment) Order 1976, (Second Proclamation Order IV of 1976) but was again omitted by the Second Proclamation (Tenth Amendment Order 1977) (Second Proclamation Order No. 1 of 1977) providing for establishment of the Supreme Court. In the case of the Bangladesh Italian Marble Works Ltd vs Bangladesh, a Division Bench of this Division declared Article 95 valid as was amended by said Second Proclamation Order No. IV of 1976. In view of such declaration, he submitted, said provision “after consultation with the Chief Justice” must be deemed to be resorted to as a part of Article 95 of the Constitution by judicial pronouncement.

52. Mr Ajmalul Hossain, QC took us through the various provisions of the Constitution. He also referred to the systems and procedures of different jurisdictions for appointment of judges in the higher judiciary including UK and USA. He submitted that there was no necessity which rendered immediate action by the President to make the, Ordinance. Power under Article 93 is very limited for the executive, which is transient in nature. This is a residual legislative power delegated by the Constitution to the President.

53. Doctrine of separation of power has been incorporated in our Constitution. The Constitution vests the executive power of Republic in the executive and the legislative power in the Parliament. Parliament consists of 300 members to be elected by the People of the Country. The President in turn is elected by the members of Parliament. Unlike some other countries, for example India, our Constitution did not make the President a part of parliament. In the scheme of the Constitution, he has no role in the legislation making of the Republic in the capacity has a part of the legislature. President has been delegated in the executive capacity legislative power under Article 93.

54. Democracy and republican character are basic features of the Constitution, which should be reflected in all matters including interpretation of the provisions of the Constitution.

55. In law making process as well, the process of accountability is placed in parliament as legislature directly accountable to the people; and when law is being made through Ordinance by the President the process of accountability is also ensured. The President is also a representative of the people in that he is elected by the members of Parliament that is people’s representatives in Parliament.

56. During the time of elected government in promulgating an Ordinance under Article 93, the President must act in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister. In other words, the Ordinance is being made by the elected government. And they are accountable to Parliament and thus, to the people. By this process under our constitutional scheme, democracy and republican character have been protected in the legislative function.

57. It is the inherent feature of democracy and theory of separation of powers that law should be made by Parliament as people’s representative in Parliament. Thus, in developed democracy like the USA, the UK and Australia, there is no provision for Ordinance making by the head of the State. Ordinance making is therefore, not the norm of democracy but an exception. Ordinance making power therefore, should be exercised sparingly and only in the rare situation and circumstances specified under Article 93.

58. Under Article 93, he submitted that Ordinance making power of the President is very limited. The limitations are placed both as to time and circumstances. If the parliament is in session, the President has no power to promulgate an Ordinance. Likewise, if the Circumstances do not exist, which required immediate action necessary, President cannot make an Ordinance. If the President is satisfied as to the existence of the circumstances, he has to make the Ordinance proportionate to the circumstances. Therefore, at least three limitations, namely, (1) absence of parliamentary session, (2) President’s objective satisfaction and (3) proportionality in respect of the Ordinance are in place when the President makes an Ordinance. There are further limitations, express and inherent, in the Ordinance namely (1) it cannot amend the Constitution, (2) cannot amend the constitutional convention and (3) cannot make law on taxation and (4) alter or amend Acts of Parliament.

59. Under Article 93 the life of an Ordinance is short and temporary. By its nature the Ordinance cannot override an act of parliament. Satisfaction of the President is objective satisfaction which is justiciable and can be questioned in the judicial review. President makes Ordinance in executive capacity and such Ordinance can always be challenged under Article 102 of the Constitution in our constitutional scheme. Such power of Ordinance is justiciable because firstly, the President acts as an executive when he promulgates an Ordinance; secondly, there is no ouster clause of jurisdiction in Article 93 like Article 48 (3) of the Constitution and thirdly, Article 93 says about proportionality which inherently requires objective satisfaction. Further in our Constitution Ordinance making power should be applied as an exceptional method which is obviously subject to judicial scrutiny. Circumstances have accordingly been placed by the respondent to justify the statement that the President was objectively satisfied.

60. During the Caretaker Government, the President is not under any obligation to act in accordance with the advice of the Caretaker Administration or Council of Advisers. In Ordinance making, the President is therefore not obliged to take advice of the caretaker administration. Ordinance making is the sole satisfaction of the President. This is because the President is elected by the people indirectly thorough members of Parliament. Whereas, the Caretaker Government is not elected at all. During the Caretaker Government, as no parliament exists, the process of check and balance, in other words, accountability is absent. During this time such accountability could only be ensured by (i) the President (ii) the Court by scrutinising whether the limitations contained in Article 93 are met or not. Application of Article 93 therefore should be more restricted than the period of elected government in power. The President has therefore a higher burden to be satisfied of the existence of the circumstances which render immediate action necessary.

61. Under Article 58D, he submitted, the Caretaker Government shall carry on the routine functions of such government and only in cases of necessity for discharge of such functions it can make a policy decision. During this time, an Ordinance could be promulgated when there is an extreme necessity of making so otherwise the Government cannot discharge its routine function.

62. As the Rules of Business amended and updated in the light of Article 58E of the Constitution, promulgation of the Ordinance at the advice of the Caretaker Administration or Council of Advisers is completely unconstitutional and ultra vires, which is not conceivable in our constitutional scheme. There was no necessity of any kind that has arisen for the President in relation to appointment of judges to promulgate the Ordinance. This Ordinance does not pass the hurdles contained in Article 93.

63. He also relied upon a decision dated 13 June, 2008 of a Division Bench of this Division in the case of Peergada Kazi Shariatulla and others vs Bangladesh in Writ Petition No. 2207 of 2008, the Muslim Marriage and Divorce (Registration) (Amendment) Ordinance, 2008 was declared to be ultra vires the Constitution as the President had no authority to promulgate such an Ordinance under Article 93.

64. He also cited another decision of the same Bench dated 23-7-08 in the case of M Shamsul Huque and others vs Bangladesh and others in Writ Petition 4300 of 2008 and Sumiton Rule No. 5 of 2008, which declared the Contempt of Court Ordinance, 2008 unconstitutional for the power of the President under Article 93 is very limited and he can make an Ordinance which is necessary for conduct of the election only fulfilling the conditions of Articles 58D and 93 of the Constitution.

65. In support, he also cited Bhagat vs Emperor: AIR 1931 PC 111; Emperor vs Bencari Lal (Lord Chancellor): AIR 1945 PC 48; Lakhi Narayan Das vs Prince of Bihar: AIR 1950 FC 59; Harla vs. Slate of Rajasthan: AIR 1951 SC 467; State of Orissa vs Bhupendra Kumar (Gajendragadkar): AIR 1962 SC 945; Makhan Singh Tarsikka vs State of Punjab: AIR 1964 SC 648; Mr Satpal Co. vs Governor of Delhi: AIR 1979 SC 1550; R K Garg vs Union of India: AIR 1981 SC 2138; A K Roy vs India: AIR 1982 SC 710, 725; Venkata Reddy vs Andhra Pradesh: AIR 1985 SC 724; K Nagrajvs Andhra Pradesh: AIR 1985 SC 551; DC Wadhwa vs State of Bihar: AIR 1987 SC 579; Surajit Sengupta vs Election Tribunal, Sylhet:1981 BLD 132; Sargodha Bhera Bus Service Ltd vs Province of West Pakistan 11 DLR (SC) 285; and Secretary, Ministry of Finance vs Md Masdar Hossain 52 DLR (AD) 82. He also submitted voluminous documents and papers containing talks, speeches and writings of eminent jurists and judges on the appointment of judges in different nations.

66. Mr Abdul Matin Khasru submitted that the Caretaker Government is an interim government. Meaning that they cannot do what an elected government can do. They will perform only the routine day to day functions of such government. The country is passing through an extraordinary time in the absence of an elected government. Under the scheme of the Constitution not a single day should pass under an unelected government.

67. He submitted that the present system for appointment and no appointment of judges is full of flaws and lacks transparency. It is always subject to external influence bringing arbitrariness in the process. The Ordinance is good and needs amendment by Parliament and could survive with certain amendments. The President has authority to make the Ordinance, if the Ordinance falls within the limitations of the Constitution. In the absence of any system for consultation, the Ordinance has provided a system. But the Chief Justice must have primacy and judiciary must have last say in the matter of appointment of judges.

68. Mr MK Rahman referred to Articles 7,11, 58D, 58E and 93 of the Constitution and submitted that in making the Ordinance, the President interfered with the independence of the judiciary and put obstructions to the appointment of judges in the Supreme Court of Bangladesh on the basis of recommendation of the Chief Justice.

69. Mr Idrisur Rahman in person submitted that the Constitution comprising 153 Articles in 11 parts is a well organised document which demands respect from all functionaries. Democracy, the rule of law and the separation of the judiciary from the executive are cornerstones of the Constitution. Every functionary under the Constitution is defined and with their powers and limitations specified. The Supreme Court is given the power to review any action or omission of such functionary. He submitted that the Ordinance was unnecessary, uncalled for and unconstitutional.

70. Mr Syed Ahmed Raja submitted that the Ordinance achieved no purpose, economic, social or legal.

71. In the writ petition, the powers of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution were invoked for a declaration that the Ordinance is void being ultra vires certain provisions of the Constitution, namely, Articles 7, 22, 94, 111 and 112.

72. Article 102 has incorporated the concept of the judicial review by this Division of administrative actions or omissions of the executive, legislature and other statutory and/or public bodies or authorities. In a proper case, this Division is empowered, inter alia, to direct a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that when he is required by law to do or declare any act or proceeding taken by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority has been done or taken, without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. This Division is also empowered to strike down any law or part of a law for being inconsistent with the Constitution under Article 7 and/or for being inconsistent with the provisions of Part III enumerating fundamental rights under Article 26.

73. Save as to the above provisions of the Constitution, I do not know of any law of the land, which could declare any other law or part of such law void for being inconsistent with the object and/or purpose of such law only or any part of such law. This Division is therefore not empowered to declare any such law or part of such law void for being inconsistent with the object or purpose of such law only or any part of such law.

74. Under Article 102 of the Constitution orders in the nature of popular English writs could be issued. The scope of judicial review is vast and multifaceted that does not need to be traced or addressed in this matter. What I want to say, a Rule Nisi could and should only be issued in the terms of Article 102 of the Constitution asking the respondent(s) to show cause as to why the action impugned or complained of should not be declared to be without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The terms of such Rule should deal and confine with the authority in making the act or omission, and the merit and legal effect of the impugned act or omission.

75. If we take liberty in issuing Rule Nisi beyond the terms of Article 102, then, where it would end up at the disposal of such Rule nobody can imagine, this case may be a perfect illustration for what I want to make out. Had the terms of the Rule been issued in the terms of Article 102, with respect, that as to why the Ordinance should not be declared to have been promulgated without any lawful authority and, as such is of no legal effect, and may further be stretched by saying, for being void for being inconsistent with or ultra vires certain provisions of the Constitution, the confusion we were put into could be avoided.

76. There is no doubt that the Rules are prepared and issued by the people sitting at the bench below our seats but definitely on the basis of the pleadings. The standard of pleadings has gone down to such an extent that unless urgent steps be taken in this regard it would be very difficult for this Division to deal with such applications under Article 102 of the Constitution in coming days.

77. Core issue facing us in the above Rule is whether or not the President has got the authority to make the Ordinance and whether the Ordinance is void for being inconsistent with any provisions of the Constitution. In order to decide such issues, we are required to examine first, the authority of the President of the Republic in making such Ordinance. Was he authorised to make such a law? In doing so, we are equally required to examine the scheme of the Constitution in empowering the President to make an Ordinance.

78. Ordinance is no doubt a bad institution in a democracy for a law left behind by the British Imperial power. In UK, the British people cannot conceive to be ruled by Ordinance. All powers there are now decentralised and delegated to the executive and/or other statutory bodies.

79. They needed Ordinance to rule the colonies for, first, the seat of Parliament was in London far away from the colonies, second, it was very easy and convenient tool to make law to consolidate the imperial power in the colonies, third, during the recess of Parliament when law was needed, the representative of the British Crown could easily invoke such Ordinance making power to make law, and last, but not the least, the making of Ordinance was not required to pass through the scrutiny of Parliament as a bill.

80. Mr Mahmudul Islam has written in his book, ‘Constitutional Law of Bangladesh’ that Ordinance is not known elsewhere in the world save India, Pakistan and Bangladesh. Mr Ajmalul  Hossain accepts such position, as he did not find anything contrary to such view in his search. In representative democracy, as an Ordinance cannot take the place of law so its utility has been done with long ago.

81. In the Subcontinent comprising India, Pakistan and Bangladesh, India adopted first its Constitution on 26 November, 1949. Certain provisions of Indian Constitution led the Supreme Court of India to make certain authorities in respect of Ordinance, particularly concerning emergency. In India, consolidation of the executive powers is so centralised in Delhi that they need the utility of Ordinance, particularly at the time of emergency and/or President’s rule in a State or when Parliament is on recess. India is an ideal example of unity in diversity. The constitutional arrangements had to take care of the conflicting interests of various states diverse in language, ethnicity, class or caste and local peculiarities in the Union. Character of the Indian Constitution is no doubt federal.

82. Article 53 of the Indian Constitution vests the executive powers in the President of the Republic and to be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with the Constitution. The supreme command of the Defence Forces of the Union also vests in the President and the exercise thereof shall be regulated by law. Article 74 however provides, inter alio, that there shall be a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President who shall, in the exercise of his functions, act in accordance with such advice. Provided that the President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider such advice, either generally or otherwise, and the President shall act in accordance with the advice tendered after such reconsideration.

83. Besides, under Article 79, Parliament for the Union shall be constituted of the President and two Houses to be known respectively as the Council of States and the House of the People. Aforesaid powers apart, the President of Indian Republic is a part of the Parliament that is the legislature for the Union. Without being aware of the peculiar powers of the President of India, the apex Courts of Pakistan and Bangladesh sometimes fell in the constitutional glitch in order to validate the Ordinance making power of the President of Pakistan or Bangladesh particularly on the basis of AK Roy vs Union of India: AIR 1982 SC 710. I shall deal with the decision a short while later. But at the moment, I shall confine my consideration of the powers of the President of Bangladesh in making an Ordinance in the scheme of our Constitution.

84. Under Article 1 of the Constitution, Bangladesh is a sovereign unitary republic. All powers of the Republic vest in the people. Such people are essentially ordinary citizen, male or women of the country. Such powers could only be exercised on behalf of the people only under and by the authority of the Constitution. The Constitution is the solemn expression of the will of the people. If any other law is inconsistent with the Constitution such law shall to the extent of the inconsistency be void that is, not legally valid.

85. The above postulates as enumerated under Article 7 are not mere wishful thinking of the framers of the Constitution. They are the pledge made on behalf of the people to be “fundamental aim of the State to realise through the democratic process a socialist society, free from exploitation, a society in which the rule of law, fundamental human rights and freedom, equality and justice, political, economic and social, will be secured for all citizens; and affirmation as “our sacred duty to safeguard, protect and defend this Constitution and to maintain its supremacy as the embodiment of the will of the  people of Bangladesh  so that we may prosper in freedom and may make our full contribution towards international peace and cooperation in keeping with the progressive aspirations of mankind;” We, the judges of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh took oath before entering the office to protect and defend the Constitution and the laws of Bangladesh.

86. Similarly, Article 26 provides, inter alia, that all existing law inconsistent with the provisions of Part III enumerating Fundamental Rights shall to the extent of such inconsistency become void on the commencement of the Constitution. The state shall pot make any law inconsistent with any provisions  of this Part and any law so made to the extent of such inconsistency be void. (underlined by me) The above limitation in the making of any law either by Parliament or President is clear and unambiguous, and must be noted to be absolute.

87. Concept of separation of the powers of the Republic is also incorporated in the scheme of the Constitution. Article 11 says the Republic shall be a democracy in which effective participation by the people through their elected representatives in administration at all levels shall be ensured. Article 22 ordains that the State shall ensure the separation of the judiciary from the executive organ of the State. Such a declared state policy endorses the concept of the independence of judiciary from the executive for enforcement of the rule of law.

88. Part IV of the Constitution deals with the executive, Part V with the legislature and VI with the Judiciary. Chapter II of Part IV provides for elected government while chapter IIA for unelected Non-Party Caretaker Government. Under Article 48(2), the President is the Head of State and shall exercise the powers and perform the functions conferred and imposed on him by the Constitution and by any other law. In the exercise of all his functions, he shall act under Article 48(3) in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister save only that of appointing the Prime Minister and the Chief Justice. Under Article 58E, the provisions requiring the President to act on the advice of the Prime Minister or upon his prior countersignature under Article 48(3), 141A and 141C shall remain ineffective during the period of the Non-Party Caretaker Government.

89. During the elected government, under Article 55 the executive power of the Republic shall be exercised by or on the authority of the Prime Minister. The Cabinet shall be collectively responsible to Parliament. A11 executive actions of the Government shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President.

90. Under Article 58B, the Non-Party Caretaker Government shall function from the date on which the Chief Adviser enters upon the office and till the date upon which the new Prime Minister enters upon his office after Constitution of Parliament. Such Government shall be collectively responsible to the President. The executive power of the Republic shall subject to Article 58D(1) be  exercised by or on the authority of the Chief Adviser in accordance with the advice of such Government,

91. Under Article 58D(1), the Non-party Caretaker Government shall discharge its functions as an interim government and shall carry on routine functions of such government and shall not make any policy decision except in case of necessity for discharge of such routine functions.

92. Making of any policy decision is entrusted with Parliament as the representative body of the people who are the repository of all powers of the Republic. To such general scheme of the Constitution is an exception provided for such an interim government to make a policy decision only when discharge of any of its routine functions necessitates so to do.

93. Such government is limited one in the sense what the elected government can do they cannot do. At the moment, such government is also functioning under emergency for which Part IX of the Constitution dealing with emergency would guide them. Under emergency fundamental and other civil rights of the people are suspended, democracy is not functioning and participation of the people in the decision making is absent. The President is the last semblance of elected government and hence, the Non-party Caretaker Government is made responsible to him.

94.
