During the period of the Non-Party Caretaker Government, even after the advice and counter signature of the Prime Minister under Articles 48(3), 141A(1) and 141C(1) made ineffective under Article 58E and when the supreme command of the defence services under Article 61 vests in the President, the President does not acquire any newer power which is not conferred under Article 48(2) of the Constitution. Certain provisions under Articles 48(3), 141A(1) and 141C(1) of the Constitution were made ineffective under Article 58E only for the reason that there would be no Prime Minister. In the absence of the Prime Minister, such provisions could not be made effective. Any other interpretation, in my opinion, would violate the scheme of the Constitution.

95. The system of government as conceived under the elected Prime Minister remains the same under the Non-party Caretaker administration. The President is not made independent of the Non-party Caretaker Government to act on his own. The President is still obliged to act at the advice of such government on the basis of constitutional convention, otherwise the very system of government would collapse.

96. Making law is the business of Parliament. Parliament shall consist of three hundred members directly elected and forty-five women members indirectly elected by said elected members. Unlike India, the President is not a part of our Parliament. So, it is wrong to assume that the President is a constituent of Parliament.

97. Power of the President under Article 93 of the Constitution during the Non-party Caretaker Government to make an Ordinance remains the same as is under an elected government. But such power is not unfettered, exercise of which is always subject to certain conditions and limitations. President can exercise such power only in the absence of Parliament. Before making of an Ordinance, he must be satisfied that circumstances exist which render immediate action necessary and appear to him to require making an Ordinance. Here the word, "necessary" is the key to the exercise of such power and the words, "to require" relate to the extent of such legislation. Mere existence of circumstances would not be sufficient for him to exercise his Ordinance-making power unless it is necessary and calls for immediate action to make the Ordinance, and the extent of the Ordinance must also correspond to the need of such circumstances.

98. Life of an Ordinance is very limited and always subject to approval of Parliament. No Ordinance shall make any provision which could not lawfully be made under the Constitution by an Act of Parliament. For instance, the Constitution (Eighth Amendment) Act, 1988 (Act XXX of 1988) was made by Parliament but part of it which dealt with the High Court Division was declared to be ultra vires the Constitution by the Appellate Division for destroying essential limb of the judiciary. Similarly, an Ordinance cannot make any provision altering or repealing any provision of the Constitution.

99. Consistent stand of the Government is that by the impugned Ordinance, constitutional provision and convention for appointment of judges in the Supreme Court were merely complemented and/ or supplemented for selection of qualified person. Dictionary meaning of word, ‘Complement’ is to complete or perfect something else and that of ‘Supplement’ is addition. “Complement” or “supplement” definitely renders alteration and/or change of the existing Constitutional provisions or conventions regarding appointment of judges to the Supreme Court. If it is so, the President then clearly transgressed the constitutional limits in making the Ordinance.

100. The framers of the Constitution did not conceive of any law for selection of persons for appointment of judges to the Supreme Court though they empowered the President to appoint persons in the judicial service or magistracy in accordance with the rules to be made by him. Under Article 95, a law could however be made prescribing additional qualifications only for appointment of judges. The President therefore cannot arrogate a power not conferred upon him by the Constitution to make an Ordinance for selection of persons for appointment of judges to the Supreme Court on the fallacy of complementing and supplementing the constitutional provisions and/or conventions.

101. Nor there existed any circumstances at the moment, which rendered immediate action necessary for making the impugned Ordinance for appointment of judges to the Supreme Court. Similarly, the Non-Party Caretaker Government is not empowered to request or advise the President to make such an Ordinance in the discharge of its routine functions. No such law, in fact, is necessary for the Non-Party Caretaker Government to make appointment of judges to the Supreme Court at the moment. Moreover, it is not the case of the respondent that the President could not make any appointment of judges to the Supreme Court without such Ordinance.

102. It is also on record that before making the Ordinance, the Supreme Court, the Attorney-General or any member of the Supreme Court Bar Association was ever taken into confidence and/or consulted. In the absence of Parliament, no debate of any form was ever initiated or generated for any opinion in making such law. It could therefore, be concluded that the opinion of the nation was never reflected or represented in the Ordinance.

103. Part VI of the Constitution deals with the judiciary with the Supreme Court at the apex and subordinate Courts at the lowest. In a recent decision dated 17 July, 2008 of the Special Bench, in which two of us were party, the norms and requirements of consultation were laid down for appointment of judges under Article 95, which is equally applicable for appointment under Article 98.

104. The Special Bench unanimously arrived at the following conclusions as to the norms and process for appointment and non-appointment of judges to the Supreme Court:

(i) the proposal and process for appointment of judges to the Supreme Court in both the High Court Division and the Appellate Division should emanate from the Chief Justice of Bangladesh;

(ii) the opinion of the Chief Justice of Bangladesh in the matter of appointment of judges to the Supreme Court is entitled to have the primacy;

(iii) in case of appointment to the High Court Division, the Chief Justice shall consult with two senior-most judges of the Appellate Division and equal number of judges of the High Court Division to form his opinion and he shall also consult senior members of the Supreme Court Bar and the Attorney-General; and in the case of appointment of judges to the Appellate Division, he shall consult with three senior-most judges of the Appellate Division to form his opinion;

(iv) the President or the Government shall have no right to directly initiate the process for appointment of judges to the Supreme Court bypassing the Chief Justice of Bangladesh but the President/ Government shall have the right of suggesting the names of suitable candidates for consideration of the Chief Justice for appointment to the Supreme Court;

(v) The non-appointment of anyone recommended, on the ground of unsuitability, must be for good reasons, disclosed and conveyed to the Chief Justice with the reasons, materials and information to enable him to reconsider and withdraw his recommendation. If the Chief Justice after consultation with the above judges in respect of particular appointments in the Division concerned, does not find it necessary to withdraw and again recommend, then the President must adhere to such recommendation;

(vi) the President as a Rule shall accept the recommendation of the Chief Justice for appointment of judges. If the recommendation of the Chief Justice for the appointment or non-appointment of any person as a judge either to the High Court or the Appellate Division could not be accepted by the Government, it cannot outright reject such recommendation and go ahead with appointment of persons of its own choice. The Government in such case shall send the recommendation back to the Chief Justice for reconsideration on the reasons supported by materials and information conveyed by the Government;

(vii) after consideration of the reasons of the Government along with the materials and the information conveyed, the Chief Justice may withdraw his recommendation. But if he again recommends the same recommendation after consultation with the aforesaid senior most judges of the Appellate Division for appointment, the Government shall be obliged to complete the process of appointment;

(viii) appointment or non-appointment of an additional judge as judge under Article 95 of the Constitution by the executive disregarding the recommendation of the Chief Justice violates the Constitution;

(ix) when the executive may not accept such recommendation of the Chief Justice for reasons to be recorded, it may request the Chief Justice for reconsideration on the materials and information conveyed;

(x) the Chief Justice shall then reconsider the case on the materials and information furnished, and, if after such reconsideration, he again recommends for appointment or no appointment, the executive would he left with no choice but to complete the process of appointment of such an additional judge on the basis of such recommendation;

(xi) after successful conclusion of the period under Article 98, an additional judge acquires legitimate expectation and he becomes entitled to be considered for appointment under Article 95 of the Constitution in the absence of positive valid reason(s) to be recorded by the Executive; and

(xii) non-appointment of the petitioners, in the circumstances, as judge of the High Court Division under Article 95 of the Constitution therefore violates the constitutional scheme and conventions and is accordingly, declared to the arbitrary, malafide, without any lawful authority and, as such„ of no legal effect.

105. The above decision not only binds Ms Nazmun Ara Sultana, J and me but also binds the Government as law of the land under Articles 111 and 112 of the Constitution unless set aside by the Appellate Division.

106. If the aforesaid consultative process is made effective, and followed, the person(s) to be selected may turn out to be the common choice of all the consulters for appointment and then, the question of primacy of any constitutional functionary would lose all its importance.

107. Now, I shall deal with the merit of the Ordinance. The object of the Ordinance is stated to establish a Commission under the name of Supreme Judicial Commission for selection and recommendation of duly qualified persons for appointment of judges in the Supreme Court. The Commission shall comprise of nine members, of them six are judges of the Supreme Court. The Ministry of Law shall send 3 to 5 names for every vacancy to the Commission for selection and recommendation as additional judge and judge of the High Court Division and judge of the Appellate Division. The Commission would select and recommend two names to make a choice between them for every vacancy. It must be noted that ‘recommendation’ does not mean to pick and/or choose from amongst the names sent but to name a person against every vacancy.

108. Moreover, the position of the Chief Justice would be that of any other eight members save permitted to decorate the chair. The President is empowered to reject the recommendation of the Commission for reasons to be recorded only, which would be final. What would happen thereafter is not spelled out. The Ministry of Law is not only made to serve as secretariat of the Commission but also guide the working of the Commission right from sending of the names up to the appointment, if any.

109. The Ordinance even if taken as a reaction to what the past administration of alliance did on political considerations in the matter of non-appointment and appointment of judges in the Supreme Court and bona fide attempt to limit the executive discretion, in effect, ultimately both altered and changed the constitutional norms, process and conventions for appointment of judges to the Supreme Court.

110. In the affidavits of Bangladesh, in order to justify the need of the Ordinance reference was made to the Constitution Reforms Act, 2005 of the United Kingdom providing for the Judicial Appointments Commission. Existence of such commission or body in some other countries including the Republic of South Africa was also referred to in the arguments. In India also, a bill was placed in Parliament. But in their wisdom, the Indian executive finds satisfied to act at the recommendation of the Chief Justice following the decisions in the 2nd Judges’ Case: (1993) 4 SCC 441 and / the answers to the Presidential Reference No. 1 of 1998: (1998) 7 SCC 739 for appointment of judges to the High Courts and the Supreme Court of India.

111. Any law prescribing the mode or procedure for appointment of judges to the higher Court always relate to and involve the independence of the judiciary and therefore, cannot be conceived of to be independent of the Constitution. It must be a part of the Constitution. It is so accepted everywhere. In the United Kingdom, aforesaid Constitution Reforms Act, 2005 was made by Parliament after public debate and deliberation for about five years. In South Africa, such commission was provided in the Constitution. Such law if felt necessary could only be made by our Parliament if need be by amendment of the Constitution. Such law cannot be made by the President through an Ordinance. I am not unaware of the necessity of a system and/or process for appointment of judges to the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. But I hope the decisions in our judges’ case would amply serve the purpose.

112. The Ordinance has no doubt succeeded in creating some confusion in the minds of some people. Reason is obvious. During the last elected government, the alliance administration packed the High Court Division with their men in such a fashion that Mr Md Ruhul Amin former Chief Justice of Bangladesh had to lament saying the appointments made such a deluge to the judiciary which could not be overcome in next 20 years. In the affidavit of the respondent, Bangladesh it is so stated in defence of the Ordinance that recent appointments were made on political considerations. Anybody now feels that the executive discretion would now be regulated by a law, which is better than nothing.

113. So, the thought may dawn to save the Ordinance by trimming off and/or removing the offending parts of it. But the scope of Article 102 of the Constitution is so limited that this Division has got no jurisdiction to ask either the Parliament or the President to legislate in order to make the Ordinance acceptable. It is a matter for Parliament for making a policy decision for selection of persons for appointment of judges if the norms and requirement of consultation as laid down hereinabove are difficult to follow and/or carry out in the absence of law. If need be, Parliament may seek amendment of the Constitution. This Division cannot permit the President to make a law for selection of judges. There could not be any reason to think that the judgment of this Division would carry lesser weight than that of the Ordinance.

114. Days of the executive prerogative in the matter of appointment of judges are long over. In India, the executive has accepted the primacy of the opinion of the Chief Justice formed through a judicially devised consultative process in the matter of appointment of judges. Pakistan has also followed suit. In UK the Prime Minister on 7 July, 2007 declared, “the Government should consider relinquishing its residual role in the appointment of judges”. The office of the Lord Chancellor which existed for about 900 years and dominated in the sphere of appointment of judges in UK was done with by said Act, 2005. In the background of such developments in the common law jurisdictions, the time is up for the executive of our nation to decide the course to follow. Choice of the day is simple and clear would it believe in age old executive discretion to pack the Supreme Court with the men of the party in power or accept the opinion of the Chief Justice made through the aforesaid consultaive process for the independence of the judiciary for enforcement of the rule of law.

115. In my considered view, the Ordinance is nothing but a device to consolidate the executive authority through the Ministry of Law in the name of the President and to the exclusion of the Prime Minister in the matter of appointment of judges to the Supreme Court. Position of the Chief Justice, whose place in the judiciary in the constitutional scheme is that of a jewel in the crown, has nakedly been degraded. In its scheme, the Ordinance has severely undermined the provisions of the Constitution and the long practiced convention for appointment of judges.

116. For reasons aforesaid, there is no escape from the conclusion that the Non-Party Caretaker Government acted beyond its functions under Article 58D in advising the President to make the impugned Ordinance and the President arrogated the power and made the impugned Ordinance in violation of the constitutional provisions and conventions. The Ordinance is also ultra vires the scheme and spirit of the Constitution and, as such„ unconstitutional.

117. In the result, the Rule is made absolute with cost.

The Supreme Judicial Commission Ordinance, 2008 (Ordinance No. 6 of 2008) is hereby declared to have been promulgated without any lawful authority and, as such of no legal effect.

Nazmun Ara Sultana J : I respectfully disagree with the view of my learned senior brother Mr. Justice Mohammad Abdur Rashid as to the constitutionality of the impugned Supreme Judicial Commission Ordinance, 2008. So, I am writing a separate judgment expressing my views with the reasoning thereof.

120. Mr Idrisur Rahman an Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh has filed this writ petition as a public interest litigant challenging the Supreme Judicial Commission Ordinance, 2008 (Ordinance No. 6 of 2008) published in Bangladesh Gazette, Extraordinary issue on March 16, 2008. This Supreme Judicial Commission Ordinance, 2008, hereinafter referred to as the impugned Ordinance, has been promulgated for the purpose of Constitution of a commission for selecting and recommending suitable persons for appointment to the post of Judges of the Supreme Court. By section 3 of this impugned Ordinance this commission namely, Supreme Judicial Commission consisting of 9 members has been constituted. Initially, i.e. at the time of promulgation of this impugned Ordinance the members of this Supreme Judicial Commission, hereinafter referred to as Commission, were Chief Justice as Chairman, Minister, Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs, 2 senior most Judges of the Appellate Division, Attorney-General, 2 members of Parliament, President, Supreme Court Bar Association and the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs. But subsequently by the Ordinance No. 29 of 2008 published on 16-6-2008 the composition of this Commission has been amended and now out of the 9 members of this Commission 6 are judges of the Supreme Court (the Chief Justice as the Chairman, 3 Senior most Judges of the Appellate Division and 2 Senior most Judges of the High Court Division), and the other 3 are the Law Minister, the Attorney-General, and the President, Supreme Court Bar Association. This composition of the Supreme Judicial Commission has not been questioned by anybody before us at the time of hearing of the Rule. Rather, one of the learned advocates who made submission before us supporting the Rule, has opined that there can be no better composition of this Supreme Judicial Commission than what it is now composed of.

121. The writ petitioner filed this writ petition before bringing of the above mentioned amendment in the composition of the Commission along with some other amendments by the Ordinance No. 29 of 2008. The main grounds stated in this writ petition for challenging the validity of the impugned Ordinance therefore, relate to the composition of the Commission which it originally was. It has been contended in the writ petition that the composition of the commission is inconsistent with the independence and separation of the judiciary inasmuch as the vast majority, i.e. 6 of the 9 members of the Commission, are from outside of judiciary, that the vast majority of this commission being from executive and legislative organs of the state and 5 members of the commission being below in rank and status to that of the judges of the Supreme Court this Ordinance not only disregards the notion and principles of independence of judiciary but it is also violative of the elementary principles of fairness and, as such, it is ultra vires of the Constitution and void.

122. Rule was issued in this writ petition on 28-4-2008 calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned Supreme Judicial Commission Ordinance, 2008 should not be declared void being ultra vires of Articles 7, 22, 94, 111 and 112 of the Constitution of the People’s Republic of Bangladesh and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

123. However at the time of hearing of the Rule the composition of this commission though has not been questioned from the side of the writ petitioner or by any of the learned Advocates who made submissions before us supporting the Rule but the learned Advocates have assailed the impugned Ordinance on the main grounds that (1) during the period of Non-party Caretaker Government the President has no power to promulgate this impugned Ordinance formulating a policy decision (2) the circumstances as specified in Article 93 of the Constitution did not exist at all necessitating promulgation of this Ordinance, (3) this Ordinance is against the Constitutional scheme as regards judiciary and (4) it is also inconsistent with the Constitution and the Constitutional convention.

124. The respondent No. 1 has contested the Rule by filing affidavit and supplementary affidavit-in-opposition. The material case of this respondent is that the President is very much authorised to promulgate this impugned Ordinance during the period of Caretaker Government also. That the President promulgated the impugned Ordinance being satisfied about the existence of emergent situation as specified in Article 93 of the Constitution of People’s Republic of Bangladesh and that this satisfaction of the President regarding the existence of the emergent situation is not justiciable.

125. Further case of this respondent No. 1 is that there were sufficient circumstances which satisfied the President to take immediate action by making and promulgating the impugned Ordinance for fair and impartial appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court holding effective consultation with the Supreme Judicial Commission headed by the Honorable Chief Justice of Bangladesh. That this impugned Ordinance is nowhere conflicting or inconsistent with the Constitution rather this Ordinance is supplementary and complementary to the principles of effective consultation with the Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of Judges of the Supreme Court. That this impugned Ordinance providing for Constitution of a commission for selection and recommendation of the suitable persons for appointment as Judges of the Supreme Court is not beyond the Constitutional scheme, inasmuch as Articles 95 and 147 of the Constitution have provided for making law determining the qualifications and other terms and conditions of service of Judges of the Supreme Court which includes pre-appointment conditions and selection procedure also.

126. However, we have heard the learned Advocates appearing for the writ petitioner, the learned Additional Attorney-General and Assistant Attorney-General appeared for the respondent No. 1 the learned Advocates who made submission as amicus curiae and also the learned Advocates who volunteered. All the learned advocates made elaborate submissions on the issues raised before us and have enlightened us by citing several authorities both from home and from abroad on the subject before us. They have also narrated the procedures which are in practice in different countries of the world for appointment of judges of the superior Courts. It should be mentioned here that Mr Rafique-ul-Haque, Senior Advocate of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, as amicus curiae, has favoured us by supplying the relevant constitutional provisions of different countries of the world as regards appointment of judges of Superior Courts.

127. We have taken into notice that in many countries of the world including UK South Africa, Sri Lanka there are commissions in different names for selection of suitable persons for appointment as judges of Superior Courts. Some of the learned Advocates have stated that they are not against the formation of such commission for selection of suitable persons for appointment as Supreme Court Judges in our country also but their concern is that this impugned Ordinance has been promulgated in contravention of Constitutional dispensation.

128. However, before we start examining the grounds agitated for invalidating the impugned Ordinance we require to answer an important question raised from the side of the respondent. The respondent No.1 has pleaded that the power of the President to make and promulgate an Ordinance depends on the subjective satisfaction of the President and that the satisfaction of the President regarding the existence of the circumstances requiring immediate action cannot be questioned in Court. The respondent’s contention is that the satisfaction of the President regarding the existence of the emergent situation as specified in Article 93 of the Constitution being non justiciable this Court cannot entertain the plea of absence of requisite circumstances for invalidating the impugned Ordinance.

129. In view of this specific pleading of the respondent No. 1, it is evident that the question whether the satisfaction of the President regarding existence of emergent situation is justiciable or not needs to be decided first before we examine the grounds agitated by the learned Advocates for challenging the impugned Ordinance.

130. Article 93 of the Constitution deals with the Ordinance making power of the President. Article 93 provides

“At any time when Parliament stands dissolved or is not in session, if the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render immediate action necessary he may make and promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require “

131. From the above quoted Article 93 of the Constitution it is evident that the power of the President to make and promulgate Ordinances is subject to some conditions which are (i) non-existence of Parliament or absence of Parliamentary Session, (ii) existence of circumstances rendering immediate action necessary and (iii) making and promulgating the Ordinance proportionate to the circumstances (the very words of the Article 93 that “he may make and promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require” indicates this proportionality). These conditions precedent for making and promulgating Ordinances have been imposed by the Constitution .If any Ordinance is promulgated in contravention of these conditions imposed by the Constitution that Ordinance will be without lawful authority and, as such, void. Article 7 of the Constitution mandates that all powers in the Republic shall be exercised under and by the authority of the Constitution and thus no authority within the Republic can transgress the limits and conditions set by the Constitution. Therefore, if any Ordinance is challenged on the allegation that the circumstances specified in Article 93 of the Constitution did not exist at the time of promulgating the Ordinance there can be no reason for the Supreme Court to refuse to look into the case, whether the Ordinance has been promulgated in contravention of Constitutional limitations. If the executive promulgates an Ordinance which itself shows that there was no necessity of taking immediate action, the Supreme Court has the power and also the duty to prevent the executive from over-stepping the limits set by the Constitution.

132. The Indian Supreme Court in AK Roy vs India reported in AIR 1982 SC 710 has expressed its view in favour of justiciability of President’s satisfaction in the matter of promulgating Ordinance by holding thus:

“It is arguable that the 44th Constitution Amendment Act leaves no doubt that judicial review is not totally excluded in regard to the question relating to the President’s satisfaction.”

133. In K Nagaraj vs State of Andhra Pradesh reported in AIR 1985 SC 551 the Indian Supreme Court has opined that an Ordinance can be invalidated for contravention of the Constitutional limitations.

134. Seervai, in his Constitutional Law of India, 3rd Edition, has stated that the power of the President to promulgate Ordinance is subject to two conditions precedent and the fulfillment of the conditions precedent is ordinarily justiciable.

135. Mr Mahmudul. Islam in his Constitutional Law of Bangladesh, 2nd Edition at para 3.35 has made an analysis thus: “under our Constitutional dispensation there is no reason to hold the satisfaction of the President in the matter of promulgating Ordinance non justiciable. Every functionary under the Constitution has power limited and circumscribed and the Constitution professing rule of law cannot be construed as having conferred an absolute discretion on any functionary irrespective of the nature of the power exercised. When the framers of the Constitution wanted to import finality to any act they used the proper language and ousted the jurisdiction of the Court, but no such language has been used in respect of the satisfaction of the President regarding emergency. Ordinance making is an exercise of the legislative power. But that does not make an Ordinance an Act of Parliament. It will have the force and effect of an Act of Parliament only when it is validly made and it is the power, nay the duty, of the Court, when challenged to see that the conditions imposed by the Constitution are fulfilled.”

136. In para 3.35 of the same book Mr Mahmudul Islam has argued: “under our Constitutional dispensation, the requisite satisfaction is readily that of the executive Government on whose advice the President has to act and there is no reason why this satisfaction like all other satisfaction of the executive should not be justiciable and why an Ordinance shall not be declared void if it becomes absolutely clear that there was no emergency, or that it was promulgated mala fide”.

137. I fully endorse these above views of Mr Mahmudul Islam. The Constitution has clearly specified some conditions precedent for promulgating Ordinance. There is no reason why an Ordinance shall not be declared void if it becomes absolutely clear that these conditions precedent imposed by the Constitution were not fulfilled before promulgation of the Ordinance. It should be mentioned here that unlike Article 48(3), 78(1), 81(3) of the Constitution there is nothing in Article 93 ousting the jurisdiction of the Court. So when the validity of an Ordinance is challenged on the ground of absence of requisite circumstances as specified in the Constitution the Court cannot refuse to look into the matter on the ground of nonjusticiability. Of course, “when an Ordinance i9 challenged on the ground of absence of emergency, the Court may start with a presumption of existence of emergency and the person who challenges the Ordinance will have a great burden of showing the absence of emergency.” (AK Roy vs India AIR 1982 SC 710)

138. However, in view of above discussion it is evident that there is no reason to hold that the President’s satisfaction regarding existence of emergent situation in the matter of promulgating Ordinances is not justiciable.

139. Now we can proceed to examine the grounds agitated before us for assailing the impugned Ordinance. The two most pressed grounds for challenging the validity of the impugned Ordinance are that (1) during the period of Non-party Caretaker Government the President has no power to promulgate the impugned Ordinance formulating a policy decision and that (ii) circumstances as specified in Article 93 of the Constitution did not exist at all necessitating promulgation of this Ordinance. These two grounds are inter-related and, as such, I shall discuss these two grounds together.

140. The learned advocates have argued that during the period of Non-party Caretaker Government the President cannot promulgate any Ordinance involving a policy decision inasmuch as the Caretaker Government is not authorised to make any policy decision except in the case of necessity for the discharge of its routine function in view of Article 58D of the Constitution. That there was no necessity at all for formation of the Supreme Judicial Commission for the purpose of appointment of Supreme Court Judges as there was prevailing a long practiced procedure for appointment of Supreme Court Judges in consultation with the Honorable Chief Justice.

141. The respondent No. 1 has opposed this argument of the learned advocates of the other side by making statements in his supplementary affidavit-in-opposition to the effect that though under Article 58D of the Constitution the Council of Advisers of the Caretaker Government suffers from some limitations to formulate any policy decision except for necessity, but no such legal barrier exists in the Constitution for the President to formulate legislative policy. That making and promulgating an Ordinance is an exclusive inherent legislative power of the President during Caretaker government and the President himself being satisfied about existence of emergent situation as specified in Article 93 and not at the instance of the Council of Advisors promulgates Ordinances.

142. It is, no doubt, true that making and promulgating Ordinances is the prerogative of the President only. The President, being satisfied about the emergent situation as specified in Article 93 of the Constitution, can promulgate an Ordinance at any time when Parliament stands dissolved or is not in session. But under our Constitutional dispensation President, being a titular head, cannot make any policy decision. So, obviously, when any Ordinance involves any policy decision that policy decision must be of the Government. Of course, Article 93, of the Constitution has authorised the President to consider whether circumstances exist rendering immediate promulgation of an Ordinance formulating the policy decision of the Government necessary. So if the President is not satisfied about the existence of emergent situation as specified in Article 93 of the Constitution he may not promulgate the Ordinance formulating the policy decision of the Government. In the matter of making and promulgation of an Ordinance involving a policy decision the Government is the recommending body whose recommendations are not binding on the President. But when the President promulgates an Ordinance involving a policy decision that policy decision, obviously, is of the Government.

143. However, in our instant writ petition we shall have to decide whether the Caretaker Government is empowered to make the policy decision of formation of the Supreme Judicial Commission for the purpose of selection and recommendation of suitable persons for appointment as judges of the Supreme Court and whether there was emergent situation as specified in Article 93 of the Constitution for promulgation of the impugned Ordinance providing for formation of this Supreme Judicial Commission. Article 58D and Article 93 of the Constitution require analysis for this purpose.

The relevant part of these 2 Articles are quoted below:

Article 58D—The Non-party Caretaker Government shall discharge its functions as an interim Government and shall carry on the routine functions of such Government with the aid and assistance of persons in the services of the Republic, and except in the case of necessity for the discharge of such functions it shall not make any policy decision.

Article 93—At any time when Parliament stands dissolved or is not in session, if the President is satisfied that circumstances exist which render immediate action necessary, he may make and promulgate such Ordinances as the circumstances appear to him to require, and any Ordinance so made shall, as from its promulgation, have the like force of law as an Act of Parliament.

144. The analysis of Article 58D makes it clear that the Non-party Caretaker Government can make a policy decision if it is necessary for the purpose of discharge of its routine function. The combined analysis of Article 58D and Article 93, therefore, tells that during the period of Non-party Caretaker Government the President can make and promulgate an Ordinance formulating a policy decision if it becomes urgently necessary for the discharge of routine function of the Caretaker Government. So, the argument that during the period of Nonparty Caretaker government the President has no power to promulgate any Ordinance formulating a policy decision not acceptable. The Ordinance-making power of the President during the period of Non-party Caretaker Government is somewhat restricted, no doubt, in view of Article 58D of the Constitution. The President cannot make and promulgate any Ordinance formulating a policy decision during the period of Caretaker Government if that policy decision is not urgently necessary for the discharge of routine function of the Caretaker Government. In other words it may be said that during the period of Non-party Caretaker Government if necessity arises for a law formulating a policy decision for discharge of routine function of the Caretaker Government and the President is satisfied about existence of such necessity/circumstances and also about the urgency for promulgation of such law he may promulgate an Ordinance which such necessity/circumstances require.

145. So, the conditions necessary for promulgation of an Ordinance formulating a policy decision during the period of Caretaker Government are:

(i) Necessity of the Ordinance for discharge of routine functions of the Caretaker government.

(ii) Existence of circumstances requiring immediate promulgation of the Ordinance, and

(iii) Proportionality of the Ordinance with the circumstances requiring promulgation of the same.

146. There cannot be any doubt that the appointment of judges of the Supreme Court to the vacant posts falls within the routine functions of the Caretaker Government.

147. We shall have to see whether formation of Supreme Judicial Commission is necessary for appointment of judges of the Supreme Court and whether circumstances exist requiring immediate promulgation of the impugned Ordinance providing for formation of this Supreme Judicial Commission.

148. Arguments though have been made before us to the effect that a long practiced procedure was in vogue for appointment of judges of the Supreme Court in consultation with the Honorable Chief Justice and, as such, formation of the Supreme Judicial Commission at this moment was not necessary at all, but no argument has been made before us denying the circumstances necessitating the formation of this Commission as narrated in the affidavit and the supplementary affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent No. 1. There is no denial of the fact that the appointment of the judges of the Supreme Court has been severely questioned and criticised in the recent past. Allegations raised widely that appointment of judges of the Supreme Court has been politicised. Even the former Honorable Chief Justice while addressing in a Bar Association meeting commented to the effect that “বিচারক নিয়োগ নিয়ে আদালতে মহাপ্রলয় ঘটে গেছে।” which was circulated widely in national news media. Strong demand is being made from the Bar and from Civil Society for fair and impartial appointment of judges of the Supreme Court. Mr. Shafique Ahmed, the present President of the Supreme Court Bar Association, being invited by us to be one of the amicus curiae, informed us that there is a demand from Supreme Court Bar also for constituting such Supreme Judicial Commission for fair and impartial appointment of the most suitable persons to the post of Supreme Court judges.

149. Admittedly, there are vacant posts of judges both in the Appellate Division and in the High Court Division and appointment of judges to these vacant posts has become necessary.

150. All these admitted facts and circumstances rendered the promulgation of the impugned Ordinance urgently necessary for formation of the Supreme Judicial Commission for the purpose of selection of most suitable persons for appointment as Supreme Court Judges and for making these appointments fair, beyond any controversy and acceptable to all and thereby to earn confidence of the people in the Superior Judiciary. So, I find no reason to accept the contention that circumstances as specified in Article 93 of the Constitution did not exist requiring immediate promulgation of the impugned Ordinance. Rather, considering the facts and circumstances stated above I find that there was urgent necessity for promulgating the impugned Ordinance for the purpose of making appointments to the vacant posts of Supreme Court judges which falls within the routine function of the Caretaker Government.

151. The other condition for validating the impugned Ordinance is its proportionality with the circumstances which required its promulgation. The impugned Ordinance has provided for formation of the Supreme Judicial Commission only for the purpose of selection of the suitable persons for appointment as Supreme Court judges. So, evidently this impugned Ordinance is very much proportionate with the circumstances which required its promulgation. I, therefore, find that all the conditions necessary for the promulgation of the impugned Ordinance during the period of Caretaker Government were very much in existence and this Ordinance is also proportionate with the circumstances requiring its promulgation.

152. The next two grounds for assailing the impugned Ordinance are that (3) this Ordinance is against the Constitutional scheme as regards the judiciary and that (4) it is also inconsistent with the Constitution and the Constitutional convention.

153. The Constitutional scheme as regards judiciary is that the judiciary shall be separated from the executive organs of the state (Article 22) and all judges shall be independent in the exercise of their judicial functions. (Article 94(4)). Article 94 clauses (1), (2) & (3) have provided the structural composition of the Supreme Court. Article 95(1) has stated that the President shall appoint the Chief Justice and other judges of the Supreme Court. The other clauses of Article 95 have described the required qualifications for being eligible to be appointed as a Supreme Court Judge. Article 96 and other Articles of Part VI of the Constitution have dealt with other matters relating to the Supreme Court and its judges. None of these Constitutional provisions has been contradicted or even touched by the impugned Ordinance. The impugned Ordinance has provided for only a recommending body for selecting and recommending suitable and fit persons for being appointed as judge of the Supreme Court by the President. Six out of 9 members of this commission being the senior most judges of both the Divisions of the Supreme Court including Chief Justice and other 3 members being closely related to the Supreme Court there cannot be any argument that this impugned Ordinance is conflicting with the constitutional scheme of independence of judiciary. Nowhere in this impugned Ordinance there is anything inconsistent with or contradicting the Constitutional provisions or the recognised constitutional convention Of consultation with the Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of Supreme Court Judges. Arguments have been made before us to the effect that the recognised Constitutional convention is that the President shall appoint judges of the Supreme Court in consultation with the Chief Justice. That the formation of a commission with 9 members for selection and recommendation of suitable persons for appointment as Supreme Court Judges has given a goby to this recognised convention of: consultation with the Chief Justice. It has beer. Argued that the provision of this impugned Ordinance to the effect that in case of disagreement among the members of commission the decision of the majority of the members present will be decision of the commission has ignored the primacy of the opinion of the Chief Justice. The contention is that the Chief Justice may differ with the majority view and in that case the opinion of Chief Justice will lose its primacy which will be conflicting with the recognised Constitutional convention of consultation with the Chief Justice.

154. But I am unable to accept the arguments of the learned advocates. Originally in our Constitution there was provision for consultation with the Chief Justice by the President in the matter of appointment of judges of the Supreme Court. By the 4th Amendment of the Constitution this provision was abolished. But in spite of abolishment of this provision the practice of consultation with the Chief Justice continued with a single departure in 1994. In 1994 appointment of several Supreme Court Judges was notified without any consultation with the Chief Justice at which the Bar and the Civil Society raised serious protest and consequently that appointment was cancelled and a fresh appointment was made after consultation with the Chief Justice. This fact recognised the convention of consultation with the Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of Supreme Court Judges and since then this convention was never broken. Thus consultation with the Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of Supreme Court Judges is now a recognised and established Constitutional convention. But what does “consultation” mean or what will be the scope and mode of “consultation” that has not been spelt out in the Constitution. This “consultation” has not taken any definite shape as yet in our country by convention also. But in some of our neighboring countries, e.g. in India and Pakistan it has been accepted (on the basis of judicial pronouncements) that “consultation with Chief Justice” requires consultation with a plurality of judges, a collegium, and that sole individual opinion of the Chief Justice does not constitute “consultation”. In those countries giving absolute discretion to the Chief Justice even as an individual in the matter of appointment of judges of the Superior Courts was not considered desirable In Supreme Court Advocates-on-record Association vs Union of India AIR 268 SC the majority view was recorded thus

“However, it needs hardly be stressed that the primacy of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India in this context is, in effect, primacy of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India formed collectively, that is to say, after taking into account the views of his senior colleagues who are required to be consulted by him for the formation of his opinion.”

155. I have already pointed out above that the Supreme Judicial Commission consists of 9 members of whom 6 are senior most Judges of both the Division of the Supreme Court including Chief Justice as Chairman and the other 3 also are closely related to Supreme Court. All these 9 members of this commission are undoubtedly most competent to find out the best suitable persons for the judgeship of the Supreme Court. These members of the Commission the consulters will perform the duty of selection of the suitable persons for the judgeship collectively with a view primarily to reach an agreed decision. If a consensus is not possible then the opinion of the majority will be the opinion of the Commission. However in my view this Supreme Judicial Commission headed by the Chief Justice does not at all derogate the convention of consultation with the Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of Supreme Court Judges, rather it is supplementary and complementary to this convention of consultation with the Chief Justice.

156. In our country no convention of giving primacy to the opinion of the Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of Supreme Court Judges has been built up as yet. It should be mentioned here that even in India and Pakistan also the non-appointment of the person recommended by the Chief Justice is permissible where the other senior judges consulted are of the view that the recommender is unsuitable for appointment. In the above stated Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association vs Union of India the majority judgment has said

“if the final opinion of the Chief Justice of India is contrary to the opinion of the senior Judges consulted by the Chief Justice of India and the senior Judges are of the view that the recommended is unsuitable for stated reasons, which are accepted by the President, then the non-appointment of the candidate recommended by the Chief Justice of India would be permissible.”

157. This above view has been fully supported by their Lordships in Special Reference No. 1 of 1998, Supreme Court Cases 739 by making comments thus:

“This is delicately put, having regard to the high status of the President, and implies that if the majority of the collegium is against the appointment of a particular person, that person shall not be appointed, and we think that this is what must invariably happen. We hasten to add that we cannot easily visualise a contingency of this nature, we have little doubt that if even two of the judges forming the collegium express strong views for good reasons that are adverse to the appointment of a particular person, the Chief Justice of India would not press for such appointment.”

158. However, I do not think that the formation of this Supreme Judicial Commission has contradicted any Constitutional provision or Constitutional convention. There is nothing in this impugned Ordinance against the Constitutional scheme as regards judiciary and this Ordinance does not contradict or is inconsistent with any provision of the Constitution or the Constitutional convention.

159. Argument has been made to the effect also that this impugned Ordinance is touching the basic structure of the Constitution which is beyond the Ordinance-making power of the President. But there is nothing in the Constitution to support this contention of the learned advocate. The proviso to clause (1) of Article 93 has stated only that no Ordinance shall make any provision:

(I) which could not lawfully be made under this Constitution by Act of Parliament.

(II) for altering or repealing any provision of this Constitution, or

(III) Continuing in force any provision of an Ordinance previously made.

160. The impugned Ordinance does not infringe any of these limitations. There is nothing in this Article 93 or in any other provision of the Constitution to the effect that no Ordinance touching (not altering or repealing) any basic structure of the Constitution can be made.

161. From the declaration made in this Ordinance as to the object and reasons of promulgating this Ordinance it is clear that this Ordinance has been made only for the purpose of formation of a commission for selection and recommendation of the best and most suitable persons for being appointed as Supreme Court judges. This commission namely, the Supreme Judicial Commission has been constituted with total 9 members of whom 4 are senior most judges of the Appellate Division including the Chief Justice as the Chairman of the com-mission, 2 are senior most judges of the High Court Division, the Law Minister, the Attorney-General and the President of Supreme Court Bar Association. This composition of the Supreme Judicial Com-mission should not be questioned. In fact, none of the learned advocates has raised any question as to this composition of the commission.

162. We have examined the other provisions of this Ordinance, save and except one, I do not find any other provision of this Ordinance objectionable. Section 6 of this Ordinance has provided that the list of proposed names should be sent to the Commission from the Law Ministry. I find nothing wrong in this provision. President is the appointing authority and, as such, it is normal that the list of the names of proposed candidates will come from the concerned ministry of the executive organ. It may be mentioned here that in a recently delivered judgment disposing of Writ Petition Nos. 1543 of 2003, 2975 of 2003 and 3217 of 2003 a larger bench of this Division has already expressed its view in support of this procedure. In that judgment written by Md Abdur Rashid, J, in the concluding portion, his Lordship has clearly said “.....the President/Government shall have the right of suggesting the names of the suitable candidates for consideration of the Chief Justice for appointment to the Supreme Court.” In fact, this process of sending the names of the proposed candidates by the Law Ministry on behalf of the President to the Chief Justice for his opinion is in practice since before.

<u>163. There is another provision in this Ordinance to the effect that the Commission will recommend two persons against every vacant post. Some of the learned advocates have raised objection as to this provision. But we should keep in mind that the commission is only a recommending body not the appointing authority. The only task of this commission is to find out the appropriate persons and recommend their names to the appointing authority. So there should not be any objection if the commission is required to find out 2 appropriate persons for every vacant post.</u>

164. Objection has been raised as to sub-section (6) of section 4 of this impugned Ordinance which has provided for convening meeting of the Commission by the Chief Justice on the request of the President or the Law Ministry for selecting and recommending suitable persons for appointment as Supreme Court Judges. It has beer argued that by this provision of the impugned Ordinance the Chief Justice has been made subservient to the Law Ministry. But I am unable to accept this argument also. Sub-section (4) of section 3 of this impugned Ordinance has provided that the Law Ministry will extend secretarial assistance to the commission. So when necessity arises and President is required to appoint Supreme Court Judges it becomes the duty of the Law Ministry to extend all secretarial assistance to the commission. The role of law ministry in requesting the commission for convening its meeting for the purpose of selecting and recommending suitable persons for such appointment should be considered as extending the secretarial assistance to the commission, it does not make the Honorable Chief Justice the Chairman of the Commission, subservient to the Law Ministry.

165. Argument was made before us to the effect that according to Article 48(3) of the Constitution the President is to appoint Supreme Court Judges on the advice of the Prime Minister and that since in the impugned Ordinance there is nothing as to the advice of the Prime Minister this Ordinance is inconsistent with the Constitution. But this argument is not entertain able at all. We should not forget that this Ordinance has been promulgated during the period of Non-party Caretaker Government when this provision of the Constitution requiring the President to act on the advice of the Prime Minister has been kept ineffective by the Article 58E of the Constitution. However, after coming of elected government if this Ordinance is made Act of Parliament then appropriate provision as to the advice of Prime Minister may be incorporated in that Act.

166. It needs to be mentioned here that this impugned Ordinance is a new law. Some lacuna or defects may be in this new law which may surface when actions start to be taken under this law. It is not unusual. Necessary amendments, addition, etc. to this new law can be made in due course. But for any such lacuna or defect, if any at all, the entire law cannot be declared void.

167. However, I have already hinted above that one of the provisions of this impugned Ordinance is not acceptable. This is sub-section (4) of section 9. This sub-section (4) of section 9 has provided that the President can reject the recommendation of the Commission finally after recording the reasons thereof. For better appreciation I like to reproduce the entire section 9 of the impugned Ordinance here.

৯। রাষ্ট্রপতির বিশেষ ক্ষমতঃ-(১) রাষ্ট্রপতি সাধারণতঃ কমিশনের সুপারিশ অনুযায়ী সুপ্রীম কোর্টের বিচারক পদে নিয়োগ প্রদান করিয়া থাকিবেন।

(২) কোন ক্ষেতে রাষ্ট্রপতি কমিশনের সুপারিশের সহিত দ্বিমত পোষন করিলে তিনি সুপারিশটি পুনর্বিবেচনার জন্য কমিশনের নিকট ফেরত প্রদান করিবেন।

(৩) রাষ্ট্রপতির নিকট হইতে পুনর্বিবেচনার অনুরোধ সহকারে কোন সুপারিশটি পুনর্বিবেচনা করিবে এবং সংশোধিত সুপারিশ কিংবা যুক্তিসঙ্গত কারণ উল্লেখপূর্বক পূর্বের সুপারিশ রাষ্ট্রপতির নিকট প্রেরণ করিবে।

(৪) রাষ্ট্রপতি কমিশনের সুপারিশ চুড়ান্তভাবে অগ্রাহ্য করিতে চাইলে যথাযথ কারণ লিপিবদ্ধ করিয়া কমিশনের সুপারিশ আগ্রাহ্য করিতে পারিবেন।

168. Nothing has been stated in this Ordinance as to what will be the situation then after rejection of entire process of selection and recommendation of suitable persons for appointment to the vacant post of Supreme Court Judges. In fact, this sub-section (4) of section 9 does not only defy the recognised and established Constitutional convention of consultation with the Chief Justice in the matter of appointment of Supreme Court Judges but it also frustrates the entire object and scheme of this Ordinance for selection of fit and suitable persons for appointment as Supreme Court Judges. It is inconsistent with the very object of promulgating the Ordinance. This very provision makes the entire Ordinance futile, ineffective. From the above quoted section 9 of the impugned Ordinance it appears that if the President disagrees with recommendation of the Commission he will send back the recommendation to the commission for reconsideration and the commission then will reconsider the matter promptly and send the amended recommendation or the earlier recommendation with reasonings to the President again. This entire endeavour of this high level commission consisting of senior most judges of both the Divisions of the Supreme Court including Chief Justice can be rendered meaningless by the application of this sub-section (4) of section 9 of the Ordinance which is not desirable and cannot be accepted.

169. This sub-section (4) of section 9 of the impugned Ordinance being very much inconsistent with the very object of the Ordinance and being the reason of rendering the entire Ordinance meaningless, futile and ineffective is liable to be declared void.

170. In this connection I suggest that there may be provisions in this Ordinance to the effect that after getting the recommendation from the Commission if the President does not agree he will send back the recommendation disclosing the reasons of his disagreement together with the relevant materials and information to the commission for reconsideration. The commission will then reconsider the matter promptly and send the amended recommendation or the earlier recommendation with reasonings to the President again as per sub-section (3) of section 9 of the impugned Ordinance. On getting back the recommendation from the commission again after reconsideration as per sub-section (3) of section 9 of the Ordinance the President should have no choice but to complete the process of appointment on the basis of recommendation of this high level commission all the members of which are the most competent persons to make the best selection for appointment to the post of Supreme Court Judges.

171. Before making an end of this judgment I recollect the argument advanced by some of the learned Advocates. Some learned advocates argued that we do not need any such Supreme Judicial Commission for we can adopt the procedure which is being followed in India and in Pakistan in the matter of selection and appointment of judges of superior Courts. It has already been indicated earlier that in India and Pakistan the executive has accepted the judicially devised procedure for appointment of judges of superior Courts. But I want to remind the learned advocates that in India also an endeavour was made to constitute a National Judicial Commission for selecting competent persons for appointment to the post of judges of Supreme Court and High Court and the hearing and disposal of the SC Advocates-on-Record Association vs Union of India case was kept pending in the hope that formation of such National Judicial Commission will relieve the grievances long felt by the judiciary in the matter of selection of proper and fit personnel and their appointment to the superior judiciary and in that event the correctness of the ratio in the SP Gupta’s case would not be required to be examined. (Vide SC Advocate son-record Association vs Union of India AIR 268 SC pars 26). It should be mentioned here that since the endeavour for constituting a National Judicial Commission could not be successful the Supreme Court of India laid down in the above mentioned case principles and prescribed procedural norms in regard to the appointment of judges of the superior Courts after reconsideration of the correctness of the opinion of the majority in SP Gupta’s Case (AIR 1982 SC 149) relating to status and primacy of the opinion of the Chief Justice of India in the matter of appointment of judges of superior Courts.

172. However it is not necessary that we should adopt the procedure of other countries if we can have our own unique one which is not less good than what is being followed in India, in Pakistan or in other countries of the world in regard to appointment of judges of the superior Courts.

173. Mr Md Abdur Rashid, J in his judgment has reproduced the conclusions arrived at in the judgment disposing of Writ Petition Nos. 1543 of 2003, 2975 of 2003 and 3217 of 2003 as to the norms and process for appointment of judges of the Supreme Court and has commented that these are binding on all including the government. In this connection I need to say that the impugned Ordinance was promulgated long before passing of the above mentioned judgment and in this instant writ petition we require to examine whether this impugned Ordinance was promulgated in contravention of any Constitutional provision.

174. However, from the above discussion it is evident that save and except the sub-section (4) of section 9 of this impugned Ordinance I do not find any other provision of this Ordinance unconstitutional or ultra vires of the Constitution. The promulgation of this impugned Ordinance also, in my opinion, has been quite in accordance with the Constitutional dispensations.

175. Accordingly, I will make the Rule absolute in part and declare that the sub-section (4) of section 9 only of this Supreme Judicial Commission Ordinance, 2008 be void being inconsistent with the very object of the Ordinance and being the reason of rendering the Ordinance meaningless and futile.

176. Before I part with this judgment I want to express my gratitude to the learned Counsels who appeared before us for the parties and also as amicus curiae and rendered very useful and commendable assistance to us.

Md Ashfaqul Islam J: I have had the occasion to go through the judgment written by their Lordships Mr Justice Mohammad Abdur Rashid and Ms Justice Nazmun Ara Sultana. I concur with Justice Nazmun Ara Sultana and record my reasons as under.

178. At the very outset I would like to highlight very basic and admitted position which to my mind, has an indelible bearing on the subject we are dealing with. Hence, it is indicated that when the entire country is under the governance of Non-party Caretaker Government and also under ‘Emergency’, the Supreme Judicial Commission Ordinance, 2008 (Ordinance No. 6 of 2008), hereinafter referred to as the ‘Ordinance’ was promulgated and that has been challenged on the question of its’ Constitutionality and the same is sought to be declared void being ultra vires of the Constitution as it is repugnant to the various provisions of the Constitution as well as long practiced convention.

179. Pertinently, different provisions of the Constitution relating to “Non-party Caretaker Government” (Articles 58B to 58E), “Emergency Provisions” (Article 141A to 141C) and “Ordinance Making Power” (Article 93) have become relevant for deciding the issue before us by interpreting those provisions in their true spirit and perspective in a given situation.

180. Consequently, the provisions of the Constitution governing the appointment of Judges (Article 95), the appointment of additional Judges of the Supreme Court (Article 98) together with the limitation of power of the President under Article 48(3) have to be interpreted in equal footing as they are significantly focused on the issue since the Ordinance under challenge aims to set up a Commission purporting to select and recommend eligible persons to be appointed as the judge of the Supreme Court.

181. Inevitably, the interpretation of the above provisions in this context has to be made by taking recourse to the methods which are suggested by the Constitution itself to be followed in so doing. Regard must the taken in this respect that the provisions of the Constitution as stated above are the outcome of the positive and cohesive thinking of the framers of the Constitution which they in their wisdom thought it proper to be incorporated in the Constitution in the manner as they exist in the Constitution to meet different situations, exigencies and requirements. Otherwise those provisions would not have been there.

182. Keeping primarily in mind what I have discussed let me now dwell upon the issue before me. The moot question that falls for consideration is, whether the Ordinance under challenge can operate as a valid piece of legislation within the framework of the Constitution or, in other words, with the mandate of the Constitution.

183. The Hon'ble President of the Republic of Bangladesh promulgated the Ordinance which came into force with the publication in the official Gazette on 16-3-2008. The Ordinance made provisions for matters relating to the appointment of the Judges in both the Divisions of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh by setting up a Commission to achieve the purpose. Thereafter a vital amendment was made in the Ordinance on 16-6-2008 during pendency of this Rule by reconstituting the organogram of the Commission. With the change in the organogram of the Commission by the amendment, the judges of the Supreme Court of both the Divisions with the Chief Justice as the chairman of the Commission now commands absolute majority of 9 (nine) member Commission.

184. The Ordinance postulates modus operandi of Commission by specifying its powers and functions in order to furthering appointment of the Judges of both the Divisions of the Supreme Court by recommending and selecting names of the eligible persons after scrutiny. Undoubtedly, the object for which the Ordinance apparently seems to be made is noble as it endeavors to concrete the process of the appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court ensuring the primacy of the Chief Justice and Judges of both the Divisions of the Supreme Court for searching who are the best choice according to them to become member of their own fraternity.

185. Whole gamut of the topic needs to be clarified upon critical appraisal of two vital aspects. Firstly, whether this Ordinance can sustain under the scheme of the Constitution and secondly, if the Ordinance survives, whether with this Ordinance as it stands, the NOBLE objective can be achieved in its’ true perspective.

186. It is mentioned that the country is now under the governance of the Non-party Caretaker Government and also under Emergency. Under the elected Government, the parliament legislates. But when the parliament stands dissolved or is not in session, the legislative function vests in the President and the President by promulgating Ordinance under Article 93 of the Constitution legislates which have the force of law as an Act of Parliament. As per Article 152 law is interpreted which includes ‘Ordinance’. Further Article 93(1) proviso enumerates that no Ordinance can be made which could not lawfully be made under this Constitution by Act of Parliament and which could alter or repeal any provision of this Constitution.

187. So a logical inference can be deducted that an Ordinance can be made which parliament can lawfully make under its plenary legislative power and also an Ordinance can be made without altering or repealing any provision of the Constitution. If these tests are satisfied, legislation by way of Ordinance is absolutely valid and has the like force of law as if the same has been passed by the parliament. In this regard, it would be relevant to mention that no implied limitation, can be applied while interpreting a written Constitution like ours when the limitations are clearly spelled out in the provision of the Constitution itself.

188. Provisions have been made under Articles 58B to 58E of the Constitution for the Non-party Caretaker Government. Article 58B(2) points out that the said government shall be collectively responsible to the President. Article 58D states that the said Government shall only function in a limited capacity and without making any policy decision shall discharge on the routine functions excepting when in the discharge of its’ routine function it is necessity to make any policy decision. Article 58E has rendered ineffective those provisions of the Constitution requiring the President to act on the advice of the Prime Minister as it is commonly found in Articles 48(3), 141A(1) and 141 (C) of the Constitution. But unlike Article 48(3) proviso Judicial review is open in this context.

189. Under Article 48(3) excepting the appointment of the Prime Minister and the Chief Justice, the President shall be acting in accordance with the advice of the Prime Minister. So the express Constitutional provision which limits the power of the President under Article 48(3) remains ineffective due to Article 58E during the tenure of Non-party Caretaker Government as it has been already explained. Therefore, while making any Ordinance during an elected Government under Article 93, the President acts according to the advice of the Prime Minister but we do not find any such EXPRESS provision in the Constitution like that of Article 48 (3) during the tenure of Nonparty Caretaker Government and for that reason it can he logically interpreted that the Ordinance making power of the President during Nonparty Caretaker Government seems to be more weighty. Likewise, same induction can be applied in respect of Emergency Period when Article 141(A)1 and 141C(1) of Emergency Provision is read within the meaning of Article 58E of the Constitution.

190. Another significant aspect which needs to be addressed in this context is, whether there had existed any situation for which the President to his satisfaction felt it necessary to take immediate action by promulgating the Ordinance in question as contemplated under Article 93(1) of the Constitution. The reasons that actuated the President to promulgate the Ordinance which have been vividly described in paragraph 4 of the Supplementary Affidavit filed by the respondent No. 1, to my mind, were justified in terms of Article 93(1). It is needless to mention that the situation that existed at the relevant time certainly demanded a change and transparency in the whole process of the appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court. An effective and immediate remedy to meet such popular demand was echoed in every public perception. What more is required to promulgate an Ordinance to fit in a situation other than this when we find that the very Ordinance aims only to set up a selecting body for ensuring the best appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court? Can it be perceived with any earthly reason that the Ordinance is tainted with malafide and colour able exercise of power? Why then an innocuous Ordinance of this kind should have to be tested and construed by inducting Article 58D and accordingly an interpretation would be given that since the Ordinance is an outcome of the policy decision it cannot be passed by an interim government is not understood. This is absolutely against rationale. In the case of Kudrat-e-Elahi Panir. 44 DLR (AD) 319. The President’s Ordinance making power was questioned on the plea of mala-fide and colour able exercise of power, Shahabuddin Ahmed CJ repelled the argument by holding at paragraph 36 as under:

“The question of colour able legislation arises when a thing which cannot the done directly is sought to be done indirectly. A thing is colour able which exists in appearance and not in reality. It is “what it purports to be” Colour ability is linked up with incompetency, that is, an authority doing a thing which he got no power to do. “Colourable” is not tainted with bad faith; it is just lack of jurisdiction. In other words, in the case of lawmaking, the doctrine of colourable legislation does not involve any question of bonafide on the part of the legislature, If the legislature is competent to pass a particular law, the motives which impelled it to act are really irrelevant.”

191. On a plain reading of the Ordinance I find that the commission set up under the Ordinance is absolutely a recommending body and not the appointing authority. The power of the appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court lies with the President who exercises the power within the limitations of Article 48(3) of the Constitution. The President appoints additional judges of the Supreme Court and the Judges of the Supreme Court under Articles 98 and 95 of the Constitution respectively. When the President is satisfied that the number of Judges of the Supreme Court should he increased he makes appointment. Before the Fourth Amendment of the Constitution, the Chief Justice was to be consulted while making the appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court. Since that provision of Constitution had been amended by the Fourth amendment now consultation with the Chief Justice does not find place in the Constitution. But even after 4th Amendment it has been consistently followed the CONVENTION’ of consulting with the Chief Justice before making any appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court. A deviation of the said convention that took place in 1994 was cured forthwith reaffirming the convention as it used to be followed before. I have already discussed that the object of the Ordinance is intended to set up a commission for selection and recommendation of eligible and duly qualified persons for appointment of the Judges in both the Divisions of the Supreme Court. Initiation of the names of the prospective persons for selection by the commission would he made by the Ministry of Law and the Commission would select and recommend two names for consideration between them against any vacancy.

192. Up to this, I do not think exercise of the Ordinance has in any way infringed expressly or by implication any provision of the Constitution or the convention for which it can be held that the Ordinance has flouted the Constitution or convention. Neither the Ordinance can be termed unconstitutional for destroying basic structure of the Constitution. It would be also unwise to infer by any stretch of imagination that since the respondent No.1 Government has interpreted the Ordinance as 'complementary’ and ‘supplementary’ of the Constitutional provision for the appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court for that reason alone express provisions of the Constitution has been altered or changed. Certainly this trend of interpretation would be termed as a travesty of interpreting Constitutional provision when Article 8(2) of the Constitution hinted amply what would be the guideline in interpreting a written Constitution like ours. Tools are in our hands, we can very well exercise our own volition for interpreting the supreme law of the land.

193. To my interpretation, the Ordinance has rather fortified and strengthened the Convention followed over the years consistently for the appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court. It has ventured to ensure primacy of the Chief Justice and other Judges for selecting and recommending fit persons to be appointed as the Judge of the Supreme Court by setting up a Commission admittedly when there is no provision for consultation with the Chief Justice in the Constitution itself. Further, life of the Ordinance would eventually depend upon the parliament whether to accept it or not (Article 93(2).

<u>194. But the provision of the Ordinance as laid down in section 9(4) which empowers the President to reject the recommendation of the Commission for reasons to be recorded, which would he final, is indeed, unconstitutional. Definitely this particular provision is inconsistent with the Constitutional provision and Convention for the appointment of the Judges of the Supreme Court. It flouts the main object of securing primacy of the Commission’s decision. To make the Ordinance effective this section is a bar for the reasons stated above. I declare this section 9(4) of the Ordinance void.</u>

The Rule is thus, made absolute in part.

Order of the Court

By majority of 2:1, the Rule is made absolute in part without cost.

195. Sub-section (4) of section 9 of the Supreme Judicial Commission Ordinance, 2008 (Ordinance No. VI of 2008) is declared to be void.

We, however, certify under Article 103(2)(a) of the Constitution that the case involves substantial questions of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, which may be decided by the Appellate Division.

End.
