full_judgment:
Farid Ahmed J : This Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the inclusion of the petitioner's building situated at House No. 1/15 Block-D, Mohammadpur, Dhaka as abandoned property in Bangladesh Gazette Extra-ordinary 'Kha' list published under the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 at page No. 9764 (17), serial No. 42 and judgment and order dated 28-5-2000 (Annexure-1) passed by the 1st. Court of Settlement, Bangladesh, Segunbagicha, Dhaka, in Case No. 172 of 1995 (Kha-42, B1ock-D, Mohammadpur) of House No. 1/15, Block-D, Mohammadpur, Dhaka shall not be declared to have been published and passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and why the respondent No.2 should not be directed to exclude the building situated at House No. 1/15, Block-D, Mohammadpur, Dhaka, from the list of the abandoned property and pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts of the case as stated in the petition are that the House No. 1/15, Block-D, Razia Sultana Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka, measuring an area of 144 square yards originally belonged to the then Government of East Pakistan and that the Government leased out the aforesaid property to Syed Md Yunus by a registered deed of lease being No. 2067 dated 2-2-1960; that after taking delivery of possession of the aforesaid property the original allottee Syed Md Yunus built a two-storied building on the leasehold land and had been living therein with his family members and that said Syed Md Yunus being in need of urgent cash money sold out the aforesaid building to Md Abdul Quayum by a registered deed being No. 881 dated 3-2-1969 and delivered physical possession of the building in question to said Abdul Quayum and that thereafter, Abdul Quayum while was in ownership and possession of the property he again sold out the same to one Habiba Banu wife of Abdul Ash by a registered deed being No. 3998 dated 30-4-1970 and handed over the physical possession of the house to her on the same day on 30-4-1970; that Habiba Banu, while was in ownership and possession of the aforesaid house she being in need of money sold out the same to the petitioners at a consideration of Taka 40,000 (Taka forty thousand) vide four registered sale deeds being Nos. 2498, 2499, 2500 and 2501 dated 9-12-1972 and handed over the physical possession of the case property along with all original documents of the building in question; that thereafter, aforesaid Habiba Banu left the property and shifted her family to a rented house situated at 22 Bangshal Road, under PS Kotwali, District-Dhaka. The petitioners also stated that Abdul Ash, the husband of Habiba Banu, was a Bangladesh national and a resident of village Ashugonj, under PS and District Brahmanbaria, that the petitioners mutated their names in the office of the City Corporation and got electricity, gas and WASA connection in the case property in their own names and Khatians in respect of the case property has been opened in their names and they have been paying taxes and other bills regularly; that while the petitioners were in ownership and possession of the case property the State Officer under the Ministry of Public Works entered into a lease agreement on 10-4-1974 with Abdul Halim, father of the petitioner, in respect of the case property for the residential accommodation of a Government officer and that after hiring the property the government allotted the same to one Mr Md Arifur Rahman, Administrative Officer, Ministry of Planning, Government of Bangladesh on 30-5-1974 for a period of leone) year and that the said agreement was renewed from time to time upto 1987 and paid rent regularly to the petitioners; that after the death of their father, aforesaid Abdul Halirn, petitioner's mother Rahima Khatun accepted the rent from the Government on behalf of the petitioners. The petitioners filed an application to the Assistant Commissioner of Housing and Settlement, Ministry of Public Works, Segunbagicha, Dhaka on 23-1-1984 and 12-4-1984 for mutating their names in place of the previous owner. On receipt of the applications the Assistant Commissioners held an inquiry through their local Administrative Officer who after holding inquiry submitted a report on 25-4-1985 stating that the petitioners are in possession of the case property by purchase from Habiba Banu. The petitioners further stated that they are in exclusive ownership and possession of the case property by purchase from lawful owner but the Government has published a Gazette on 23-9-1986 enlisting the abandoned building and in the said list the house of the petitioners has been included in the kha list of the abandoned building. The petitioners thereafter filed an application before the Court of Settlement under section 7 of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 for the exclusion of the property from the Kha list which was registered as Settlement case No. 172 of 1995. The Court of Settlement after hearing by judgment and order dated 28-5-2000 rejected the case and thereby refused to exclude the case property from the abandoned list. Being aggrieved thereby the petitioners moved this court and obtained the present Rule.

3. The respondent No.2 Government of Bangladesh has filed affidavit-in-opposition denying all allegations made in the writ petition. The specific case of this respondent is, that the disputed plot was allotted to one Syed Md Yunus, a refugee from India by then Government of East Pakistan in the year 1960 and said Md Yunus built his house therein and lived therein with his family members and then sold the same to one Md Abdul Quayum in the year 1969, who again sold the same to one Habiba Banu, wife of Abdul Ash on 30-4-1970, that said Habiba Banu left the house with her family members during the War of Liberation and the house was in uncared for condition and the Government took possession of the house and listed the same as abandoned property under PO 16 of 1972. The whereabouts of Habiba Banu was not known during liberation of Bangladesh and, as such, the property was rightly included in the abandoned list. The predecessors of the petitioners have created 4(four) sale deeds by false personation and forging the signature of Habiba Banu.

4. Mr MA Quddus Sheikh, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners, submitted that the Court of Settlement has taken adverse inference about the title deeds of the petitioners without taking into consideration that those are registered deeds and have got some presumptive value and, as such, the judgment passed by the Court of Settlement is not lawful and the same has got no legal effect. Mr Quddus thereafter, submitted that the Court of Settlement did not consider that the respondent being satisfied with the title of the petitioners hired the same from the petitioners for their residential accommodation and they paid rent to the petitioners and, as such, the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement refusing to release the case property from abandoned list is liable to be declared to have been passed without any lawful authority. Mr Quddus Sheikh lastly submitted that the property has been included in the 'Kha' list of the abandoned buildings without serving any notice for taking or surrendering possession of the same to the respondents.

5. Mr Karuna Moy Chakma, the learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2, submitted that the petitioners have failed to prove that the alleged vendor of the petitioners Habiba Banu purchased the property in question by a deed dated 30-4-1970 and she did not leave the property uncared for and thereafter sold the same to the petitioners in the year 1972 remaining herself in possession of the case property The Deputy Attorney-General thereafter submitted that the Court of Settlement found that the LTI of Habiba Banu appearing in the petitioner's purchase deeds are not the product of the same hand and, as such, it cannot be held that those are LTI of petitioners' vendor Habiba Banu or that she ever sold the case property to the petitioners.

6. Admittedly, the case property was leased out to one Syed Yunus on 2-2-1960 by the then Government of East Pakistan. It is also admitted that said Md Yunus subsequently sold the case property to Md Abdul, Quayum through registered deed dated 3-2-1969 and while he was in possession in the case property he again sold the same to one Habiba Banu, wife of Md Ash through registered. deed dated 30-4-1970. The case of the petitioners is, that said Habiba Banu sold the case property to these petitioners vide four registered sale deeds dated 9-12-1972 and handed over physical possession to them and that said Habiba Banu also, handed over all original documents in respect of the case property to the petitioners and thereafter, she shifted her family members to 22 Bangshal Road under PS Kotwali, Dhaka, and that Habiba Banu never left this country during the liberation war and her whereabouts was not unknown. The petitioners have submitted all the original documents including the original lease deed and lease agreement granted by the then Government of East Pakistan in favour of the original allottee Syed Md Yunus. The original deed of subsequent purchasers Md Abdul Quayum and thereafter Abdul Quayum to Habiba Banu have also been annexed as Annexure-D and D1 respectively with this writ petition. Four title deeds of the petitioners have also been annexed as Annexure-E Series. The petitioners thereafter mutated their names in the office of the Dhaka City Corporation and took gas, electricity and WASA connection in their own names and copy of the same has been annexed as Annexure-F series.

7. The Court of Settlement rejected the case of petitioners holding, that the LTI of Habiba Banu, the vendor of the petitioners, appearing in the title deed of the petitioners, is not product of the same hand and that some of the LTI are highly indistinct, some contain most insufficient ink and that none of the attesting witnesses of the title deeds of the petitioners have been examined to prove the genuineness of those deeds. The respondents did not submit any written objection before the Court of Settlement and they have also failed to produce the concerned file regarding the abandoned house. The Court of Settlement lastly held that the petitioners have failed to prove that Habiba Banu ever sold the case property to them through their title deeds. Specific case of the petitioners is that they purchased the case property from Habiba Banu and while they were in ownership and possession of the case property they let out the said house to the Government for the residential accommodation of an Administrative Officer of the Ministry of Planning, Government of Bangladesh vide Arlnexure-G(1) an agreement dated 10-4-1974 and thereafter, the said house was allotted to Md M Arifur Rahman on 30- 5-1974. From the said annexures it appears that one Abdul Halim signed the said agreement on behalf of the landlord. These petitioners claim that this Abdul Halim is their father. In their title deeds the petitioners have mentioned their father's name as Abdul Halim. After the death of aforesaid Abdul Halim the mother of the petitioners Rahima Khatun received rents of the house in question from the Government on behalf of the petitioners. The respondents have not denied that the property was sold to Md Abdul Quayum by the original lessee Syed Md Yunus and that Abdul Quayum thereafter sold the case property to Habiba Banu.

<u>8. The respondents only stated that Habiba Banu never sold the case property to the petitioners in the year 1972 remaining herself in possession of the case property. The respondent No. 2 hired the case property for residential accommodation of their officers vide Annexure-G1 and paid rent to the petitioners. We get support of the said fact from the documents filed by the respondent No. 2 as Annexure-1 series along with the supplementary affidavit dated 1-2-2007. Annexure-1 is a letter dated 7-12-2006 sent by the Assistant Director of the Government Accommodation Directorate, to the learned Deputy Attorney-General stating that the case property was hired by their Directorate at a rent of Taka 1350 from 1-7-1983 and was allotted and that the case file of the property is not traceable from their office. Annexure-1A is a rent receipt which shows that the rent of the house in question was paid to (Halima Khatun) mother of the petitioners) on 1-7-1983. Annexure-I(b) is an attested photo copy of the rent receiving register which shows that the respondent paid rent against the case property for several months to Rahima Khatun. On being directed by the Court the learned Deputy Attorney-General has produced the rent receipt register of the Accommodation Directorate in original. From pages 4376 and 4377 it appears that Rahima Khatunis the owner of the house situated at 1/15 Razia Sultana Road, Mohammadpur, Dhaka which is the case property and the Government paid rent to Rahima Khatun for several months in the year 1983 and 84. The learned Advocate for the petitioners orally submitted that the Government after 1984 did not extend rent agreement and handed over the vacant possession to the petitioners and since then they are in possession of the case property. The respondents though claimed that the Government took possession of the case property in the year 1972 but they are quite silent as to how the petitioners thereafter went into possession of the case property. The petitioners have submitted all the original documents including their title deeds. The Court of Settlement without going through the contents of those documents held, that the LTI alleged to have been put by Habiba Banu in the title deeds of the petitioners do not tally with each other and the same are not the product of same hand. We have examined the title deeds of the petitioners Annexure-E series. From the LTI of those deeds it cannot be said that those are not the products of same hand. We did not find any reason to disbelieve the execution and registration of those title deeds by Habiba Banu in favour of the petitioners. The Court of Settlement was not justified in discarding those title deeds without obtaining any expert opinion from a fingerprint expert to ascertain the genuineness of LTI of Habiba Banu. In the case of Tarak Chandra Majhi vs Atahar Ali Howlader and others reported in 8 BLC (AD) 67 their Lordships held that-</u>

<u>"to avoid the risk of falling into error as to genuineness of writing, signature, etc., upon resorting to unsatisfactory and dangerous mode or process of examining the contentious signature, writing, etc. by the Court through comparison, the best course, in our opinion, is to avoid said unsatisfactory and dangerous procedure and the desired course should be to go for microscopic enlargement and expert advice, since the science of examination of signature, writing, etc. for determination of similarity through microscopic enlargement has advanced enough and has reached to the stage of accuracy and certainty as well, as expertise skill is also available."</u>

<u>The petitioners had filed all the original documents before the Court of Settlement and the court did not make any doubt about the genuineness of the original documents but rejected the case only on the ground that the LTI of Habiba Banu put in the title deeds of the petitioners do not tally with each other. This finding of the Court of Settlement is not lawful. Since the original documents have been produced by the petitioners, it was the duty of the Court of Settlement to come to a finding about the genuineness of those documents after obtaining the expert opinion on the LTI of Habib a Banu with her admitted signature. The Court of settlement dis- believed the title deeds of the petitioners on the ground that some of the LTI are highly indistinct and some contain excess ink. For this indistinct and excess ink in the LTI of vendor of the petitioners in the title deeds it cannot be said that those were not executed by the vendor or the same cannot be disbelieved.</u>

9. The petitioners were not served with a notice for surrendering the property before inclusion in the 'Kha' list of abandoned property and thereby it did not comply with the mandatory provision under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985.

10. The petitioners have annexed the death certificate of Mosammat Habiba Banu as Annexure- K, From the said annexure it appears that Habiba Banu, wife of Late Abdul Ash died on 31-1-1993 in Bangladesh and the said certificate was issued by the Dhaka City Corporation and as per death register said Habiba Banu died on 31-1-1993 in Bangladesh. From the above circumstances, we come to the conclusion that the Court of Settlement was not justified in rejecting the case and refusing to exclude the case property from 'Kha' list of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property and the said judgment is not lawful and the same has got no legal effect.

11. In the result, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The Judgment and order dated 28-5-2000 passed by the Court of Settlement, 1st Court, Dhaka, in Case No, 172 of 1995 is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and the same has got no legal effect.

The respondents are directed to exclude the house in question situated at 1/15, Block-D, Mohammadpur, Dhaka, from the "Kha" list of abandoned property published in Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary 'Kha' dated 23-9-1986 under Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, Ordinance 54 of 1985 at page No. 9764 (17), Serial No. 42 (Annexure-1).

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 9-11-1997 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 1320 of 1993).
full_judgment:
Md Fazlul Karim J: This appeal at the instance of the writ-respondent No.2. as the appellant is directed against the judgment arid order dated 9-11-1997 of the High Court Division passed in Writ Petition No. 1320 of 1993 making the Rule absolute declaring the inclusion of the respondent's property at Plot Nos. 537 and 538 of holding No. 14, Road No.8, Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned property published on 23rd September 1986 in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary at No. 9762(14) against serial No. 31 and the judgment and order dated 26-11-1992 in Case No.3 of 1992 by the First Court of Settlement refusing to exclude the house from the said 'Ka' list on the purported ground that the application before the First Court of Settlement was barred by limitation.

2. The writ-petitioner-respondents filed the writ petition stating, inter alia, that Dr Mahmood Hasan, former Vice-Chancellor of Dhaka University and Secretary, Ministry of Foreign Affairs of erstwhile Pakistan was allotted holding No. 14, Road No.8, Dhanmondi Residential Area, Dhaka on the basis of a lease deed executed on 24- 8-1956 and registered on 25-9-1956 by the Dhaka Improvement Trust (DIT). Dr Mahmood Hasan constructed a building on the said holding which is known as "Hasan House", now on plot Nos. 537 and 538. During the lifetime of Dr Mahmood Hasan the building was let out to the American Embassy and the lease deed expired on 1970. Thereafter a second lease deed was executed which also expired on 15th November, 1973. Meanwhile, Dr Mahmood Hasan distributed his properties to his wife, sons and daughters by Notarial deed being, Notarial Deed No. 911 which was accepted by his heirs. The aforesaid building was equally bequeathed to his daughters, namely, Mrs Rehana Kamal (petitioner No. 1 in writ petition) and Rifat Alam (mother of petitioner No. 2 in writ petition). Mrs Rifat Alam made an oral gift to her minor son. Syed Ayyad Alam (present respondent No.2) on 27-2-1971 in Dhaka and confirmed the same by a Notarial Declaration in Canada on 28-11-88. After making the deed to the heirs Dr Mahmood Hasan died on 25-12-1970 in Karachi, Pakistan. The American Embassy which was a tenant in the he use used to deposit rents in the joint SB Account of both the sisters in American Express International Banking Corporation, Dhaka, Meanwhile the Ministry of Works by its letter dated 23-10-1973 informed the tenant, American Embassy not to pay the rents to the absentee owners as there is a dispute with regard to the legal status of the house. In such situation Major (Retd) Mahmud Kamal, the husband of Mrs Rehana Kamal, respondent No. I, came to Bangladesh from Germany and met the Secretary, Ministry of Works on 7-5-1976 and submitted a written representation to decide about the legal status of the house which was pending before the Ministry of Works. The Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka advised them on 6-1-91 to contact with the Management Board of the Abandoned Property Cell. On 23-9-1986 the aforesaid building was published in the Gazette Extraordinary as an abandoned building at its 'Ka' list. Respondent No.2 (writ petitioner No.2) came to Bangladesh from Canada and learnt that the house was declared as an abandoned property. Thereafter, a case was filed in the Court of Settlement, Dhaka for exclusion of the house from the list but the case was dismissed on the ground of limitation. Thereafter, the respondents (petitioners in writ petition) filed the writ petition. By supplementary affidavit the writ petitioners filed certain documents including the passport, etc showing that the writ petitioners are Bangladeshi nationals and their whereabouts were very much known to the Government and they did not abandon their citizenship.

3. The appellant as respondent No. 2 Government of Bangladesh filed affidavit-in-opposition stating, inter alia, and admitting about the granting of lease to Dr Mahmood Hasan but asserted that none of the owners returned to Bangladesh after the Liberation War and ceased to occupy, manage and supervise the case property in person. They were the citizens of a state which was engaged in military operation with the People's Republic of Bangladesh and the property was legally taken over by the Government as abandoned property under President's Order No. 16 of 1972. It is further stated that the petitioner's petition before the 1st Court of Settlement was hopelessly barred by limitation and they filed the writ petition before the High Court Division by creating some false, fabricated, baseless, antedated papers and the petitioners are not the citizens of Bangladesh and they are not entitled to any relief sought for.

4. The writ-petitioners thereafter, filed affidavit-in-reply denying the assertions in the affidavit-in-opposition while reiterating the statements made in the writ petition.

5. Leave was granted in this appeal to consider the grounds, namely,:

(1) For that the petitioners, holding Pakistan passport staying in Karachi in 1971 and never returning to Bangladesh and there having been no verified pleading to the effect that they were stranded in Pakistan, the High Court Division relying on inadmissible piece of document and upon erroneous view of the provisions of

President's Order No. 149 of 1972 wrongly assumed that the writ petitioners are Bangladeshi citizens and on that basis wrongly held that the property in question is not an abandoned property.

(2) For that the petitioners being Pakistani citizens, the property in question is an abandoned property and the High Court Division was wrong in holding the said property to be not an abandoned property.

(3) For that the petitioners not being Bangladeshi citizens, the question of enforcement of their right to property does not arise and the writ petition was not maintainable for not availing the efficacious remedy within the period of limitation.

(4) For that the High Court Division was wrong in treating the writ petitioners to be the owners of the property in question without properly examining the evidence produced and considering the legal deficiencies.

6. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Additional Attorney-General, appearing for the appellant, has submitted that the writ-petitioners-respondents holding Pakistani passport staying in Karachi in 1971 and there being no material to show that they were stranded in Pakistan, the High Court Division erred in law on wrong assumption of the provision of President's Order No. 149 of 1972 that the respondents are Bangladeshi citizens and their property could not be an abandoned property inasmuch as the respondents not being citizens of Bangladesh the enforcement of their alleged fundamental right by way of writ petition was not maintainable once their application before the Court of Settlement has been dismissed as barred by limitation.

7. Mr TH Khan, the learned Counsel appearing for the respondents, has, however, submitted that admittedly Dr Mahmood Hasan, the original owner of the property in question, died in Karachi on 25-11-1970 leaving behind the writ petitioners and others as the heirs to whom he gifted the property on 23-10-1970 and that the American Embassy, tenant of Dr Hasan, accepted the respondents as landladies who as well mutated their names with the Dhaka Municipality, paid rent and taxes and were very much available and their whereabouts were not unknown and they were very much present in Bangladesh executing a power of attorney to possess the case property through tenant. The learned Counsel further submitted that the respondent No. 1 and her sister the mother of respondent No.2, were stranded in Pakistan and subsequently, had to escape to Germany and Canada respectively in 1973 and obtained the citizenship in those countries which are not at war with Bangladesh or in any way were not engaged themselves in any prejudicial activities against Bangladesh retaining their citizenship of Bangladesh by operation of law inasmuch as no attempt was ever made by the Government to form an opinion that the absence of the respondent owners outside Bangladesh was prejudicial to the war of liberation and that no attempt was made to take over-possession of the case building treating the same as, abandoned property. The learned Counsel has however submitted that the Gazette notification dated 23-9-1986 regarding the case building in "Ka" list without taking possession has rendered the listing to have been made without any lawful authority.

8. Admittedly it appears from Annexure-V that the respondents were born in Dhaka and that they were daughters of Dr Mahmood Hasan, a former Vice-Chancellor of Dhaka University and Foreign Secretary of Government of Pakistan. Dr Mahmood, the admitted owner, died in Pakistan on 25-11-1970 and prior to that on 23-10-1970 he gifted the property in favour of the respondent No. 1 and the mother of the respondent No.2. The tenant American Embassy had acknowledged the respondents as the landladies and paid rent and the agreement was renewed in 1973 and had .been paying rent regularly in their account with American Express Bank at Dhaka.

9. Article of the Bangladesh Citizenship Temporary Order 1972 (President's Order No. 149 of 1972) provides that-

"Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, on the commencement of this order, every person shall be deemed to be a citizen of Bangladesh-

(i) who or whose father or grandfather was born in the territories now comprised in Bangladesh and who was a permanent resident of such limitation on the 25th day of March, 1971 and continues to be so resident; or

(ii) who was a permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh on the 25th day of March, 1971 and continues to be so resident and is not otherwise disqualified for being a citizen by or under any law for the time being in force;

Provided that if any person is permanent resident of the territories now comprised in Bangladesh or its dependent is, in the course of his employment or for pursuit of his studies, residing in a country which was at war with, or engaged in military operation against Bangladesh and is being prevented from returning to Bangladesh, such person, or his dependents, shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh."

10. The respondents were admittedly born in territory now comprising in Bangladesh. The y were temporarily staying in Pakistan at a time when Pakistan was at war with Bangladesh and no communication between these two countries was available and in 1973 the said writ-petitioner and the mother of respondent No.2 had to escape from Pakistan and went to West Germany and Canada respectively but during their absence from Bangladesh they continued to occupy, supervise and manage the case property admittedly through their tenant who as well have been depositing rent in the writ-petitioner's Bank account.

<u>11. The words "to occupy, supervise and manage in person" came up for consideration in the case of Speed Bird Navigation vs Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 170 are given below:</u>

<u>"To occupy, supervise or manage in person as has been used in the definition clause cannot be taken in the literal sense for the considerations already noticed. The words 'in person' in the said clause may not necessarily imply physical presence of the owner in all cases: that may as well be understood in the sense that occupation, supervision or management, as has been referred to therein, is to be done with the concurrence and under the authority of the owner concerned. Any other construction will lead to some astounding consequences. An owner of a house property may find that he has been completely divested of his property on the ground that he ceased to occupy in person the said property during his temporary absence from the place although the entire members of his family had been residing at the. said house all the time. It can never be the legislative intent that a person who was required to go outside his country on account of some lawful purpose or had been held up in some foreign land and prevented from returning to his homeland by the circumstances over which he had no control, should be deprived of his property simply because he was not physically present to occupy, supervise or manage the said property, although it was being administered and managed according to his own arrangement and will. The words 'in person' in the definition clause should therefore be liberally construed. "</u>

<u>Thus the writ-petitioners occupying and managing the case building through a tenant and realising rent could not be said that they have not been occupying, supervising and/or managing the case property.</u>

12. Similarly, in the case of Bangladesh vs Abdul Hoque reported in 1982 BLD (AD) 143 it has been held that:

"The respondent was born in the territory now comprised in Bangladesh but his temporary absence is covered by the proviso quoted above and the law says "he shall be deemed to continue to be resident in Bangladesh," notwithstanding his temporary residence in a country which was at war or engaged in military operations against Bangladesh. "

<u>13. The definition of the word 'abandoned property' necessarily implies a meaning that if the residence of the owner of a property staying outside Bangladesh is, in the opinion of the Government, for a purpose prejudicial to the interest of the State but in the absence of any formation of any opinion as to any prejudicial activities indulged by such a person, he shall be deemed to continue to be resident of Bangladesh notwithstanding his temporary residence in the country which was at war or engaged in military operation against Bangladesh.</u>

14. In the case of Bangladesh vs ATJ Industries reported in 28 DLR (AD) 120 it has been held, inter alia, that:

"The definition clause with inclusion and exclusion clauses have been so framed that we do not find any other reasonable construction to bestow on entire clause of Article 2(1) than we have given. On the formation of opinion of the Government the definition clause comes into operation, but once opinion has been formed the law takes effect from 28-2-72, the day President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was promulgated. The Government is to form its opinion on the events as they stood on 28-2-72."

<u>15. The Government of Bangladesh during the absence of the writ petitioners could not form any opinion that the residence of the owners of the case property in Pakistan was for the purpose of prejudicial activities to the interest of the State in order to render the property to come within the mischief of the definition of abandoned property.</u>

<u>16. Moreover, the property was being managed, controlled and supervised by the power of attorney holders and duly occupied by the American Embassy as the tenant and though they were outside Bangladesh but their whereabouts were not unknown and they did not cease to occupy, supervise or manage the property before declaring the property as abandoned property and admittedly even in December, 1995, the Government could not form any opinion as to the status of the property.</u>

17. The tenant's possession of the case building being the possession of the landlord the Government also could not and did not take possession of the house on the plea of absence of the owners from the tenant and thus the property does not fall within the meaning of an abandoned property. Reference in this regard may be had to the case of Farida Aziz vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 45 DLR 12 wherein it has been held that:

"The Government in such a position is not empowered to take possession of the house on plea of absence of the owner and the property does not fall within the meaning of abandoned property."

18. Admittedly, the Government could not form any opinion as to the status of the property and thus, though the owner stayed abroad the Government has not formed any adverse opinion so as to deem the case property as an abandoned property. In the case of Speed Navigation vs Bangladesh reported in 27 DLR 170 wherein it has been held that:

"The words 'in person' in the said clause may not necessarily imply physical presence of the owner in all cases: that may as well be understood in the sense that occupation, supervision or management, as has been referred to therein, is to be done with the concurrence and under the authority of the owner concerned."

19. The object of forming an opinion as to the purpose of staying outside by the owner is to form an adverse opinion for declaring the property to be an abandoned property. Admittedly, in this case no notice under section 7(3) of the President's Order No. 16 of 1972 was issued till December 1975 so as to vest the property in the Government under section 4 thereof treating the property to be an abandoned property under section 2(1) of the Order.

20. Similarly, no notice, which is a mandatory requirement under section 5(b) of the Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, was served on the person in possession of the abandoned building requiring him to surrender possession so as to make the listing of the property as an abandoned in schedule 'Ka' and publication in the Gazette in respect of which the notice has not been issued making the listing illegal. Similarly, although the property has been listed in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned buildings, admittedly no possession of the building has been taken treating the same as abandoned property. Admittedly, American Embassy as the tenant of the owner had been in possession, but no attempt was taken by the Government to recover possession of the case building so as to entitle the authority to list the same in 'Ka' list rendering the said listing per se illegal.

21. In the case of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary. Ministry of Works and others vs Helaluddin Ahmed reported in 4 MLR (AD) 140 it has been held that:

"The High Court Division upon examining the provisions of section 5 of the Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985 (Ordinance No. 54 of 1985) observed that In the instant case no notice for surrendering or taking over possession of the disputed building could be produced by the Government. In view of section 5 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 providing for listing in the official gazette of those buildings for which notice has been issued or served or possession pursuant to such notice has been taken as abandoned property condition precedent for listing in the impugned gazette as in the instant case the issuance of notice for surrendering or taking possession of the abandoned building, failure of which has rendered the listing in the Official gazette of the petitioner's building illegal. This view finds support in the case of Iqbal Ahmed Qurishi vs Bangladesh reported in 45 DLR 416 in which one of us was a party."

22. In the case of Bangladesh vs Professor Golam Azam reported in 46 DLR (AD) 192 it has been held that:

"Thus, even though a person leaves the country of his origin with intention of never returning to it, his domicile of origin in that country is never lost, until he actually settled in another country with the intention of making that country his permanent home. In other words, the domicile of origin is not lost by mere temporary abandonment. Domicile of origin acquired subsists until it is replaced by a fresh domicile of choice."

23. The law of abandoned property contains in its definition the clause on exclusion and inclusion. Thus, for bringing the property within the periphery of abandoned property it must be shown that it has come strictly within the mischief of the law clearly, for it betrays the fundamental right of a citizen to hold the property.

24. In the case of Bangladesh vs MS Ispahani reported in 40 DLR (AD) 116 it has been held:

"The law of abandoned property is a stringent law no doubt, but as has been noticed in 28 DLR and 30 DLR (AD) the definition contains the clause on exclusion and inclusion. One thing is very well settled that no person shall be deprived of his life and property unless it comes within the clear provision of law itself. He cannot be deprived of his property by fallacious approach nor by provisions of enactment which merely by sidewind points a finger to such property. To be taken away of any property it must be shown that his property has come within the mischief of law clearly. There is no doubt that when the Act itself provides a dictionary for the words used, we must look into the dictionary first for an interpretation of the words used in the statute. The Court is not concerned with any presumed intention of the legislature-its task is to get at the intention as expressed in the statute. Therefrom we examined the language of the definition to see if the ordinary accepted notion of abandoned property fits in with the language used. Why this law and when was it promulgated become a relevant point. As Lord Atkinson pointed out in his speech in 1928 AC (at page 164).

"An Act of parliament does not alter the law by merely betraying an erroneous opinion of it."

25.	In American jurisdiction it has been said:

"We are not limited to the lifeless words of the statute and formalistic canons of construction in our search of the intent of the Congress and in construing a statute, we may with propriety record to the history of times when it was passed." (1942) 315 US 262 (L). "

<u>26.	From all these discussions above, It is clear that the respondents though filed nationality certificate and the power of attorney to show that they are citizens of Bangladesh which had not been controverted by any tangible material on record, the birth right of anyone to be a citizen of any particular country could not be brushed aside in the absence of any positive contrary intention manifested so as to deprive him of the right to be a citizen of a country where he was born.</u>

27. In that view of the matter, we do not find any merit in the submissions of the learned Counsel for the appellant.

The appeal is, accordingly, dismissed without any order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the Judgment and Order dated May 26, 1997 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 343 of 1995).
full_judgment:
Md Ruhul Amin J: This is pre-emptors appeal by leave against the judgment dated May 26, 1997 of a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 343 of 1995 discharging the Rule obtained against the judgment and order dated October 22, 1994 of the 2nd Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Narsingdi in Miscellaneous Appeal (preemption) No. 16 of 1994 allowing the same upon setting aside the judgment and order dated May 14, 1994 of the Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Narsingdi in Miscellaneous Case (preemption) No.3 of 1992 allowing the same.

2. The Miscellaneous case was filed under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 seeking preemption of 57 decimals of land as cosharer of the holding by purchase and contiguous land owner of the land sought to be preempted.

3. The case of the pre-emptor, inter alia, was that the case land belonged to Durga Charan Saha and on his death the same devolved upon his son Jogendra Chandra Saha who transferred the case land to Ramizuddin and on his death opposite party (in the Miscellaneous case) Nos. 3-10 inherited the property, that Moti Mia and his brother Lokman purchased .26 acre of land of plot No. 2125 of Khatian No. 1151 from Jogendra Chandra Saha and he also transferred 13 acre of land of the aforesaid plot to the pre-emptor on September 12, 1985 and thus he became cosharer of the holding in question i.e. holding No. 1151, that opposite party Nos. 3-10 without serving any notice on the pre-emptor transferred the property sought to be preempted to the opposite party (in the Miscellaneous case) Nos. 1 and 2 on November 21, 1991, that the pre-emptor is also the owner of the plot No. 2108 which is contiguous to the case plot No. 2109.

4. The Miscellaneous case was opposed by the opposite party Nos.1 and 2 i.e. pre-emptees stating, inter alia, that their father Subed Ali purchased .28 acre of land of plot No. 2344 by the kabala dated October 11, 1969; that on the death of their father in 1985 they have become co-sharers of the holding land of which sought to be preempted by the pre-emptor claiming to be a co-sharer, that they purchased the land sought to be pre-empted at a time when they are already co-sharers of the holding on the death of their father who purchased the land of the holding in question in 1969, that the pre-emptors purchased the land sought to be preempted with an agreement of reconveyance and in the light of the agreement of reconveyance they have transferred the land to the opposite party Nos. 310 on August 11, 1992, that the preemptees are co-sharers of the holding in question by inheritance, by purchase as well as they are contiguous land owners of the holding in question.

5. The trial Court allowed the prayer for preemption on the finding that the pre-emptees were neither co-sharers by purchase or by inheritance. As against the judgment of the trial Court the pre-emptees went on appeal. The appellate Court allowed the appeal on the finding that land purchased by the pre-emptees father on October 11, 1969 was of SA Khatian No. 1151, that the land of CS Khatian No. 986 has been listed in SA Khatian No. 1151, that the finding of the trial Court as to pre-emptees of not being co-sharers on the ground that there was no mention of the SA khatian in the kabala (Exhibit 'Uma') in the name of the plaintiffs' father is not correct since the land of CS khatian No. 986 has been listed in SA khatian No. 1151, that the pre-emptees as heirs of their father who purchased land of the holding in question on October 11, 1969 are the co- sharers of the holding in question by inheritance and, as such, pre-emptor is not entitled to the relief sought i.e. pre-emptor cannot seek preemption in respect of the transfer that took place on November 21, 1991 in favour of the pre-emptees.

6. The pre-emptor moved the High Court Division in revisional jurisdiction as against the judgment and order of the appellate Court and obtained Rule. The High Court Division on consideration of the materials on record held that the pre-emptees are the co-sharers of the holding by inheritance and they already being co sharers of the holding made the purchase in question in 1991 and the pre-emptees having had made the purchase at a time when they were already co-sharers by inheritance of the holding land of which sought to be preempted, the Miscellaneous case filed seeking preemption was not maintainable since a co-sharer by purchase as well as claiming to be a contiguous owner of the land sought to be preempted sought preemption against the co-sharers who long before the purchase sought to be preempted became co- sharers of the holding by inheritance.

7. It may be mentioned the pre-emptees pleaded that they purchased the land sought to be preempted with an agreement for reconveyance and in pursuant to the said agreement for reconveyance they have reconveyed the land on October 11, 1992 to the opposite party Nos. 3-10 (seller). In the background of the said pleading of the pre-emptees the High Court Division observed that on the reconveyance of the land sought to be preempted by the pre-emptees to the seller opposite party Nos. 3-10 "the cause of action for preemption has been extinguished". It appears the High Court Division has made the aforesaid observation in the light of the decision in the case of Md Abbas Ali vs Md Osman Ali (minor) and others reported in 37 DLR 324. In the light of the aforesaid decision the High Court Division further observed "on this ground as well as the Rule is liable to be discharged". On the aforesaid observations and findings the High Court Division discharged the Rule.

8. It may be observed that trial Court as well as appellate Court did not address to the question of contiguity claimed by the pre-emptor as the said Courts proceeded on the question of co-sharership of the pre-emptor and the pre-emptees. The High Court Division on consideration of the materials on record having had found that the pre-emptees are the co- sharers of the holding land of which sought to be preempted concurred with the finding of the appellate Court that the pre-emptees are co-sharers of the holding land of which sought to be preempted.

9. Leave was granted to consider the contentions that the High Court Division was wrong in holding that after reconveyance there remained nothing to be preempted as title of the land sought to be preempted vested with the original owner and the cause of action for which the case for preemption was filed no longer existed, that as the deed of reconveyance was made during the pendency of the Miscellaneous case for preemption and, as such, the reconveyance so made cannot defeat the right of pre-emptor to preempt the case land, that the proposition of law as laid down in the case of Md Abbas Ali vs Md Osman Ali (minor) and others reported in 37 DLR 324 relied upon by the High Court Division in rejecting the prayer for preemption in case is not reviewed then by the transaction of the said kind the whole purpose of filing of a preemption case will be defeated.

10. It is pertinent to mention that the appellant has not taken any leave as regard the question of pre-emptees being co-sharers by inheritance prior to the sale sought to be preempted as held by the High Court Division as well as by the appellate Court. In the background of the said state of the matter the learned Advocate-on-Record for the appellant felt difficulty to proceed with the appeal. It may be mentioned the finding as to pre-emptees being the co-sharers by inheritance is a finding of fact by the appellate Court and the same has been affirmed by the High Court Division on consideration of the materials on record. Since no exception has been taken in the present appeal as to pre-emptees being the co-sharers of the holding by inheritance prior to sale sought to be preempted the appeal is not a well conceived one and also not legally competent. The contention upon making which the leave was obtained is of no avail in any respect in the background of the finding that the pre-emptees are co sharers by inheritance prior to their purchase of the holding land of which sought to be preempted.

<u>11. The state of right of preemption in the background of reconveyance of the land intended to be preempted prior to the filing of the case seeking preemption and reconveyance of the land during pendency of the case filed seeking preemption came up for consideration before this Division as well as before the High Court Division on several occasions. The decision that has been made in the reported cases as regard the state of right of preemption in respect of the land intended to be preempted but reconveyed to the original owner (vendor) and thereupon right, title and interest have vested with him and that on such reconveyance the original owner is possessing the land is that with such reconveyance right of preemption no longer exists. There is also one line of decisions that a transfer followed by a deed of reconveyance would not defeat the right of preemption and that the pre-emptor would take the preemption with the encumbrance of reconveyance. The transaction i.e. reconveyance, pursuant to an agreement for reconveyance said to have been executed at the time of sale would be a clog on preemption provided the reconveyance is not a sham and colourable transaction or, in other words, is not a transaction of the kind sole object whereof is to defeat the right of preemption. The other view is that if the deed of re- conveyance is a genuine one and that on the basis thereof if the pre-emptee reconveyed the land to the original owner (vendor) and the right, title and interest vest in the vendor and the possession of the land sought to be preempted has also gone back to him in that case even though the reconveyance has been made during the pendency of the case seeking preemption the case so filed would become infructuous since with the reconveyance right of preemption ceased to exist. In case of reconveyance either before the filing of the case seeking preemption or at a time when the case seeking preemption is pending the Court would be required to examine whether the transaction is a genuine one or the same is a sham and colourable transaction. If by reconveyance right, title and interest does not vest with the original owner and that the possession of the land also does not go back to the original owner in that case the transaction i.e. reconveyance would be considered a sham and colourable transaction and the right of preemption will exist. The transaction i.e. reconveyance, whether is genuine or a sham and colourable one is to be determined in the background of the evidence brought on record by the parties: If the evidence is in the affirmative i.e. right, title and interest in the land sought to be pre-empted has gone back to the vendor and the land sought to be preempted is possessed by the vendor, in that case there would be no right of pre-emption whether the reconveyance is made before the filing of the case seeking preemption or during the pendency of the case. The contrary of the aforesaid state of the matter would not defeat the right of pre-emption.</u>

12. Since in the instant appeal finding of the Court of fact being that the pre-emptees are the co- sharers by inheritance of the holding land of which sought to be preempted and the same having been affirmed by the High Court Division on consideration of the materials on record we are of the view the contention making on which leave was obtained is of no merit. The matter of reconveyance was rightly not addressed by the trial Court as well as the appellate Court. The High Court Division was not required to address itself to the question of reconveyance since the said Division held that the pre-emptees are co-sharers by inheritance of the holding land of which sought to be preempted.

<u>13. Even if for argument's sake it is accepted that reconveyance having been made during pendency of the case seeking preemption the same could not be a clog for allowing preemption is accepted, then too pre-emptor was not entitled to preempt the land sought to be pre-empted since on consideration of the materials on record last Court of fact found that the pre-emptees were co-sharers by inheritance of the holding land of which sought to be preempted. The High Court Division, on independent consideration of the materials on record, concurred with the finding of the appellate Court that the pre-emptees are the co-sharers of the holding by inheritance long before purchase and the pre-emptor is cosharer by purchase. At the time of purchase sought to be preempted, the pre-emptees were co-sharers of the holding in question by inheritance. The learned Advocate-on-Record could not refer to any material to take exception to the finding of the High Court Division and the Court of appeal that the pre-emptees are co-sharers of the holding land of which sought to be preempted by inheritance at the material time i.e. at the time of sale sought to be preempted.</u>

14. In the background of the discussions made hereinabove we find no merit in the appeal.

15. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed.

There is no order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 3rd March, 1997 passed by the High Court Division  in Civil Revision No. 323 of 1994)
full_judgment:
Syed JR Mudassir Husain J : This appeal has arisen out of leave granting order dated 7th June, 1998 passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1200 of 1997 against the judgment and order dated 3rd March, 1997 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 323 of 1994 making the Rule absolute against the judgment and decree passed on 21st September, 1993 by the learned Additional District Judge, Dinajpur in Other Appeal No. 91 of 1981 dismissing the same and affirming those of dated 27th August, 1989 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Dinajpur in the Other Suit No. 206 of 1997 decreeing the same.

2. The appellant as plaintiff instituted the aforesaid suit for declaration of her title in the suit land and also for further declaration that the order passed by defendant No.2, the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Dinajpur on 12-10-1976 in VP Case No. 15(JA)FU/76-77 treating the suit property as vested property is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff.

3. Plaintiffs case, inter alia, is that her father Upendra Nath Paul and her uncle Nripendra Nath Pual being Bangladeshi citizens were the recorded owners of the suit property under both in RS and SA Khatian. Her father by registered deed gift dated 25-3-1975 made a gift of 'Ka' schedule property in her favour and handed over possession thereof; that her uncle Nripendra Nath Paul used to maintain her from her childhood out of love and affection and, as such, he (Nripendra Nath Paul) also by another  registered deed of gift dated 26-6-1975 transferred 'Kha' schedule property in her favour and also handed over the possession thereof. Having received the said property, the plaintiff has been possessing the same. But the defendant No.2 being influenced by some local people started the aforesaid Vested Property Case on the basis of a collusive report from defendant No. 3 the local Circle Officer (Rev) and illegally passed an order on 12-10-1976 in the aforesaid VP Case treating the said property as Vested Property. Hence the suit.

4. The defendant No.2 contested the suit by filing written statement denied the material allegations made in the plaint, contending, infer alia, that the suit was not maintainable in its present form; that the aforesaid recorded owners Upendra Nath Paul and Nripendra Nath Paul left for India permanently and, as such, the property in question has been rightly declared as an enemy property and subsequently, as vested and non resident property; that the deeds of gift are collusive and fabricated documents.

5. Defendant Nos. 6-8, the alleged lessees of the disputed land under the government (present respondent Nos. 1-3) also contested the suit by filing separate written statement supporting the case of defendant No. 2 as made out in their written statement.

6. The trial Court decreed the suit holding that Upendra Nath Paul and Nripendra Nath Paul, the father and uncle respectively of the plaintiff being Bangladeshi citizens had gifted the suit property in her favour by genuine registered deed of gift vide Exhibit 5 and Exhibit 6 respectively dated 24-3-1975 and, as such, the (plaintiff) acquired valid right, title, interest and possession in the suit property, and the defendant No.2 illegally treated the suit property as vested property.

7. Against the aforesaid decree, neither the government nor the vested property authority preferred any appeal challenging the said decree but only the alleged year-to-year lease holders, the defendant Nos. 6-8, preferred an appeal although they have no locus standi to challenge the aforesaid judgment and decree of the trial Court, that the learned Additional District Judge who heard the appeal dismissed the same on contest affirming the findings of the trial Court upon proper consideration of materials on record and relying upon the relevant decisions.

8. Against the aforesaid judgment of affirmance, the aforesaid defendant Nos. 6-8 lessees moved the High Court Division in revision and the Rule issued therein was made absolute upon setting aside the concurrent legal findings and decisions of both the lower Courts below. Hence the appeal.

<u>9. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiya, the learned Counsel for the appellant, placed the judgments of the Courts below as well as the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and thereafter he submitted that in view of concurrent findings of fact as to possession of the suit property by the plaintiff appellant prior to the giving of the so-called lease by the government in the above mentioned VP Case No. 15(JA) FU/76-77, was based on proper consideration of the material evidence on record with reference to the case of the contesting parties and, as such, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in law in setting aside the judgment and decrees of the Courts below based on concurrent findings off act and thereby exceeded the revisional jurisdiction under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure which resulted in an error in the decision causing failure of justice and, in such view of the matter, the findings and decisions as arrived at by the High Court Division cannot be sustained in law and the same are liaible to be set aside.</u>

10. Mr Bhuiyan has next submitted that the High Court Division erred in law in holding that the registered deeds of gift in favour of the plaintiff appellant by Exhibit 5 and Exhibit 6 respectively dated 24-3-1975 and 26-6-1975 are not valid for the reasons that the joint property had not been partitioned by metes and bounds amongst the co-sharers and thereby laid down an erroneous principle that unpartitioned property cannot be gifted by registered instrument.

<u>11. The learned Counsel has further argued that the suit property cannot be declared as enemy property in the year 1976 in view of the provisions of Ordinance No.1 of 1969 and lack of evidence on the side of the Government as to possession of the suit land by government as enemy property prior to 'Ekhsona' lease allegedly granted to the defendant respondent Nos. 1-3 (defendant Nos. 6-8) in the aforesaid VP Case by order passed on 12-10-1976 by defendant No.2, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division erred in reversing the decree of affirmance of the Courts below holding that the said land is enemy property. In support of his above contention Mr Bhuiyan has cited a decision in the case of Laxmi Kanta Roy vs Upazila Nirbahi Officer and another reported in 46 DLR 136.</u>

12. Mr Bhuiya has lastly, submitted that Hindu Law as administered by the Courts in Bangladesh is applied to Hindus in East Bengal and the Bangladeshi Hindus are governed by the Dayabhag School of Hindu Law, while non Bengalee Hindus in Bangladesh or in other parts of India are governed by the Mitakshara School of Hindu Law. According to Mitakshara, son acquires at his birth an equal interest with his father in all ancestral property held by the father and on the death of the father the son takes the property, not as his heir, but by survivorship and, according to Dayabhag, the son does not acquire any interest by birth in ancestral property, their rights arise for the first time on the father's death and at the same time a father, according to Dayabhag Law, can dispose of ancestral property whether movable or immovable by sale, gift, will or otherwise in the same way as he can dispose of his separate property. As regards the transfer of the suit property by will by Dayabhag. Mr Bhuiyan has cited a decision in the case of Debendra Coomar Roy Chowdhury and another vs Brojendra Coomar Roy Chowdhury and another reported in the India Law Reports, Volume 17, Calcutta 886, wherein it was held that under the Hindu Law in Bengal a person has the right to dispose of his property by will.

13. Drawing an analogy from the above cited case, Mr Bhuiyan argued that the transfer of the suit property by registered deed of gift vide Exhibits 5 and 6 of 1975 as stated above are legal and valid, we find substance in this argument of Mr Bhuiyan.

14. We have perused the judgments of the Courts below as well as the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. It appears that, both the Courts below having considered the oral and documentary evidence, concurrently held that the transfer by registered deeds of 1975 vide Exhibits 5 and 6 as made by father and uncle living in a joint undivided Hindu family under the Dayabhag School of Law, is valid. Since the father and uncle being in Bangladesh in the year 1975, transferred the suit property, by the aforesaid registered deeds of gift, cannot be declared an enemy property in view of the aforesaid decision as referred to above in 46 DLR 136 and we accepted the argument of Mr Bhuiyan that since the law of enemy property itself died with the repeal of Ordinance No.1 of 1969 on 23-3-1974 no further Vested Property case can be started thereafter on the basis of the law which is already dead.

15. Admittedly, plaintiffs father and uncle were in joint mess and there was no partition amongst themselves as co-sharers. According to Dayabhag Law, father can dispose of ancestral property and plaintiffs uncle being in joint family can also dispose of his ancestral property by sale, gift and will or otherwise.

16. Having regard to above, the finding of the High court  Division to the effect that the gift in favour of the plaintiff-petitioner by Exhibits 5 and 6 are not valid for the reason that joint property had not been partitioned by metes and bounds amongst the co-sharers, cannot be sustained in law.

17. It further appears that neither the Government or the Vested Property Authority challenged the decree of the trial Court and it is the defendant Nos. 6-8, being lessees of the Vested Property for one year, cannot have any locus standi to challenge the decree or prefer an appeal against such decree. It is for the Vested Property Authority to challenge the decree. We therefore, hold that the defendant Nos. 6-8 being year-to-year lease holders had no locus standi to prefer any appeal before the appellate Court as well as in the High Court Division and, as such, the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division having failed to consider this aspect of the case, committed an error of law which resulted in an error in the decision causing failure of justice.

For the above reasons, we hold that the High Court Division exceeded in its revisional jurisdiction in setting aside the findings of the lower Courts below concluded by concurrent findings of fact. In view of the facts and circumstances, we find merit in this appeal and accordingly, we set aside the findings and decisions of the High Court Division and consequently the appeal is allowed without any order as to cost.

End.
