full_judgment:
Nozrul Islam Chowdhury J: This, Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause why the judgment and order dated 20-2-1994 passed by 1st Court of Settlement, Dhaka in Case No. 51 of 1992 relating to House No.3/4 Segun-bagica, Dhaka dismissing the petition for releasing the petitioners property (by majority judgment) should not be declared to have been" passed without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect.

2. Heard the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners and Mr Sukumar Biswas the learned Assistant Attorney-General. appearing on behalf of the respondents, perused the petition and the materials placed before us including the impugned judgment wherefrom it transpires that the 1st Court of Settlement was constituted by two other members of them The Chairman delivered the impugned judgment with whom one of the Members i.e. Mr Md Amanullah a member agreed with the Chairman in rejecting the case brought under section 7 of the Ordinance being Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 brought by the petitioner and thereby upheld the inclusion of the property in the Ka list of the abandoned buildings by the respondents, while by the dissenting judgment one of the Member of the Court Mr Muhammad Habibur Raman Bhuiyan allowed the case brought by the petitioner directing exclusion of the case property from the 'Ka' list of the abandoned building with a further direction to restore possession of the case property to the applicant.

3. We have gone through the entire judgment in minute details where from it is revealed that the majority views disclosed in the impugned judgment is based on a report available with the records maintained by the government where from the learned Chairman and one of its member held the view that the case property formerly belonged to Khan Bahadur Nazir Uddin Ahmed and on his death his sons and daughters inherited the case property including other building and house left by him. It was also detected in the majority judgment that Mr Kamal Uddin got the case property in his exclusive share upon an. amicable partition amongst his co sharers and Kamal Uddin joined Pakistan Foreign Service and after liberation of Bangladesh he opted for Pakistan and died in Etiophya where he was serving as Ambassador of Pakistan, on the death of Kamaluddin his wife and children also opted for Pakistan, therefore, the government respondents declared the property as abandoned bringing it in the Ka list of the abandoned buildings. The other view in the dissenting judgment we find that the learned Member arrived at a finding that the case property was requisitioned by the government on 11-7-73 and it was de-requisitioned on 21-4-80 and the case property was in the possession of the respondents at the time of its inclusion or enlistment. The order of requisition shows that the respondents acknowledged Mrs Shamsunnessa wife of Iate KB Naziruddin Ahmed as the owner of the case property who neither left the country nor relinquished the citizenship of Bangladesh nor abandoned the property, therefore, the learned Member of the Settlement Court was also of the opinion that the respondents cannot disown its owner Mrs Shamsunnessa and on de-requisition of the property on 21-04-80 it instantly devolved on the original owner from whom the property was requisitioned and never on the government respondents. The learned Member of the Settlement Court in his dissenting judgment has also elaborately mentioned the reasons upon which he had dissented with the majority view passed by the Court of Settlement without going in details about the same. We have also noticed that the government at the time of declaring the property as abandoned included the same in the Ka list as also based its decision on an amicable partition amongst the sharers treating the case property in the exclusive share of Mr Kamaluddin. It may be mentioned in this connection that an amicable partition is a partition as long as it is admitted by the co-sharer but the moment when the co-sharers do not admit the amicable partition such partition cannot have any legal effect. In the instant case we find that the petitioners before us are the admitted co-sharers of Mr Kamal Uddin in the property left behind by Mr KB Naziruddin Ahmed and the petitioners are claiming before us that the property left. behind by KB Naziruddin Ahmed are not partitioned amongst its co-sharers. In such view of the matter, we are of the opinion, that the property of Mr Kamal Uddin one of the sons of KB Naziruddin Ahmed must be ascertained first by the government respondent by away of partition and after a legal partition the property belonged to Kamal Uddin can be treated as abandoned, if the law permits, but before ascertainment of the· exclusive share of Kamal Uddin the declaration of the case property as abandoned as has been done by the government respondents is not accept- able. Therefore, we affirm the opinion disclosed in the judgment by the dissenting judgment delivered by the learned Member Mr Muhammad Habibur Rahman Bhuiyan in Case No. 51 of 1992 ( Ka-82- Segunbagicha, Dhaka) so far as it relates to House No.3/4 Segunbagicha, Dhaka. It may also be noted that after the death of Naziruddin Ahmed ownership devolved upon the heirs of Naziruddin Ahmed and Kamauddin Ahmed is one of those heirs left behind by KB Naziruddin Ahmed. The minority view shall prevail over the majority view delivered by the learned Chairman along with another Member in the said case.

4. In the result the rule is made absolute with an observation to the effect that the government, if willing to declare and bring the property of Kamaluddin within the mischief of Ordinance 54 of 1985 as an abandoned property in that case the government is at liberty to bring a partition suit within 6 months from date for the purpose of ascertainment of exclusive share of Kamauddin in House No. 3/4 Segunbagicha, Dhaka and then they are at liberty to proceed in accordance with law, in the meantime both the parties are directed to maintain status quo in respect of possession and position of the property, in the event of failure of the Respondents to bring a partition suit within six months, the minority Judgment shall take immediate effect.

End.

full_judgment:
Syed Mahmud Hossain J: This appeal by the pre-emptors as the appellants following leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 2-7- 2003 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2387 of 1995 making the Rule absolute reversing those dated 22-10-1994 passed in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 233 of 1992 of the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat, Third Court, Chittagong allowing pre-emption case reversing those dated 30-7-1992 in pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1992 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Third Court, Sadar, Chittagong dismissing the pre-emption case under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act or in the alternative under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

2. The facts, leading to this appeal, are precised below:-

The appellants as the pre-emptors filed Miscellaneous Case No. 1 of 1992 in the Third Court of Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Chittagong stating, inter alia, that the case land appertaining to RS Plot No. 3797 under RS Khatian No. 3836 belonged to Md. Ismail, grandfather of the appellants, measuring .07 acre of land out of .17 acre. The remaining .10 acre was record in the names of Atarjan and Salima Khatun in equal shares in RS Khatian No. 3838. RS Plot No. 3797 has been recorded in the aforesaid two khatians but the same belonged to one holding. After that, Ismail, the owner of RS Khatian No. 3836, died leaving behind one son and five daughters,- namely, Sajaba, Masma Khatun, Zohura Khatun, Bibi Jan and Masuda Khatun. Bibi Jan died leaving behind two daughters, namely, Jahanara Begum and Ayesha Khatun and sisters, namely, Sajaba, Masma, Zahura and Masuda Khatun. Later, Masuda Khatun died leaving behind husband, Amir Ahmed and other sisters. On 15-11-1977, the appellants and Rahmatullah purchased the shares of other co-sharers of RS Khatian No. 3836 in RS Plot No. 3797. After that, the cousin of the pre-emptors, namely, Ayesha Khatun also transferred her share to the pre-emptors and thus they were co-sharers by inheritance and purchase in the case holding and khatian, Abdun Nabi, grandson of Atarjan, inherited the entire share of Atarjan Abdun Nabi obtained 1ganda of land from RS Khatian No. 3838 but wrongly stated RS Khatian No. 3836 in the registered deed of sale dated 16-9- 1991 showing an inflated amount of Taka 20,000. Pre-emptee Nos. 1 and 2 are strangers to the case land. After that, the pre-emptors collected the certified copy of the deed of sale dated 16-9-1991 and became aware of the trans- action and filed the miscellaneous case for pre- emption.

3. The pre-emptees contested the case by filing written objection denying all the material statements made in the application for pre-emption. Their case, in short, is that the case pond of RS Plot No. 3797 comprising 0.17 acre out of which .07 acre was recorded in RS Khatian No. 3836 and the remaining .10 acre in RS Khatian No. 3838 but both the jama and holding are separate. The pre-emptors are co-sharers in RS Khatian No. 3836 but not in RS Khatian No. 3838. Abdun Nabi purchased .09 acre of land of RS Plot No. 3797 under RS Khatian No. 3838 on 7-7-1933 from Solima Bibi, Amena Bibi, Asma Khatun. In the deed of sale, Abdun Nabi was shown to have purchased .07 acre of land of RS Plot No. 3797 under RS Khatian No. 3838. Abdun Nabi by inheritance and purchase got title in .10 acre of land which later devolved upon his heir Mahfuza Khatun. After that, Mahfuza Khatun transferred .20 acre of land from RS Plot No. 3838 for consideration of Taka 20,000 to the pre-emptees by a deed of sale dated 16-9-1991. The pre-emptors were asked to purchase the case property and they offered only Taka 5,000 for which their offer was turned down. The pre-emptees developed the case land by spending huge amount of money. Hence, they prayed for dismissal of the pre-emption case.

4. The trial Court by his judgment and order dated 30-7-1992 dismissed the case. Against the judgment and order of the trial Court, the pre-emptors preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No. 233 of 1992 before the learned District Judge, Chittagong. On transfer, the appeal was heard by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat, Third Court, Chittagong, who by judgment and order dated 22-10-1994 allowed the appeal reversing the judgment and order passed by the trial Court. After that, the pre-emptees filed an application for review under Order XL Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure but the application for review was rejected on 27-3- 1995.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order dated 22-10-1994, pre, emptees filed a revisional application under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure before the High Court Division in Which Rule was issued in Civil Revision No. 2387 of 1995. The High Court Division by the judgment and order dated 2-7-2003 made the Rule absolute reversing the judgment and order of the appellate Court dated 22-10-1994.

6. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with judgment and order dated 2-7-2003 passed by the High Court Division, the pre-emptors moved this Division by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1631 of 2003 in which leave was granted on 5-1-2005 resulting in the initiation of Civil Appeal No. 108 of 2005.

7. Mr Omar Farook, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellants, submits that the High Court Division came to a finding that the pre-emptors are non co-sharers in RS Khatian No. 3838 and that on the contrary they are co-sharers in RS Khatian No. 3836 although the pre-emptors by filling an application for amendment before the appellate Court amended the application for pre- emption stating that they are also co-sharer tenants in RS Khatian No. 3838 and that the High Court Division without taking into consideration that fact delivered the judgment and, as such, the impugned judgment should be set-aside. He further submits that in case of a pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act if a tenant is co-sharer in the plot he is also treated as a co-sharer in that plot even if the said plot is recorded in more than one khatian.

8. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocate, impugned judgment and the papers incorporated in the paper-book.

9. Initially, the pre-emptors filed the pre-emption case stating that they are co-sharers of RS Plot No. 3797 appertaining to RS Khatian No. 3836.

10. Admittedly, the pre-emptors own a portion of land in RS plot No. 3797. There is nothing on record to show that this plot was partitioned by meets and bounds between the parties and that mutation in accordance with such partition has been effected. Admittedly, the case land is situated with-in Chittagong City Corporation and, as such, section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is attracted, not section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

11. In the case in hand, it appears that in the appellate Court the pre-emptors filed an application under Order VI Rule 17 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for amendment of the application for pre-emption filed under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural and Tenancy Act stating that they are also co-sharer tenants in RS Khatian No. 3838. In support of their contention, they produced a registered deed of sale dated 27-11-1940 to show that their father Md. Younus purchased land from RS Khatian No. 3838 and, as such, they are also co-sharer tenants by inheritance in that khatian. The application for' amendment was allowed by the appellate Court by Order No. 12 dated 3-6-1993. The High Court Division came to a wrong finding that the: pre-emptors are not co-sharers in RS Khatian No. 3838 and, as such, reversed the findings of the appellate Court holding that the pre-emptors are not entitled to pre-empt the case land. By amendment of the application for pre-emption, the pre-emptees could prove that they have got interest in RS Khatian No. 3838.

<u>12. In a case of pre-emption filed under section 24, of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act if a co-sharer tenant owns a portion of land in any plot, he is to be. treated as co-sharer in the entire plot even if the land of that plot is recorded in more than one khatian. Therefore, in the event of transfer of a portion of land of that plot appertaining to another khatian a co-sharer tenant can file a pre-emption case under section .24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act notwithstanding the fact that he does not have any interest in that khatian. The words "one or more co- sharer tenants of such land" occurring in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act means a co- sharer in the plot not the holding as mentioned in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Such being the position of law, the pre-emptors were not even required to file an application for amendment to show that they have also interest in RS Khatian No. 3838.</u>

13. In the case of SM Basiruddin vs Z Islam, 35 DLR (AD) 230, it has been held that the expression 'non-agricultural land' used in section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act is not synonymous with the word 'holding' as used the "Bengal Tenancy Act or State Acquisition of Tenancy Act."

14. Without looking into that legal aspect, the High Court Division came to a finding that the pre-emptors could not prove that they have also interest in RS Khatian No. 3838.

15. The findings arrived at and the decision made by the High Court Division are based on wrong appreciation of laws and facts and, as such, the impugned judgment and order is liable to be set-aside.

Accordingly, the appeal is allowed and the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is set-aside and the impugned judgment and order passed by the appellate Court is restored. There is no order as to costs.

End.
